It was only natural that I saw everything as it was . A value . Some would think I was cold , distant . Perhaps . Observance , however , had proven to be a virtue . No human being is without flaw . <newline> I liked to think that . But when you 're thrown a nasty curcurveball , it 's up to you to hit it . Always . That one curveball , that person I could never understand . Perhaps my thoughts were captious on this day , but the man I met was average looking to me at best , I swear . I payed him no mind , though intrigued . I sulked over my ice cream , watching it 's appeal stat drop like a rock . Looking up , I went cold . Perfect stats ? Impossible . Impossible . My viscid day had transpired into a paradox . Perfection ? Perfection is relative , it ca n't exist , not even through a machine . No , it could n't be . There it was . 100 . 100 . 100 . 100 . The numbers swam in my head , mocking me . I snapped back to the scene unfolding before me , realizing I had annihilated my Ill-fated ice cream cone to smithereens , cold liquid dripping nonchalantly onto the dolorous colors on the pavement . A drop of strawberry ice cream , how tragic it looked , against the dullness of the ground . Colder still , were the stares I felt blazing behind me . I twitched , unsure of how to continue , attempting to comprehend it . `` Excuse me , miss ? '' An amused voice strayed across the cracks in the pavement . `` Icecream lasts longer if you savor it , you know . ''

samples.MiMo-V2.5-Pro_story:
# The Perfect Man

I was five years old the first time I saw the numbers.

They hovered above my kindergarten teacher, Mrs. Huang, like a translucent video game HUD — glowing digits only I could read. Intelligence: 62. Charisma: 78. Patience: 41. I didn't understand what they meant yet, but I remember thinking the patience number seemed too high.

By the time I was ten, I'd learned to read them fluently. Every person I looked at carried their own floating stat sheet, drifting just above their heads like a private weather system. Intelligence, Strength, Dexterity, Charisma, Wisdom, Empathy — six numbers, always. My mother had Empathy at 91, which explained why she cried at commercials. My father had Intelligence at 88 but Charisma at 23, which explained why he ate lunch alone at every family gathering.

I never told anyone. What would I say? *Hey Dad, your social skills are a 23 out of 100?* Besides, I'd tested it. When I described the numbers to a school counselor at age twelve, she recommended I see a therapist. The therapist's Empathy was 34. I stopped going after two sessions.

Over the years, I developed my own internal database. The average person scores between 40 and 60 in any given stat. Anything above 80 is exceptional. I'd met a concert pianist with Dexterity at 94. A philosophy professor with Wisdom at 89. A con artist in a Shanghai train station with Charisma at 97 — I watched him sell fake jade to three people in twenty minutes.

But I had never — not once in twenty-six years — seen anyone break 95 in more than one category.

Until the morning I met Xu Chen.

I was sitting in a coffee shop in Hangzhou, nursing a latte and pretending to work on my laptop, when the door opened and he walked in. I glanced up the way I always do — a reflex as natural as blinking — and the numbers above his head made me set my coffee down so hard it splashed onto the table.

Intelligence: 99. Strength: 97. Dexterity: 98. Charisma: 99. Wisdom: 96. Empathy: 99.

I stared. I rubbed my eyes. I stared again. The numbers didn't change. They glowed brighter than anyone's I'd ever seen, almost pulsing with warmth, as if the universe itself was showing off.

He was average-looking — maybe thirty, with a plain face, unremarkable clothes, and a slight slouch. Nothing about his appearance suggested what floated above him. He ordered a black coffee, sat down three tables away, and opened a worn paperback.

I couldn't focus. Every few seconds, my eyes drifted back to those impossible numbers. After twenty minutes, he looked up and caught me staring.

"You keep looking over here," he said. His voice was calm, almost amused. "Do I have something on my face?"

"Sorry," I managed. "I just — you remind me of someone."

He smiled. "Happens all the time."

We talked. His name was Xu Chen, a freelance translator who'd just moved to Hangzhou. He was warm without being pushy, funny without trying too hard, and listened in a way that made you feel like the only person in the room. Every quality his stats promised, delivered in real time.

Over the following weeks, we became friends. Coffee turned into dinners, dinners into long walks along West Lake. I kept waiting for the catch — the hidden flaw, the stat I'd misread. But it never came. He was exactly what the numbers said: extraordinary in every measurable way.

And it terrified me.

Because here's the thing about seeing everyone's stats — it strips away mystery. I'd spent my whole life reducing people to six numbers, using those numbers to decide who was worth my time. A coworker with low Empathy? Not worth befriending. A date with Intelligence below 70? No second meeting. I had built my entire social life around a spreadsheet only I could see.

But Xu Chen, with his perfect scores, taught me something I hadn't expected. One evening, sitting by the lake, I finally confessed my ability. I expected disbelief. Instead, he was quiet for a long time.

"So what's my Empathy?" he asked.

"Ninety-nine."

He nodded slowly. "Then let me tell you what I see in you. No numbers. Just what I feel." He turned to face me. "You're kind, but you're lonely. You've been watching people your whole life instead of connecting with them. And I think those numbers you see — they're not a gift. They're a wall."

I opened my mouth to argue, but nothing came out.

That night, I went home and stood in front of my bathroom mirror. For the first time in my life, I looked above my own head. There, glowing softly, were my own six numbers. Every single one of them was average.

And for the first time, I thought — maybe that was enough.
samples.DeepSeek-V4-Flash_story:
Ever since you were a child, you have been able to see people’s stats. It wasn’t a choice. They hung in the air above every head like museum labels: Intelligence, Dexterity, Charisma, Wisdom, Luck, and dozens of smaller ones. Your mother’s numbers: Intelligence 88, Charisma 71, Patience 23. Your father’s: Strength 62, Intelligence 44, Kindness 90. You loved them anyway, but the numbers made love complicated. You knew where they were faulty.

By adulthood, you had become an expert. You could predict a person’s behavior in seconds. You used the gift as a shield, never getting too close to anyone whose stats revealed a fatal flaw. Everyone had one.

Except the man on the 5:14 train.

He stepped through the doors, and the air around him seemed to fold. Above his head, written in the same familiar green font, were stats you had never seen in nature: Strength 100, Dexterity 100, Constitution 100, Intelligence 100, Wisdom 100, Charisma 100, Luck 100. No gaps. No negatives. Perfect.

You sat up. Your heart hammered. The train lurched, and he didn’t stumble. Of course he didn’t.

You followed him when he got off, one stop past your own. He didn’t look back. He helped a woman with a stroller up the stairs. Her stats were unremarkable; his didn’t waver. He bought a sandwich from a street vendor and gave it to a man sleeping in a doorway. The vendor’s eyebrows rose. The sleeping man’s stats flickered with confusion and gratitude. The perfect man walked on.

You followed him for three days. You were sure it was a trick. No one is all 100s. Everyone has hidden debuffs. But his numbers never changed. Not when a cyclist nearly struck him—his Dexterity evaded instantly. Not when an angry man shouted at him—his Charisma turned the confrontation into a conversation. The stats remained.

On the third day, he turned a corner, stopped, and waited. “You’re good,” he said. “But I’ve known you were following me since the first train. Your sneaking skill is a 6.”

You froze. “How do you know that?”

“Because I can see your stats,” he said.

You had never told anyone about your ability. “That’s impossible. Only I—”

“Only you can see theirs? No.” He smiled. “You can see the surface. I can see the whole sheet.”

He recited them: your Intelligence, 91. Dexterity, 73. Charisma, 82. Fear, 99. Loneliness, 100. “You’ve spent your whole life reading other people’s statistics,” he said. “But you’ve never once asked what your own numbers mean.”

“I can’t see my own,” you said.

“No,” he said. “You don’t want to. Because if you did, you would see the only real deficit you have is one you created yourself: Hope. Four.”

The word hit like a bullet. “That’s not fair.”

“Fair?” He laughed, and his stats remained perfect—but for the first time, the numbers above his head flickered. They didn’t drop. They didn’t rise. They flickered like a bad signal.

“What are you?” you asked.

He looked at you for a long time. “I’m what you’ll be in thirty years,” he said, “if you stop counting other people’s points and start earning your own.”

Then the train came. He boarded, and the doors closed. The last thing you saw was
samples.Muse-Spark-1.2-Contributor_story:
You don't remember a time before the numbers.

When you were four years old you thought everyone could see them. Pale, translucent boxes hovering just over people's heads, like subtitles. Your mother had [INT 6/10] [DEX 5/10] [STR 4/10] [CHA 7/10] [EMP 9/10] floating above her ponytail while she made you peanut butter sandwiches. Your father had [INT 7/10] [DEX 6/10] [STR 8/10] [CHA 5/10] [EMP 6/10] over his balding head while he watched football. Your kindergarten teacher, Mrs. Jensen, had [INT 8/10] [DEX 4/10] [STR 3/10] [CHA 6/10] [EMP 7/10] and [PAT 9/10] — patience, you learned later, was a stat that only showed up on people who worked with children.

You asked Mrs. Jensen why her patience was so high and she laughed and asked what you meant. You pointed at the box over her head. Her smile went tight. She sent you to the school counselor.

By the time you were seven you learned to stop talking about it. By ten you had learned to catalog people silently.

No one ever had a perfect score. Most adults hovered around fives and sixes. A college athlete who came to your high school for a career day had [STR 9/10] [DEX 9/10] but [INT 4/10]. Your brilliant but anxious physics teacher had [INT 9/10] [CHA 3/10]. Everyone was lopsided. Everyone was human. The numbers flickered slightly, too — you watched your mother’s [EMP 9/10] drop to [EMP 6/10] for two weeks after your grandmother died, and watched your best friend’s [DEX 7/10] climb to [8/10] after a summer of skateboarding.

You learned not to judge people by them, or at least to try not to. But you couldn’t unsee them. It was like being the only person in the world who could see color.

You are twenty-six now. You work at a library downtown, reshelving books, because it’s quiet and people don’t expect you to make too much conversation. You see hundreds of boxes a week. You’ve gotten good at pretending you don’t.

Then on a Tuesday in October, at 11:42 in the morning, the door chimes and a man walks in out of the rain.

He is not tall. Not particularly handsome. Early thirties, maybe, in a cheap gray raincoat that drips onto the linoleum. He smiles politely at you as he shakes out his umbrella, and you glance up, out of habit, to read him.

And you freeze.

[STR 10/10]
[DEX 10/10]
[INT 10/10]
[CHA 10/10]
[EMP 10/10]
[LCK 10/10]

Every bar is full. Every number is maxed. The boxes are not pale and translucent like everyone else’s. They are solid, sharp-edged, burning white-gold, as if someone turned the brightness all the way up. You have never seen a ten in any stat, ever. You have never seen anyone with all six. You stare so long your eyes start to water.

He notices.

He looks right at you — not at your face, but at the space about six inches above your head where your own box must be — and his perfect smile falters for the first time.

“You can see them,” he says quietly.

You should deny it. You have denied it for twenty years. But your mouth is dry and you manage only, “Can you?”

He walks closer, past the new arrivals cart, until he’s on your side of the circulation desk. Up close his stats are almost too bright to look at. You can see fine lines around his eyes that don’t match a man with [STR 10/10] and [DEX 10/10]. He looks tired.

“Do you know what perfect stats actually mean?” he asks, and he doesn’t wait for you to answer. “It means you’ve stopped. Nothing moves anymore. Nothing grows, nothing fades. The first time I saw mine hit ten, I was nineteen. I thought I’d won something.” He laughs, a short, rusted sound. “I haven’t had a cold in twelve years. I also haven’t learned a single new thing that stuck. My mother died last spring and my empathy stayed right there. Ten out of ten. Didn’t flicker.”

You glance again at that [EMP 10/10] and for the first time you understand it isn’t perfection. It’s a ceiling.

“What are you?” you whisper.

He shrugs. “The same as you. Just… later. You have [PER 10/10], by the way. Perception. It’s the only reason you can see us. Mine was a nine when I was your age.” He taps his temple. “Yours is going to hit ten someday too, if you keep looking.”

You think of Mrs. Jensen’s patience, your mother’s empathy dropping after your grandmother died, your friend’s dexterity climbing with practice. You thought the numbers described people. You never considered they might be describing movement.

He picks up his wet umbrella. His bright box follows him, unwavering.

“You can still change yours,” he tells you, heading back toward the door. “That’s the good part. You’re still all sevens and eights. You’re still messy. Try to keep it that way as long as you can.”

The door chimes again as he leaves. The rain keeps falling. You sit alone behind the desk for a long time, looking at your hands, wondering what your own flickering numbers look like right now, and feeling, for the first time in your life, grateful that they are not perfect.
samples.Gemini-3.6-Flash_story:
Ever since I was seven years old, the world has come with subtitles. Floating just above everyone’s head, in faint, glowing blue numbers, are their attributes: Strength, Dexterity, Intelligence, Wisdom, Charisma, and Luck.

Humanity, I learned early on, is defined by compromise. The world operates on a strict bell curve. My high school track coach boasted an impressive 84 in Strength, but his Wisdom hovered around a tragic 38. My college professor possessed a 91 in Intelligence, though his Charisma barely scraped past 40. Most people sit comfortably in the fifties—a messy, beautifully flawed collection of average numbers. Flaws, I realized, were what made people human.

Then came a rainy Tuesday afternoon at a corner café.

I was sipping cold coffee, idly scanning the patrons. The barista had a 74 in Dexterity—useful for pulling espresso shots—and a 42 in Luck. A businessman near the window rocked an 80 in Charisma, though his low Wisdom suggested he was about to make a terrible investment.

Then the front door chimed, and he walked in.

I nearly choked on my drink. Above his head, the numbers didn’t glow faint blue; they shimmered in a brilliant, blinding gold.

*Strength: 100*  
*Dexterity: 100*  
*Intelligence: 100*  
*Wisdom: 100*  
*Charisma: 100*  
*Luck: 100*  

He was dressed simply—a plain gray coat, dark jeans—but he moved with a fluid, terrifying grace. When a distracted patron accidentally knocked a ceramic mug off a nearby table, the man caught it mid-fall without even turning his head, sliding it smoothly back onto the wooden surface before it could shatter. When he spoke to the cashier, his voice possessed a warm, melodic resonance that caused every person in the room to subtly relax.

He was, by every mathematical definition, absolute perfection.

I couldn't stop staring. He ordered a black coffee, picked up his cup, and walked straight toward my corner table. Before I could look away, he pulled out the chair across from me and sat down.

"You're squinting," he said softly. His eyes were clear, bright, and impossibly deep. "Most people just admire the posture. But you’re reading the numbers, aren't you?"

My throat went dry. "You... you can tell?"

"I used to see them too," he replied, taking a slow sip of his coffee. "Until I maxed them all out."

"How?" I whispered, leaning in. "Is it a glitch? Are you an alien? A god?"

He chuckled, a sound so pleasant it felt like sunlight breaking through clouds. "Nothing so grand. Just a life consumed by relentless optimization. Forty years of absolute discipline. Biohacking, polyphasic sleep, mastering dozens of languages, memorizing entire libraries, physical conditioning, emotional mastery. Every waking second dedicated to pushing every single stat to its cap."

"That's incredible," I said, awestruck. "You're the pinnacle of human achievement."

The man looked down at his coffee cup, a small, weary smile touching his lips. "That's what I thought I was building. But do you know what happens when your Luck is 100? Nothing unexpected ever occurs. When your Intelligence and Wisdom are maxed out, every conversation is completely predictable before it even starts. When Dexterity and Strength are flawless, you never stumble, but you also never feel the thrill of overcoming your own weakness."

He met my gaze. "Perfection isn't a victory. It's a cage. I built a prison out of high scores."

I sat back, stunned. I looked above his head again. The golden numbers remained, brilliant and unyielding.

"Why talk to me?" I asked.

"Because when I look at you," he said gently, "I see a 52 in Strength, a 61 in Intelligence, and a 48 in Luck. You are chaotic. You are incomplete. You still have room to surprise yourself." He set a crisp hundred-dollar bill on the table to cover his four-dollar coffee—a classic maxed-Charisma gesture that felt entirely genuine.

He stood up, adjusting his collar. "Don't envy the finished product," he said with a quiet nod. "The game is only fun while you're still playing."

He turned and walked out into the downpour. I watched him go, his golden stats fading into the gray mist outside, leaving me sitting in the quiet café, surrounded by the beautiful, messy averages of the world.
samples.Kimi-K3_story:
The numbers showed up when I was six, floating over my kindergarten teacher's head like a thought bubble in a cartoon. INT: 6. DEX: 3. CHA: 8. WIS: 5. LCK: 2. I thought everyone saw them. By the time I learned they didn't, I'd also learned to keep quiet. Kids who announce the teacher's stats out loud get sent to the school psychologist.

The categories mapped cleanly onto the video games of my childhood, which made it feel less like witchcraft and more like a HUD God forgot to switch off. Ten was the ceiling. Most people lived between three and six. A seven could make somebody the star of a small town. I once watched an INT: 9 argue a case on the courthouse steps; I swear the pigeons applauded.

You'd think the gift would make me rich. It mostly made me an unnaturally good triage nurse. I admit the hemorrhaging guy, defer the man whose LCK is a 9 and whose cut is cosmetic, and once — only once — I watched a CON: 9 walk away from a bus crash with a paper cut. My colleagues call me uncanny. I've stopped correcting them.

The man came in on a Tuesday, peak flu season, the waiting room an orchestra of coughs. I looked up from my clipboard and the numbers over his head were ten, ten, ten — all of them, INT, STR, DEX, CHA, WIS, CON, LCK — not glowing, not flashing, just sitting there with the calm of a completed form. Perfect. I dropped my pen. He picked it up before it finished falling and handed it back with a smile that could have ended wars.

"I'm here about the trial," he said. "Volunteer." He held out his arm for the blood draw, and his chart told the rest: he was donating his body to science, weekly, because his blood made antibodies like a factory. Perfect CON will do that.

Eli Mercer came back every Tuesday, and over a year of Tuesdays we became something between friends and a control group. He beat the ICU chess pool blindfolded. He talked a jumper down from the parking structure in the courtyard between draws. He fixed the vending machine with a paper clip. He remembered everyone's name, everyone's grandchildren, everyone's odds.

"Do you know?" I asked finally, while he sat in the phlebotomy chair. "What you are?"

"Statistically improbable," he said. "I did the math. I had the math to do it." Then, quieter: "You see them, don't you? The numbers. You've never once asked me what I see over your head."

I told him everything. He nodded like a man confirming a diagnosis. "I wondered when I'd find one of you. People who can check." He rolled his sleeve down. "Here's the secret no one believes: the scales lie. They max out, sure. But the only stat that matters never gets a number. It's whether the numbers get *spent*."

He died at forty-two — a perfect CON finally spent, on a remission timeline he'd predicted to the day. His blood trial has saved, last I checked, about forty thousand people. I'm one of sixteen nurses he told his secret to; we trade his Tuesdays sometimes, like an inheritance.

Last week a janitor stopped me in the hall — INT: 4, gray hair, knees shot. "You're the one Eli Mercer talked about," he said. "The one who can check." He smiled like a man holding a winning ticket, and over his head, faint as a draft under a door, a new stat flickered where I'd never seen one before.

I didn't read it. I didn't need to. That night I looked in the mirror, and for the first time in my life I saw my own numbers — and one of them, just one, had ticked up.
samples.GPT-5.6-Luna_story:
# Perfect Stats

Ever since I was a child, I had been able to see people’s stats.

The first time it happened, I was six. My mother was standing in the kitchen, smiling down at me while holding a plate of sliced apples.

**MOTHER**
Intelligence: 74
Strength: 31
Dexterity: 42
Endurance: 38
Luck: 61

I thought everyone could see those numbers. I spent years assuming they were as ordinary as someone’s name or height.

Then, at school, I discovered they weren't.

By the time I was twelve, I had learned not to stare. By sixteen, I had learned to use the numbers.

Teachers with high Intelligence were easy to impress. Bullies with low Dexterity were easy to dodge. Friends with high Luck somehow always found money on the sidewalk or arrived five minutes before a bus left.

I never told anyone about my ability.

It was the kind of secret that could ruin a life.

I used my gift quietly. I chose good partners for group projects, avoided dangerous people, and eventually got a job at a small accounting firm where numbers were already a respectable obsession.

My life was ordinary.

Until I met him.

It happened on a rainy Tuesday.

I was leaving work when I saw a man standing beneath the awning across the street. He was perhaps thirty years old, dressed in a dark coat, with black hair plastered against his forehead by the rain.

I looked at him.

And froze.

His stats appeared.

**MAN**
Strength: 100
Intelligence: 100
Dexterity: 100
Endurance: 100
Luck: 100
Perception: 100
Charisma: 100

I blinked.

The numbers didn't disappear.

Perfect stats.

I had seen thousands of people in my life. The highest Intelligence I'd ever encountered was 96. The highest Luck was 93.

Nobody had ever reached 100 in everything.

The man looked directly at me.

“You can see them, can't you?”

My stomach dropped.

I turned to leave.

“Don't,” he said.

There was something in his voice that stopped me.

I slowly faced him.

“See what?”

He smiled.

“The numbers.”

Rain hammered the pavement around us.

“How long have you known?” I asked.

“Since I was born.”

My mouth went dry.

“You have this ability too?”

“No.”

He stepped closer.

“I have the stats.”

That answer made even less sense.

He reached into his coat and pulled out a small notebook.

“I've spent years looking for people like you.”

“Why?”

“Because the world isn't supposed to have people with perfect stats.”

He opened the notebook. Inside were dozens of names, dates, and numbers. Most had been crossed out.

“I don't understand.”

“You think those numbers describe what you are,” he said. “They don't. They describe what you are *allowed* to become.”

I stared at him.

He continued.

“Everyone has limits. Invisible walls. Strength can improve, intelligence can improve, luck can change. But the system keeps people within certain boundaries.”

“The system?”

He looked up at me.

“Call it whatever you want. Fate. God. Reality.”

Then his smile vanished.

“I found a way to break it.”

A chill ran through me.

“And that's why you have 100 in everything?”

“No.”

He closed the notebook.

“That's why you're here.”

Before I could ask what he meant, he grabbed my wrist.

For the first time in my life, my vision changed.

The numbers surrounding him shattered like glass.

Behind them was another line of text.

**LEVEL: 1**
**UNALLOCATED POINTS: 10,000**

I couldn't breathe.

The man released me.

“You can see stats because you're not part of the system in the same way everyone else is.”

“Then what am I?”

He looked almost sad.

“The administrator.”

Thunder rolled overhead.

I laughed because the alternative was screaming.

“You're insane.”

“Maybe.”

He pointed at the city.

“Tomorrow morning, you will look at someone and see a stat you've never seen before.”

“What stat?”

“Potential.”

He walked into the rain.

I watched him disappear between the headlights and umbrellas.

The next morning, I tested his prediction.

On the train, I looked at an old woman.

Nothing unusual.

A businessman.

Nothing.

A child.

Nothing.

Then I looked at the young woman sitting beside the window.

Her usual stats appeared.

But beneath them was something new.

**POTENTIAL: 100%**

And beneath that:

**CURRENT LEVEL: 1**

Then another message appeared.

**Would you like to allocate points?**

For the first time since childhood, I wished I had never been able to see the numbers.

Because beneath the question was a list.

**Strength. Intelligence. Dexterity. Luck.**

And at the very bottom:

**Reality.**

I stared at it for a long time.

Then I smiled.

I'd spent my entire life believing the numbers told me what people were.

Now I understood.

They were only telling me what people could become.

And, apparently, someone had finally given me the power to change the answer.

I've seen numbers hovering over people's heads since I was six years old. My mother thought I was inventing imaginary friends when I told her the mailman had a Strength of 34 and a Charisma of 12. By the time I was ten, I'd stopped mentioning it to anyone. By twenty, I'd built a quiet life around it—learning which stats mattered for which situations, using the knowledge like a secret currency nobody else could spend.

Intelligence, Strength, Dexterity, Charisma, Wisdom, Constitution. Six numbers, usually capped somewhere in the 20s for exceptional people, most folks clustering in the 8-14 range like the world's most boring bell curve. I'd seen a chess grandmaster with 27 Intelligence once and thought that was the ceiling of human possibility.

Then I met Daniel.

He worked the register at a coffee shop I'd never been to before, in a town I was only passing through for a wedding. I almost didn't look up from my phone when I ordered, but something made me glance at him—maybe the stillness in his voice, maybe just habit.

The numbers over his head stopped me cold.

Intelligence: 99. Strength: 99. Dexterity: 99. Charisma: 99. Wisdom: 99. Constitution: 99.

I'd never seen anything above a 40. I stood there long enough that he raised an eyebrow and asked if I was okay.

"Fine," I said. "Sorry. Long day."

I took my coffee to a corner table and didn't drink it. I just watched him work the register, refill the pastry case, laugh at some customer's joke. Nothing about him suggested a man operating at the theoretical maximum of human capability. He wasn't leaping over counters or reciting pi to the ten-thousandth digit. He was just... a guy, making lattes, occasionally missing the exact center of a to-go lid.

I came back the next day. And the day after that. I told myself I was investigating a phenomenon, but really I think I just wanted to understand what perfection looked like when it wasn't trying to prove anything.

On the fourth day, I worked up the nerve to sit at the counter during a lull and ask him, carefully, hypothetically, whether he'd ever felt like he could do anything—like there was no ceiling on him at all.

He laughed, not unkindly. "Everybody feels that at twenty-two, don't they?"

"No," I said. "I mean it differently."

Something in my tone made him look at me properly, the way people rarely do. "You're the one who's been staring at me since Tuesday."

I admitted it, then—haltingly, half-expecting him to call security. Instead he listened, turning a cup absently in his hands, and when I finished he was quiet for a long moment.

"I don't feel like anything special," he said finally. "I forget where I put my keys. I was bad at math until I was fifteen. My mom says I was a colicky baby who wouldn't sleep." He shrugged. "Maybe your numbers are wrong."

"They've never been wrong before."

"Then maybe," he said, "the numbers aren't the point."

I didn't understand what he meant until weeks later, back home, turning the memory over the way you turn over a stone looking for what's underneath. Daniel wasn't extraordinary because of his stats. He didn't win a Nobel Prize or bench-press a car. He was, as far as I could tell, unfailingly kind, endlessly curious, and utterly unimpressed with himself. Whatever those numbers measured, it wasn't the thing that made someone worth knowing.

I still see the numbers now, everywhere, all the time. But I've stopped believing they tell me anything true. Somewhere out there is a man with a perfect 99 in every category, pulling espresso shots and forgetting his car keys, living a life no more remarkable than anyone else's—except that he taught me, without meaning to, that the score was never the story.

**The Numbers We Carry**

The first time you saw them, you were four years old, sitting in your mother's lap at the kitchen table. Above her head, glowing faintly in your vision, floated a small window: **Katherine Mavis. INT 84. DEX 62. CHA 71. WIS 79. CON 65.** You reached for it with a chubby toddler's hand, and your mother laughed and asked what you were grabbing at. You couldn't explain. There weren't words for it yet.

By eight, you understood. Everyone had numbers. The bully on the playground had STR 91 and INT 42, which made you smile even as he shoved you into the dirt. Your teacher, Mrs. Caldwell, had WIS 95, the highest you'd ever seen, and you respected her deeply for reasons you could never articulate to your classmates. Your father, who left when you were six, had CHA 88 — you only learned what that meant years later, watching the way women turned their heads when he walked into a room.

You learned not to mention the windows. By twelve, you'd tested enough to know that mentioning them got you sent to counselors, stared at by worried parents, shuffled between specialists. The windows were yours. They were real. They were yours.

In high school, you began to understand the patterns. STR meant muscle and stubbornness. INT was thinking speed, problem-solving, the mind's quickness. DEX was grace and coordination — athletes had it high, as did dancers and surgeons. CHA was presence, charm, the thing that made rooms listen. WIS was judgment, the wisdom of knowing what to do with everything else. CON was resilience, endurance, the body's quiet refusal to quit.

You learned that high stats weren't everything. A man you met at twenty-two had INT 99 — the highest you'd ever seen at the time — and he was unemployed, bitter, washing dishes at a diner, because his CHA was 31 and his WIS was 40. Brilliant mind, no wisdom, no warmth. He couldn't keep a friend or a job.

You learned that low stats weren't death sentences either. Your best friend since college, Mia, had STR 38 and CON 41. She was a librarian with chronic fatigue, but she had INT 84, CHA 82, WIS 90. She was the wisest person you knew, kind and perceptive in a way that her numbers couldn't capture but somehow did. The stats were guides, not destinies. They were rough maps of a person, not the territory.

So when you walked into the coffee shop on a rainy Thursday morning, you weren't expecting anything remarkable. You were tired. You'd slept poorly. You ordered an oat milk latte and waited, watching the rain bead on the window.

Then the door opened.

He was ordinary-looking. Tall, brown hair, a gray coat, mid-thirties perhaps. Nothing about his appearance announced him. But the window above his head was — 

You blinked. Looked again.

**INT 100. DEX 100. STR 100. CHA 100. WIS 100. CON 100.**

All of them. Maxed. Every category. The numbers glowed brighter than any you'd ever seen, as if the window itself were made of light.

You stared. He ordered a black coffee. He paid. He turned, scanning for a seat, and his eyes met yours. He paused. Something flickered across his face — recognition, or surprise, or perhaps the look of someone who's been caught.

He walked over. He sat down across from you without asking, as if it were the most natural thing in the world.

"You can see them," he said quietly. Not a question.

Your throat closed. In thirty years, no one had ever — 

"It's alright," he said, and his voice was calm, warm, the kind of voice you'd trust instantly. "I'm not going to hurt you. I've been looking for someone like you for a very long time."

"Why?"

"Because I need help." He smiled, and there was sadness in it. "I have perfect stats, as you can see. I always have. From the moment I was born." He leaned forward. "Do you know what that's like? To be perfect at everything and still be utterly, completely alone? No one can beat me at anything. No one can challenge me. I've never had an equal. I've never had a friend."

You looked at the perfect numbers above his head. You thought of your mother, her laugh, her good-but-not-great stats. You thought of Mia, who was sleeping right now, tired but kind.

"You need a friend," you said slowly. "Not a perfect one. Just a friend."

He looked at you, and for the first time, the window seemed to dim slightly. The numbers still glowed. But something behind them softened.

"Yes," he said. "I think I do."

Outside, the rain kept falling. Inside, two lonely people began to talk.

samples.MiMo-V2.5-Pro_story:
# The Fog

I had lived in the coastal town of Mirren for thirty-seven years, and in all that time, I had never seen fog like this.

It rolled in on a Tuesday evening in late October, thick as cotton batting pressed against the windows. By the time I noticed it from my kitchen sink, the streetlights across the road had already vanished. The neighbor's house — close enough that I could normally see the color of their curtains — was simply gone, swallowed whole.

"Strange weather," I muttered to no one, drying my hands on a dish towel.

My wife, Helen, had passed the previous spring. The house was full of the particular silence that follows a death — not empty, exactly, but rearranged, as though the furniture itself was holding its breath. I had grown accustomed to talking aloud to fill the space. The fog, I decided, was just another thing to remark upon.

By morning, it hadn't lifted. If anything, it had thickened. I opened the front door and could see perhaps three feet ahead before the world dissolved into gray. The air tasted of salt and something older — wet stone, maybe, or the underside of the pier where the barnacles clung.

I walked to the end of my driveway. The mailbox stood like a ghost of itself. Beyond it, there was nothing.

"Tom?" A voice materialized from the blankness. I startled, gripping the mailbox post.

"Who's there?"

It was Gerald, my neighbor from two doors down. He emerged from the fog like a figure stepping through a curtain, his face pale and bewildered. "You seeing this? Radio says it's just a marine layer. Should burn off by noon."

It didn't burn off by noon.

By the second day, people began to behave strangely. Not dramatically — nothing you could point to and name. But I noticed that Mrs. Calloway, who walked her terrier every morning at seven sharp, hadn't been seen. The lights in the harbormaster's office stayed dark. At the grocery store, the shelves were still stocked, but the cashier — a young woman named Dana who had always been cheerful — stared at her register as though she'd forgotten what it was for.

"Are you alright?" I asked her.

She looked up at me, and for a moment, I wasn't sure she recognized me. Then she blinked and smiled thinly. "Just tired, Mr. Alden. This fog. It gets into your head."

She was right about that. By the third day, I found myself standing in Helen's garden, staring at the dead stalks of her rose bushes, unable to remember why I had walked outside. The fog pressed against my face like a damp hand. I could hear the ocean — it was always there, the rhythm of Mirren — but the sound seemed wrong, too close, as though the tide had crept up the hill and was lapping at the foundations of the town itself.

On the fourth day, I heard Helen's voice.

I was sitting in the living room, reading the same paragraph for the fifth time, when it came from the hallway. Soft, unmistakable. My name, spoken the way she used to say it when dinner was ready — half question, half declaration.

"Tom."

I set down the book. My heart hammered. I knew, rationally, that it was impossible. Helen was buried in the churchyard on Elm Street. I had stood in the rain and watched them lower the casket. I had thrown the handful of dirt. I knew these things.

But the fog didn't care what I knew.

I stood and walked to the hallway. The fog had found its way inside — I could see it curling along the baseboards, seeping beneath the door like something alive. And at the end of the hall, where the bedroom door stood half-open, there was a shape. Not Helen, not exactly. A suggestion of her. The way light bends around something that used to be there.

I took one step forward. Then another.

On the fifth day, the fog lifted.

Gerald found my front door open that morning and let himself in, worried. He found me sitting in the kitchen, a cup of cold tea in my hands, staring at the garden through the window. The roses were still dead. The world was sharp and ordinary and bright.

"You alright, Tom?" Gerald asked.

I considered the question for a long time. The fog was gone, but I could still feel it — a coolness in the rooms that hadn't been there before, a faint smell of salt in the hallway, a lingering sense that something had been offered and I had, wisely or not, declined.

"Yes," I said finally. "I think I am."

But I slept with the bedroom door closed after that.
samples.DeepSeek-V4-Flash_story:
The fog came in off the river just after dusk, soft and white as a sheet drawn over the world. Arthur stood at the end of his street, hands in his pockets, and watched it swallow the houses one by one. The lamplights became smudges, then ghosts, then nothing. He should have headed home, but the fog had a way of erasing reasons, and he found himself walking instead.

He knew this neighborhood. He had lived here eleven years. But the fog stripped the familiar landmarks away—the blue mailbox, the crooked fence, the Harrisons’ barking terrier—and left only the wet black asphalt and the sound of his own footsteps. Each step was a question. Each question went unanswered.

At the corner he stopped. There was a bench there, usually facing the bakery. Through the murk he saw a shape that shouldn't have been. A small red balloon, tied to the bench’s armrest, tugging faintly in the still air. No one was around. Arthur stood and looked at it. For no good reason, he felt the fog thicken behind his eyes, and he remembered his daughter’s sixth birthday. How she had let go of a red balloon in the park and cried for an hour, and he had promised they would find it. They never did.

He left the balloon and walked on.

The fog grew deeper. The sidewalk narrowed. Arthur had the sensation of wading, not walking. Somewhere ahead, a voice rose and fell—a woman singing, or perhaps crying. It came from the direction of the old church. He followed it, because the fog seemed to leave a trail in the sound.

The church steps appeared like a shoreline. On them sat an old woman in a gray coat, her head bowed. She looked up as he approached, and her face was wet. “You came back,” she said.

Arthur stopped. “I’m sorry. I don’t—do you need help?”

“You came back,” she repeated. “I knew you would. You always left the gate open, and I always closed it, but now I can’t. I’m too tired.” She held out a hand. It was trembling.

He crouched down. The fog swirled around them, making a small room out of the church steps. “I’m not who you think I am,” he said gently. “But I can help you get wherever you need to go.”

“You don’t know where that is,” she said. “I don’t either. But I waited here because I thought maybe the fog would bring you. It brings everything back, doesn’t it?”

Arthur felt a coldness seep through his coat. He thought of the balloon again. He thought of his daughter’s small hand waving as she grew up and stopped waving. He thought of the house where he slept alone now, and the kitchen light he left burning every night for no one. The fog was inside him, too—a soft, white erasure of the edges of things.

“Yes,” he said quietly. “It does.”

The old woman nodded. “That’s why I came out. To see what the fog carries. Better than the things I carry alone.”

Arthur didn’t know what to say. He sat down beside her on the cold stone, and for a while they watched the fog drift past the streetlights like a slow river of ghosts. Then the woman sighed and said, “My husband used to tell me that the fog was the world breathing. When you can’t see ahead, he said, it’s because the world is taking a breath before it sighs.”

“A nice idea,” Arthur said.

“It was a lie,” she said, and laughed. “But a kind one.” She stood, steadied herself on his shoulder, and looked down at him. “You should go home. There’s someone waiting for you, even if you don’t believe it.”

She walked off into the white, and the fog swallowed her like everything else.

Arthur remained for a long time. Eventually he rose and walked back the way he came. The red balloon was gone. The blue mailbox appeared, then the crooked fence, then the Harrisons’ terrier barked as he passed. His own front door seemed smaller than he remembered, but he had the key in his hand.

He opened the kitchen light, left it burning, and stood at the window. The fog was thinning now, revealing the dim shapes of rooftops, a tree, the far-off lights of the town. He thought of the old woman’s lie—the world breathing—and of his daughter, grown and living three states away, who sometimes called him just to say goodnight. He picked up the phone. There was no answer, but the voicemail was kind.

“I just wanted you to know,” Arthur said, “that I’m sorry about the balloon.”

He let the fog close around the house, and for the first time in years, he slept without dreaming.
samples.Muse-Spark-1.2-Contributor_story:
I have lived in Greyhaven for thirty-one years, long enough to know there are two kinds of fog. The first is the honest kind, the thin veil that rolls off the Atlantic at dawn and is gone by breakfast. Tourists take pictures of it, fishermen wait it out, and by nine o'clock the sun has burned it away. The second kind is different. My mother called it the hungry fog. It doesn't roll. It arrives. It settles low and thick and does not leave until it wants to.

I had not seen the hungry fog in fifteen years, not since the night my father disappeared from the lighthouse.

The weather radio warned about it yesterday afternoon while I was closing up the hardware store. "Dense fog advisory until further notice," the voice crackled. I looked out the window at the harbor and saw it forming, a wall of white advancing across the water, swallowing the buoys one by one. No wind. No sound. I locked the door and walked home quickly, pulling my collar up though it wasn't cold.

By dusk, Greyhaven had vanished. From my porch I could not see the house across the street, only a pale, luminous blankness where it should be. The streetlamps were halos, faint and useless. The fog dampened every sound. Even the gulls were silent.

I told myself I would stay inside. I made tea. I tried to read. But at about eleven, the lighthouse horn sounded.

That was impossible. The lighthouse has been automated for a decade, and its horn was decommissioned years ago. My father was its last keeper. When they found his coat folded neatly on the catwalk and the light still turning, they said he must have fallen. They never found a body. I had not heard that horn since I was sixteen.

I stood at my window with my tea going cold in my hands, listening as it sounded again — a long, mournful bellow that vibrated in my chest, muffled by the fog. Without thinking, I put on my boots and my father's old oilskin that still hung by the door and stepped out.

The fog was colder than I expected. It clung to my skin, damp and close. I could see perhaps five feet in any direction. The world was narrowed to the slick asphalt under my boots and the white around me. I followed the hill down toward the harbor, toward the sound, counting the cracks in the sidewalk the way I did as a child.

The town was empty, or seemed empty. I passed dark houses where I knew my neighbors were awake behind curtains, waiting it out like I should have been. The fog made ghosts of everything. A bicycle left on a lawn looked like a hunched animal. A stop sign floated, bodiless.

At the harbor, the water was invisible, but I could hear it lapping. The lighthouse stood on its rock, its beam sweeping — or I thought it was sweeping — but the fog ate the light after a few feet, so it pulsed like a faint heartbeat instead of a blade. And there, on the path to the causeway, I saw a figure walking ahead of me.

My breath caught. The shape, the gait, the oilskin. For a second I was sixteen again, watching my father leave for his night shift.

"Dad?" I called, and my voice was swallowed instantly.

The figure did not turn, but it stopped. It waited.

I ran then, or as close to running as I could on the wet stones, the fog parting just enough for me to see. When I was close enough to touch him, I realized it was not my father. It was only a piling draped with a tarp, half-collapsed.

And then, behind me, the horn sounded a third time and a hand touched my shoulder.

I spun around. No one was there. But the fog was suddenly thinner, just for a moment, and I saw my town again — the harbor, the houses on the hill, the light in my own kitchen window where I had left it on. I saw it clearly, the way I see something after I thought I had lost it forever.

I understood then what my mother had meant. The hungry fog doesn't take. It shows me what I have been looking for, and it waits to see if I will chase it forever or let it go.

I walked home. The fog stayed all night, thick as cotton, but I slept with the window open, listening to the silence where the horn had been. By morning it was gone. The sun was out. The harbor was blue and ordinary and honest. I went to the lighthouse rock and found no footprints but my own, already drying in the sun.
samples.Gemini-3.6-Flash_story:
It didn’t drift in like normal sea mist; it spilled over the jagged lip of the bluffs like milk poured into a bowl. Within ten minutes, the Atlantic had vanished. Then the tall cedar trees at the edge of my yard disappeared, leaving me suspended in a featureless, woolly void.

In Blackwood Cove, we called it the Harbor Breath. My grandfather used to say that every thirty years, the ocean held its breath, exhaling a fog so thick it erased the border between what was real and what was remembered.

Standing on the porch of my cottage, I watched the final shreds of afternoon daylight get swallowed whole. The temperature plummeted, carrying a dampness that seeped straight into my bones. But I couldn’t go inside just yet. I had left the *Mariner*, my grandfather’s handcrafted oak skiff, loosely tethered at the end of the lower dock. If the midnight surge hit while she was adrift, she’d be battered to splinters against the rocks.

I clicked on my heavy brass lantern, but the beam died less than three feet from the glass, illuminating nothing but swirling suspended droplets. Sighing, I stepped off the porch into the white gloom.

Instantly, the world went dead silent. The steady, rhythmic rumble of the surf was gone, replaced by a heavy, suffocating stillness. Even my footsteps on the gravel path sounded muffled, as if I were walking on wet velvet.

I reached out, relying on muscle memory to guide me down the steep wooden stairs leading to the shoreline. One step, two steps, three. The wood beneath my boots felt slick with condensation.

Then the sound began.

It started as a low humming, vibrating right in the back of my teeth. Then it resolved into a voice—clear, sweet, and entirely impossible.

"Arthur?"

I froze, my hand hovering over the wooden handrail. That was my sister Clara’s voice. Clara, who had walked out onto the tide flats during the winter storm of 1998 and never returned.

"Arthur, down here. The water is so calm today."

My heart hammered against my ribs. Reason screamed at me that it was a trick of the mist, an auditory illusion born of cold air and old grief. But my feet moved on their own, drawing me down toward the sound.

"I've been waiting for you," the voice drifted from the darkness below.

The lantern cast useless amber halos into the wall of gray. I reached the bottom of the stairs and felt the slick planks of the dock beneath me. The smell of rot and old brine was overwhelming.

Through the white veil, a silhouette took shape at the very edge of the pier. It was slight, wearing the familiar yellow rain slicker Clara had loved.

"Clara?" my voice trembled, swallowed instantly by the fog.

The figure turned. It had no face—only an expanse of shifting, gray vapor that reached out with tendrils of white frost. 

Panic flared, hot and sharp. The fog wasn't just weather; it was a hungry thing, luring the lonely into its depth. 

The figure stepped closer, extending a pale mist-hand. The cold radiating off it was absolute, threatening to freeze the breath in my lungs. It wanted me to take one more step off the dock, to plunge into the icy dark below.

I forced my eyes shut. I remembered my grandfather’s warnings: *When the Harbor Breath takes the world, trust only what your hands can hold.*

I dropped the lantern. It shattered against the wood with a dull clatter. I dropped to my knees and slammed my bare hand onto the thick, wet hemp rope tied to the pier's mooring cleat. The coarse fibers bit into my palm, grounding me in reality.

I pulled on the rope with everything I had. The oak hull of the *Mariner* bumped against the pilings. I grabbed the secondary line, looped it twice around the post, and tied a double-half hitch with shaking fingers.

The voice shrieked—a sound like tearing metal—and a cold tendril brushed my cheek, leaving a trail of numb frost.

"You aren't her," I whispered into the damp wood of the dock. "She’s gone."

I kept my eyes squeezed shut. Keeping my hand firmly on the thick rope, I crawled backward, finding the bottom riser of the wooden stairs. Step by step, I hauled myself up the cliff path, blindly climbing out of the shroud.

When my boots finally struck the firm gravel of my yard, the air grew thinner and warmer. I scrambled onto the porch, threw open the door, and slammed it shut, sliding the heavy deadbolt home.

Leaning against the solid wood, gasping for breath, I looked out the window. The fog pressed against the glass, flat and white, like a face waiting to be let in. But inside, the fire was lit, and the wood was real.

# The Fog

The fog came in the way it always did here—silent, total, as if the world had decided to stop existing three feet past my door. I'd been back in Grey Harbor for two days, sleeping in my mother's cottage with the windows open, when it rolled in off the water and erased the town.

The lawyer had told me to take whatever I wanted; the house was to be sold. My mother had kept everything. My father's wool coat still hung by the door. His compass, its brass worn to a soft glow, sat on the sill above the kitchen sink where she could touch it while washing dishes.

I hadn't intended to keep either. I hadn't intended to keep much of anything.

But the fog, when it came, felt like an invitation, or a dare. I took the coat, the compass, and the small tin box from the mantel—the one I'd been avoiding since the funeral—and walked down toward the lighthouse the way my father used to walk: head down, hands deep in pockets, as if he knew the world by memory and had no need of looking at it.

People here say the fog has a personality. Ours was patient. It didn't rush the rocks; it settled over them like something that had decided to stay. My father went out into fog like this when I was nine, and the sea, which we'd always treated as a neighbor, took him and never apologized. My mother walked to the lighthouse every day afterward, for twenty years. I used to think she went to look for him. Now, standing at the base of the white tower with the coat too big on my shoulders and the compass cold in my palm, I wondered if she'd gone to learn the fog's language instead—how to live in a world that refuses to be seen clearly.

I sat on the flat rock where she always sat, the granite polished smooth by her patience, and opened the tin box. Her ashes, pale as the fog itself. She'd asked to be scattered at the lighthouse, and I'd told the funeral director we'd do it, and then I'd carried her home to Portland in my carry-on luggage like a secret I wasn't ready to say out loud.

The fog pressed close. Somewhere beyond it, a bell buoy sounded, patient as a heartbeat.

"I couldn't do it," I said, and my voice went nowhere, absorbed by all that white. "I kept thinking there'd be a clear day. A right day."

The fog, being patient, waited.

So I did it badly—the way most true things get done. I opened the lid and the wind took some of her and the rocks took the rest, and for one terrible, perfect moment she was part of the fog itself, everywhere, touching everything, the way grief does, the way love did. I cried until the buoy's bell sounded like an answer, and then I laughed, because she'd have laughed at me making a ceremony of a gray afternoon.

When I stood to go, I looked at the compass out of old habit. The needle held steady, as needles do. North doesn't care whether you can see it. That was, I think, the thing my mother had spent twenty years learning at the end of this island, and the thing she'd left in a brass instrument on her windowsill for me to find.

The fog did not lift as I walked home. The cottage appeared only when I was nearly upon it, pale windows glowing like something remembered rather than seen. But I kept the coat on, and I kept the compass, and I found my way—not because the path was clear, but because it wasn't, and I had finally learned to go anyway.

# The Fog

The fog arrived just before midnight.

At first, I thought it was only mist rising from the river. I was standing at the kitchen window, washing the last cup of the evening, when I noticed a pale whiteness gathering between the houses. It moved slowly at first, curling around fences and garden walls. Within minutes, the streetlamp outside had become a faint yellow blur.

I dried my hands and stepped onto the porch.

The air was cold and wet against my face. I could barely see the mailbox at the end of the path. Somewhere beyond it, a dog barked once, then fell silent.

That was when I heard the bell.

It was a small, distant sound.

*Ding.*

I froze.

*Ding.*

The sound came again, somewhere down the road.

There was an old railway line beyond the village, abandoned for nearly twenty years. Trains no longer ran there, and the station had been closed even longer. Yet everyone in the village knew the story about the night the last train disappeared into the fog.

My grandfather had told it to me when I was a child.

The train had been carrying twelve passengers. It entered the tunnel just after midnight and never came out. Searchers found nothing: no wreckage, no bodies, not even a broken piece of track. The railway company eventually declared it an accident, but no one could explain where the train had gone.

Grandfather always ended the story with the same warning.

“If you ever hear a bell in the fog,” he would say, “don't follow it.”

I laughed at the memory.

Then the bell rang again.

*Ding.*

I should have gone inside.

Instead, I grabbed my coat and flashlight.

The village was strangely quiet as I walked down the road. The fog swallowed everything beyond a few steps. My own footsteps sounded unfamiliar, as though someone were walking beside me.

Then I saw a light.

Far ahead, a warm yellow glow appeared in the mist.

I walked toward it.

The light grew brighter until I could make out an old railway station. I had never seen it before. Not in photographs, not even in my grandfather's stories. Yet there it stood, perfectly preserved, its wooden sign hanging above the platform.

**RAVEN'S END**

The station clock showed midnight.

The bell rang.

*Ding.*

A train emerged from the fog.

It was an old passenger train, black and silver, its windows glowing softly. It stopped without making a sound.

One door opened.

I stepped backward.

Someone was standing inside.

An old man in a dark railway uniform.

My breath caught.

He looked exactly like my grandfather.

“Grandpa?”

The man smiled sadly.

“You shouldn't have come.”

I wanted to run, but my legs refused to move.

“What is this place?”

“A place between leaving and arriving.”

He looked toward the train.

“I waited a long time for you.”

I shook my head. “You're dead.”

“I know.”

The train bell rang again.

Behind him, I saw twelve passengers sitting silently in the carriages. Their faces were pale and strangely familiar. Then I realized they were the people from the old photograph my grandfather had kept in his study—the twelve passengers who had vanished all those years ago.

My grandfather stepped down onto the platform.

“Every year,” he said, “the train returns for one night. It carries those who were lost. But tonight, it has come for someone else.”

“Who?”

He looked at me.

I understood.

“No.”

He reached into his coat and handed me a small brass railway whistle.

“Your father was supposed to take this journey. He died before he could. The train came for him instead.”

The fog began to thicken around us.

“Go home,” Grandpa whispered. “And don't look back.”

I ran.

I ran until my lungs burned, clutching the whistle in my hand. The fog chased me through the streets, curling around my ankles. Behind me, the bell rang again and again.

I did not turn around.

At dawn, I reached my house.

The fog disappeared as suddenly as it had come.

For several minutes, I stood on the porch, shaking.

Then I looked down at my hand.

The brass whistle was gone.

In its place was an old photograph.

I turned it over.

Written on the back in my grandfather's handwriting were six words:

**Some journeys are meant to end.**

I never heard the bell again.

But every year, on the night the fog returns, I leave my porch light on until morning.

Just in case someone else hears it.

# The Fog

I remember the morning it came—not as weather, but as something alive.

I was seven years old, standing at my bedroom window, watching the world outside dissolve into gray. Mom said it was just fog, nothing more, but I knew better even then. Fog doesn't swallow the Hendersons' oak tree whole in the span of a blink. Fog doesn't make the streetlights hum with a sound like something breathing.

By noon, the whole town had gone quiet. Not silent—quiet in the way a held breath is quiet. Dad tried to drive to work anyway, said the fog would burn off by the time he reached the highway. He came back twenty minutes later, face pale, saying he'd driven in circles for an hour and ended up right back at our driveway.

We didn't leave the house after that.

The days blurred together. Mom kept the radio on, but all we got was static laced with something that might have been voices, might have been our own imaginations filling gaps with meaning. Dad boarded the windows, not because anything tried to get in, but because none of us could stand to look at the gray anymore. It pressed against the glass like it wanted to be let inside, patient and endless.

I was the one who saw her first—a woman standing at the edge of our yard, right where the fog began. She wasn't moving, just standing there, facing our house. I called for Dad, but by the time he came, she was gone, swallowed back into the gray like she'd never existed.

"You imagined it," he said, but his hands were shaking when he nailed the last board over the window.

That night, I heard my name. Not shouted, not screamed—just spoken, soft and familiar, like someone who loved me was calling me to dinner. I lay frozen in bed, listening to it drift through the walls, through the boarded windows, until Mom came in and held me until morning.

We lasted eleven days like that, rationing canned food, listening to the fog breathe against our house. On the twelfth day, Dad said we couldn't stay any longer. We were nearly out of food, and the water had started tasting strange, like it was absorbing the grayness too.

We left at dawn, the three of us holding hands, walking into a fog so thick I couldn't see my own feet. Dad led us by memory alone, counting steps to the Hendersons' house, then the Miller's, then the old church on the corner. The voices came again, closer now, calling each of our names in turns, trying to pull us apart. I felt Mom's grip tighten like a vice.

We walked for what felt like hours, though Dad said later it had only been twenty minutes. Then, all at once, the gray began to thin. Sunlight broke through in fractured beams, and I saw the shape of the water tower on Route 9, the one that marked the edge of town.

We didn't look back. We didn't stop until we reached the next town over, where people stared at us like we were ghosts ourselves, covered in a strange residue that clung to our clothes for days after.

They said the fog lifted a week later, revealing a town that looked untouched—houses standing, cars parked, nothing disturbed. But no one ever went back to live there. The government fenced it off, called it an environmental hazard, gave it a name full of syllables that meant nothing.

Sometimes I still hear my name in the quiet moments, in the gray hush before sleep takes me. I never answer.

The fog came down so fast I almost missed the turn. One minute the sky was that pale, washed-out blue of early autumn, and the next, the world was swallowed in white. I slowed the car, my hands tightening on the wheel as the road disappeared beneath the hood.

I had not been back to this town in seventeen years. Seventeen years since I left for college with a suitcase and a promise to my mother that I would visit more often. I had not visited more often. I had visited three times, and now I was returning for the last thing she would ever need from me.

The fog pressed against the windows like something alive. I could not see the ditches on either side of the road, and the yellow line became the only proof that the world still existed beyond my headlights. I thought of turning around, of finding a motel in the next town over, of waiting until the weather cleared. But there was nothing waiting for me in the next town. There was nothing waiting for me at all, except the house, and the boxes, and the quiet work of closing a life.

I passed the old Walker farm without seeing it. I knew it by the curve of the road, by the place where the pavement dipped and the trees drew back. The barn had burned down when I was eleven, and I had cried for weeks over a cat named Buttons who had not, in the end, been inside. My mother had held me in the kitchen and said, "Some things are gone before you can save them, but you keep loving them anyway. That's the trick."

The fog seemed to thicken at the memory, or perhaps it was simply the road climbing into the hills. I turned on the radio, but there was only static, only a soft hiss that sounded like breathing. I turned it off. The silence was worse.

Then, ahead of me, a shape moved through the white.

I slowed. A woman was walking along the shoulder of the road, her head bare, her coat the color of dried leaves. She did not turn as my car approached, and I pulled alongside her, rolling down my window. The air that came in was cold and tasted, faintly, of smoke and apples.

"Are you all right?" I called. "Do you need a ride?"

She turned then, and my heart stuttered in my chest. She had my mother's face. Not exactly — the nose was wrong, the eyes were set differently — but the shape of her jaw, the way her mouth was preparing to speak, those were my mother's. She looked at me with an expression I could not read.

"You're going to miss the turn," she said.

"I'm sorry?"

"The road forks ahead. You're going to miss the turn to the house." She pointed, and I saw, in the fog, a faint shadow that might have been a road sign. "Don't miss it. She'll be waiting."

I opened my mouth to ask who she meant, but when I looked again, the shoulder of the road was empty. The fog closed over the place where she had stood, smooth and undisturbed, as if no one had ever walked there.

I drove on. The road did, in fact, fork, and I almost took the left branch out of habit, out of the memory of a different trip, a different autumn. But I saw the sign — faded, half-hidden by a growth of ivy — and I turned right.

The house appeared as if the fog had been keeping it for me. The porch light was on, though no one had lived there for months. I sat in the car for a long moment, watching the light flicker in the white air. Then I turned off the engine, and the quiet that came down around me was the quiet of a held breath.

I walked up the steps. The door opened before I could find the key.

The house was warm inside, and it smelled of apples, and somewhere, very softly, a woman was humming a song I had not heard since I was seven years old.

I stepped inside. The fog closed behind me, gentle as a held hand.

# The Ring on Maple Street

You almost didn't see it. You were walking home from work, the same route you'd taken a thousand times, eyes half-focused on your phone, when something caught the late afternoon light and threw it back at you like a tiny mirror. You stopped, tilted your head, and there it was—a gold ring sitting right in the middle of the sidewalk on Maple Street, as if someone had placed it there on purpose.

You picked it up. It was heavier than you expected, warm despite the November chill, and engraved on the inside with words in a language you didn't recognize. The band was smooth, almost liquid to the touch, and it fit your right ring finger perfectly. Too perfectly. Like it had been made for you.

You slipped it into your pocket and kept walking.

That night, you dreamed of a woman standing at the edge of a cliff overlooking an ocean you'd never seen. She turned to face you, and her eyes were the color of storm clouds. "You found it," she said, not as a question but as a confirmation. "Now you'll see what I saw."

You woke up at 3:17 a.m. with your heart hammering and the ring glowing faintly on your nightstand. You told yourself it was a trick of the streetlight through the curtains. You went back to sleep.

The next morning, the world looked different. Not dramatically—nothing so crude as colors being brighter or sounds being sharper. It was subtler than that. You could see the weight people carried. Your neighbor, Mrs. Huang, who always smiled and waved from her garden, had a shimmering gray haze around her shoulders, and you *knew*—without knowing how—that she was grieving. Her sister had died three days ago. You hadn't heard. You shouldn't have known.

At work, your coworker Derek laughed at something on his phone, but the haze around him was the color of rust, and you understood he was terrified of losing his job. Your boss, Linda, moved through the office with a golden aura so bright it almost hurt to look at—she'd just received news she was going to be a grandmother.

You took the ring off at lunch. The world snapped back to its ordinary flatness. You put it on again, and the auras returned, pulsing and layered and achingly honest.

Over the following days, you tested it. You walked through the park and saw a teenager sitting alone on a bench, surrounded by a haze so dark and tangled that you sat down beside him. You didn't mention the ring. You just talked. He told you things he said he'd never told anyone. When you stood to leave, the darkness had thinned, just slightly, and he looked at you with wet eyes and said, "Thanks. I don't know why I told you all that."

You didn't either. But you suspected the ring had something to do with it—not because it gave you power, but because it gave you *sight*, and sight made you brave enough to sit down.

The woman from your dream appeared again a week later. This time, she stood in your kitchen, translucent as morning fog. "The ring was mine," she said. "I made it after I lost my daughter. I needed to understand people—their pain, their joy—so I wouldn't feel so alone. It worked. But it also broke me, because I could never turn it off."

She looked at you with those storm-cloud eyes. "You're stronger than I was. But the ring will ask a price. It always does."

You wanted to ask what price. She was already gone.

You found out three weeks later. You were standing in a hospital waiting room, the ring on your finger, surrounded by dozens of people whose grief and fear and hope crashed over you like waves. It was overwhelming—a cacophony of human feeling so intense that your vision blurred and your knees buckled. A nurse caught you. "Are you alright?" she asked.

You looked at the ring. You understood the price now. To see everyone's truth meant carrying it, too.

That evening, you walked back to Maple Street. You knelt down in the exact spot where you'd found the ring, pressed it into the concrete seam between two sidewalk squares, and whispered, "Find someone stronger than me."

You stood up, bare-handed, and the world looked ordinary again. But you carried something with you that the ring had taught you before it asked too much: every single person you passed was fighting something invisible, and the bravest thing you could do—ring or no ring—was simply to sit down beside them.

You spotted it between a gum stain and a cigarette butt—a gold band, no fancier than a wedding ring, but lighter, with no engraving. You picked it up. It was warm, as if someone had just taken it off. You slipped it onto your right index finger because it was too loose for your ring finger, and it fit there perfectly. You meant to post about it in the neighborhood group later, but somehow you never got around to it.

The first time it happened was at the grocery store. You bumped carts with a woman in the produce aisle. She apologized, and when her fingers brushed yours, you didn’t just see her face. You saw a memory: her kitchen, her husband, herself. The memory was about you. Three weeks ago, you had cut in front of her at the checkout, and she was replaying it, silently calling you a selfish jerk. You blinked. She smiled and walked on.

You tested it. You shook hands with a colleague. The moment skin met skin, you saw a memory of him at an office party, mimicking your voice, making fun of your presentation. You laughed along with him later, but your stomach was cold.

The ring, you realized, showed you what people really thought of you when they were alone. Not their words. Their memory-truth.

You told yourself to stop, but you couldn’t. It became an addiction. You brushed your brother’s shoulder and saw a memory of him telling your mother that you had never grown up, that you would always be the burden. You let your best friend hug you and saw her crying in her car after you forgot her birthday, wondering if you actually cared about anyone except yourself. You wanted to smash the ring with a hammer, but you didn’t. You needed to know.

Then came the night you touched your boyfriend’s hand across the dinner table. Maybe you shouldn’t have. But you did. You saw a memory: him sitting in the dark, phone in hand, looking at old photos. Not of you. Of his ex. In the memory he was whispering, “I should never have left her.” You watched it pass, and then you looked at him, and he was asking if you wanted more wine. You said yes, and you didn’t touch him again for the rest of the night.

You lay awake, and the ring seemed heavier. Every touch had become a minefield. Every handshake a hidden verdict. You wanted to take the ring off, but you were afraid. What if the memories weren’t the worst part? What if the worst part was knowing you couldn’t argue with them? They weren’t accusations from other people. They were the secret highlights of other people’s real feelings.

Near dawn, you got up. You went to the kitchen for water. Your boyfriend was asleep on the couch, because he’d let you have the bed. You looked at your own hand, the gold band glinting in the fridge light, and you thought: Who put this ring here? What kind of power shows only the moments that hurt? Maybe there were other memories too—ones where he smiled at you, where your friend laughed with you, where your brother was proud. But the ring always chose the wound. Maybe that was the real magic: not truth, but poison. It didn’t show you what people thought. It showed you what your fear wanted you to believe.

You took it off. It slid easily, leaving a pale dent in your finger. You opened the window and held it over the sill for a long time. Then you closed your fingers around it and put it in the pocket of your coat. Not to wear. To remind yourself.

When your boyfriend woke up, you touched his shoulder. No memory. Just the warmth of his skin. He asked why you were crying. You said, “I don’t know.” But you did know.

Later that afternoon, you walked the same sidewalk. The gum stain was still there. The cigarette butt. This time, you didn’t look down.

You never look down when you walk. You look ahead, at traffic lights, at your phone, at the cracks in the buildings. But this morning the rain has just stopped, the sidewalk on 5th is slick and reflecting the sky, and a glint catches your eye that doesn't belong.

It is a gold ring. Plain, heavy, without any inscription. It sits half in a puddle near the curb, as if someone dropped it without noticing. You crouch. You rub it dry on the sleeve of your jacket and slip it into your pocket, telling yourself you will take it to the lost and found at the corner store. You don't.

At the crosswalk you wait for the light. You are still holding the ring between your thumb and forefinger inside your pocket, turning it over. A bus hisses past and sprays water, a kid on a scooter nearly clips you, and without thinking you slide the ring onto your right middle finger. It fits perfectly, which is the second strange thing. You never wear rings because nothing ever fits right.

The light turns green. You step off the curb and —

— you are back on the curb. The light is red again. The bus is approaching again. The kid on the scooter is behind you again, saying "excuse me" in the same exact tone.

You stumble. Your heart does a strange double beat. You look down at the ring. It is cold now. Ice cold.

You step off again, more cautiously. No rewind. You cross safely.

You spend the next block testing it. You take the ring off, put it back on, take it off again. Nothing. You try to figure out the trigger. Was it fear? You had felt a flash of panic just before you stepped out, a certainty that the bus was too close.

At the coffee shop, you find out. You are waiting in line and you put the ring back on while you reach for your wallet. The barista calls out an order, a man in front of you trips, his hot coffee tilting toward you, and your stomach lurches —

— and you are three seconds back, standing a foot to the left, the man still upright, his coffee still in his hand. This time you step aside. He stumbles, but the coffee spills harmlessly on the floor.

It rewinds. About three to five seconds, whenever you feel a sharp jolt of dread or regret, the moment you wish you could take back. The ring gives it back.

For an hour, it feels like a miracle. You use it to not miss your train. To not say the awkward thing to your coworker. Each time, that cold pulse, that little skip backwards, that second chance.

Then at lunch, you use it to take back a conversation. Your friend Mara tells you she is moving away next month, and your face does something before you can control it — disappointment, maybe hurt — and you feel her see it. You feel the regret spike, and the ring pulls you back. You try again. You smile better, you say, "That's amazing, I'm so happy for you." It works. She doesn't notice the stutter in time. But you remember both versions. You remember your first, honest face, and your second, rehearsed one. They sit on top of each other in your mind like double-exposed photos.

That is when you understand the cost. The world rewinds, but you don't. You carry every failed version with you.

You wear the ring the rest of the afternoon and it happens again and again, small rewinds you don't even mean to trigger, until by five o'clock your head aches with memories of things that, for everyone else, never happened. You remember tripping four times on the same stair, saying the wrong thing three times in the same meeting. The day feels crowded, heavy, too full.

On your way home, you stop at the same puddle on 5th. The imprint of where the ring sat is still there, a perfect circle in the grime.

You take the ring off. It is warm again in your palm, waiting. You understand now why it was left there. Someone else got tired of carrying all their almosts.

You place it back on the sidewalk, exactly where you found it, half in the puddle. You don't look back as you walk away, because you know if you do, you might wish to take it back. And it would let you.
