samples.MiMo-V2.5-Pro_story:
I woke up to the familiar weight of my quilt and the soft grey light of a Tuesday morning filtering through the blinds. Everything was as it should be: the rumpled sheets, the glass of water on the nightstand, the faint smell of coffee already brewing from the timer I’d set. I stretched, my joints popping in a way that felt satisfyingly normal. Then I swung my legs out of bed, and my bare feet met the cold wooden floor with a soft *thump*.

Or rather, they should have.

There was no *thump*. There was no sound at all.

I froze, mid-stretch. The world outside my window was a silent film. A car slid down the street, its tires making no whisper on the asphalt. A dog barked in the distance, its mouth opening and closing in a frantic pantomime, but the bark never reached me. I could see the rustle of leaves in the wind, but the gentle shushing was absent. The only sound in the universe was the frantic, hammering beat of my own heart, a drum in a vacuum.

Panic, cold and sharp, lanced through me. I stumbled to the bathroom, my footsteps eerily silent. I turned on the faucet. Water gushed out in a perfect, shimmering arc, but it hit the porcelain sink with the silence of a falling feather. I clapped my hands in front of my face. I saw the motion, felt the sting, but the *clap* was stolen from the air. I was living in a world muted, a planet on pause.

Dressed in a daze, I walked outside. The neighborhood was a tableau of eerie normalcy. Mrs. Henderson was pruning her roses, her shears opening and closing on the stems. Mr. Garcia was washing his car, sponge moving in soapy circles. They moved with purpose, their faces calm. But when Mrs. Henderson’s shears snipped a dead bloom, there was no *snick*. When Mr. Garcia’s hose sprayed the driveway, there was no *hiss*. We were all actors in a play where the sound designer had quit.

I walked to the town square, a growing knot of dread in my stomach. There, a small crowd had gathered around the old clock tower. They weren’t panicking. They were just… looking. At each other, at the silent world, their expressions a mixture of confusion and a strange, shared resignation. I saw my friend, Lena. Her lips moved, forming my name. I saw the shape of it, but heard nothing. I shook my head, pointing to my ears. She nodded, a sad understanding in her eyes. She pointed to her own throat, then made a sweeping gesture at the silent world. We were all in the same soundless boat.

Days bled into a week. We adapted, as humans do. We communicated with exaggerated gestures, written notes, and the frantic tapping of phone screens. The initial terror subsided into a profound, aching loneliness. The silence wasn’t just an absence; it was a presence, a thick, woolen blanket smothering the world. I missed the mundane symphony: the refrigerator’s hum, the rustle of a newspaper, the simple, comforting sound of another person breathing in the same room. I started to forget what voices sounded like, including my own.

Then, one evening, sitting on my porch watching the silent sunset paint the sky, I felt it. A vibration. Not in my ears, but in my bones, in the wooden planks beneath me. It was rhythmic, deep, and utterly alien. I looked around. Others on the street were stopping, placing hands on lampposts, on the hoods of silent cars. They felt it too. The vibration grew, a subsonic pulse that seemed to emanate from the very core of the earth.

It wasn't a return of sound. It was something else. As the pulse intensified, I didn't *hear* it, but I *understood* it. It was a feeling, a raw, primal emotion that bypassed my ears and flooded my mind: a vast, ancient loneliness. It was the loneliness of deep space, of silent stars, of a universe that had never known a voice. It was the loneliness of the planet itself, finally expressing its own mute existence.

And in that shared, silent vibration, something shifted. I looked at Lena, who was standing across the street, her hand on a tree trunk. Our eyes met. I didn't need to hear her voice to know what she was feeling. The vibration connected us, a silent network of shared experience. The profound isolation cracked, not because sound returned, but because we realized we were not alone in the silence. We were all listening, together, to the same unheard song.

The world was still silent. The engines, the birds, the voices—all remained absent. But the oppressive loneliness was gone, replaced by a quiet, resonant connection. We had lost the sound of the world, but in its place, we had found a deeper way to listen to each other, and to the silent, vibrating heart of everything. I took a deep, soundless breath, and for the first time since I woke up, I felt a sense of peace. The silence was no longer an absence. It was simply the world’s new, and strangely profound, language.
samples.DeepSeek-V4-Flash_story:
You wake up from a daze. The first thing you see is the ceiling, familiar cracks running like a map. The room is exactly as it should be: alarm clock on the nightstand, shoes by the door, half-open blinds throwing stripes of sunlight across the blanket. You sit up slowly. Your head is heavy. You should hear something—the refrigerator’s low hum, the tick of the clock, the neighbor’s radio through the wall. But there is nothing. Not silence as in a library, but a deeper, thicker silence, as if the air itself has stopped vibrating.

You say, “Hello?” You feel your throat tighten. You feel the pulse of your vocal cords. But there is no sound. You clap your hands together, slap the mattress, knock your knuckles against the nightstand. The impact sends a sting up your arm, but your ears receive nothing.

Panic crawls up your spine. You stand, walk to the window. Outside, the street looks normal. A blue sedan sits at the stop sign. A woman pushes a stroller. A dog lifts its leg against a fire hydrant. The leaves on the maple tree move as if in a breeze, but perhaps you do not hear the rustle. You try to remember what sound was like. You can’t. It’s like trying to remember a color you’ve only seen in a dream.

You open the front door and step outside. The air is warm. The woman with the stroller passes by; her lips move, and she glances at you and smiles, but the words are invisible. You shout, “What happened?” You feel the roar in your chest, the hot push of breath from your lungs, but no one turns. The dog’s mouth opens in a bark, its body jerking, but the silence swallows it.

You walk to the corner. There is a construction site, workers swinging their arms, jackhammers rising and falling. The man at the stoplight wears earbuds, nodding to a beat you can’t hear. A plane crosses the sky, a silver speck dragging nothing behind it. You realize the world is still making sound. The sound is still there. It’s you who is broken.

You sit down on the curb. A child on a bicycle nearly runs into you, then swerves, mouth opening in an apology. You can’t feel the apology. You put your hands over your ears, but that changes nothing. Inside your head, there is the same muffled void. No ringing, no humming. Just emptiness.

The daze, you remember now. The dizziness that had been building all week. The loud pop in your left ear that morning, and the warmth running down your neck. The doctor’s name on the card in your pocket. You pull it out: audiologist. There is an appointment tomorrow. You had forgotten. You had hoped it was a dream.

You look at the card, then at the street. Everything is as it should be. Cars, people, light. And there is only one thing missing. But maybe that’s enough to make a world strange. You close your eyes. You feel the curb vibrating slightly—a truck somewhere, rumbling through the pavement. You press your palms flat. The vibration travels up your arms and into your chest, a low pulse that sings through bone instead of air.

You stand up. The child is still watching you. You nod, and he pedals away. You put the card back in your pocket. You walk home, feeling the thump of your own footsteps through the soles of your shoes. It isn’t sound. But it’s something. It’s a rhythm. Maybe you can learn to listen that way.

The next day, you will go to the audiologist. You will see her lips move, and you will read the words: “Can you hear me?” You will shake your head. She will nod and smile, and then she will write on a piece of paper: “We’ll work with this.” You will feel the paper in your hand, and the faint trembling of the pen lines against your fingertips.

But for now, you open your front door, step back into the silent room. You stop at the threshold and look back. The neighborhood glows under the late-afternoon sun. A woman laughs on her porch, head thrown back, but you don’t hear her. You don’t need to. You see her shoulders shake, her hand flat against her chest, and you know the shape of laughter.

You close the door. The silence wraps around you like a blanket. It’s not empty anymore. It’s full of things you can feel.
samples.Muse-Spark-1.2-Contributor_story:
You wake up from a daze on your living room floor, afternoon light cutting through the blinds in clean bars across the carpet. For a second you just lie there, cheek against the rug. Everything is as it should be. Your coffee mug is still on the table where you left it, a thin skin forming on the surface. The front door is closed, locked just the way you always lock it. 

There's only one thing missing. 

There is no sound, anywhere.

You notice it slowly, as an absence that grows heavier the longer you listen. Not the hum of the refrigerator. Your building sits two blocks from the highway, and there has never been a moment in three years when you couldn't hear a faint rush of traffic. Now there is nothing. Not even the sound of an engine in the distance.

You sit up too fast and your head swims. You slap your ears, hard, thinking they must have popped. You yawn wide to equalize the pressure the way you do on airplanes. You feel your jaw click, but no pop, no ring, no relief. Just the same perfect, heavy silence.

You try to speak. Your mouth opens, your throat moves, you feel the vibration in your chest as you say 'Hello?' But you hear nothing. Not even the inside of your own voice. Panic climbs up the back of your neck.

You stumble to the kitchen and turn on the faucet. Water arcs out, clear and normal, splashing into the sink and beading on the steel. You thrust your hand under it; it is cold and real, but it makes no sound at all.

Your phone is on the counter. You pick it up and press play on a voicemail from Maya, pressing the speaker to your ear until it hurts. Her mouth moves in the little waveform animation, but no voice comes out. You turn the volume all the way up. Nothing.

You need to get out to check if it's you or the world.

You unlock the front door — the deadbolt slides back silently — and step into the hallway. Mrs. Chen from 3B is walking her little dog down the stairs, just as she does every evening. Her mouth is open, laughing, her dog is barking, you can see its jaws working and its whole body shaking with each yap. You can see the jangle of her keys.

She waves at you. You wave back, feeling like a mime. You try to shout and you see her face falter. She is saying something you cannot hear. You shake your head, point at your ears, shrug helplessly. She nods slowly, touches her own ears, mouths 'Are you okay?' You nod even though you are not.

Outside, the street should be chaos. It is five o'clock. Buses should be hissing, cars honking, teenagers shouting outside the convenience store. Instead the world is a silent film. You watch a bus roll past, massive and close, its tires kicking up a piece of newspaper. You see the newspaper flutter, but you don't hear its engine, not even the distant whine you always complained about. A pigeon takes off right beside your foot and you flinch, but its wings make no rush of air.

You sit down hard on the curb because your legs will not hold you. You close your eyes and try to breathe. And in that moment, with your eyes shut, you finally hear something.

Not with your ears. Behind them.

A faint, high note, like a television left on in another room. It grows, just a little, just enough for you to follow it inward, away from the street, away from the panic.

You remember the daze. You remember reaching for painkillers for your headache, taking them with cold coffee, lying down on the floor because the room swam and the light was too bright.

Your eyes snap open. The street is still silent. Mrs. Chen is standing at a distance now, holding her phone to her ear, obviously calling someone for you, her mouth forming earnest, silent words.

You focus on that thin, high note again. You follow it. You pull at it.

And then, like a needle dropping onto vinyl, sound crashes back.

A car horn blares and you jolt. The dog barks, sharp and sudden. Mrs. Chen's voice, distant but clear, says, '—is on his way, sweetheart, just stay right there.'

You can hear your own breath, ragged and loud.

The world had not gone silent. You had. For a few terrifying minutes you had slipped just out of reach, and now you are back. You sit on the curb, shaking, listening to the terrible, beautiful roar of the ordinary engine in the distance, and you do not want it to ever stop again.
samples.Gemini-3.6-Flash_story:
You wake up from a daze. Everything is as it should be. The warm afternoon sun filters through the blinds, casting slatted golden light across the familiar mess of your living room. The half-empty mug of coffee sits on the side table; your dog’s bed rests by the cold fireplace; the dust motes drift lazily through the air. There’s only one thing missing. 

There’s no sound, anywhere, not even the sound of an engine in the distance.

At first, you assume your ears are blocked. You swallow hard, yawn, and press the heels of your palms against your ears, expecting that familiar pop of pressure equalization. Nothing happens. You sit up on the couch, the leather creaking beneath your weight—or at least, it should be creaking. You hear no rustle of fabric, no soft thud of your feet striking the hardwood floor.

You clap your hands together violently. You feel the sharp sting of skin meeting skin, the physical vibration traveling up your wrists, but the air around you remains utterly dead. Panic, quiet and heavy, begins to settle in your chest.

You rush to the kitchen. The refrigerator compressor usually hums with a low, reassuring thrum, but when you lay your hand against its cool side, though you feel the faint vibration of the motor working within, no noise reaches your ears. You open the cabinet, grab a ceramic plate, and let it fall. It shatters against the tile floor into a dozen sharp shards. The destruction is instant, dramatic, and entirely mute.

It isn't a problem with your hearing. You tap your own collarbone, feel your pulse thudding in your throat, and bite your lip until it hurts. The physical sensations are intact. Sound itself has simply vanished from the universe.

You pull open the front door and step outside onto the porch.

The street looks entirely mundane, yet horrific in its quietude. High above, the branches of the old oak tree sway in a stiff breeze, but there is no rustle of leaves, no sigh of the wind through the power lines. Across the street, Mrs. Gable’s retriever is at the fence, its mouth wide, throat working in frantic, soundless barks. Down the road, a silver sedan sits idling at the intersection. You can see pale heat rising from its exhaust pipe, but the deep rumble of its engine is completely absent.

You step off the porch and hurry down the driveway, your breath coming fast. You scream—or try to. You force air through your larynx, feeling your vocal cords strain and vibrate, but no sound emerges into the atmosphere. It is as if the air itself has lost the capacity to carry a wave.

Across the lawn, your neighbor, Marcus, stands near his mailbox. He is staring up at the sky, his face pale, hands trembling.

When he notices you, he rushes over. His lips move rapidly, his hands gesticulating frantically as he tries to speak. You read the shape of his mouth: *What happened? Can you hear me?*

You shake your head, pointing to your mouth and then to your ears, opening your hands in a gesture of shared powerlessness. Marcus drops his arms to his sides. A look of profound, terrifying isolation washes over his face, mirroring the cold knot tightening in your own stomach.

Together, you both turn to look down the street. Other neighbors are stepping out of their houses now. They emerge like ghosts from their front doors, looking around in bewildered terror, checking their phones, gesturing silently at one another across immaculate green lawns. Nobody can hear anything. The entire neighborhood—perhaps the entire world—has been plunged into an absolute vacuum of stillness.

You look up at the sky. A jet glides high overhead, leaving a brilliant white contrail against the blue expanse. Usually, its thunderous roar would follow seconds later, shaking the windows. Now, it slides across the atmosphere in total, eerie silence, like a needle dragging across a silent record.

You sit down on the curb next to Marcus. Without the endless background hum of modern life—the traffic, the wind, the steady beat of living—the world feels fragile, stripped down to raw geometry and light. You close your eyes, feeling the warmth of the sun on your skin and the steady, silent rhythm of your heart, waiting to see what happens next in a universe that has forgotten how to speak.
samples.Kimi-K3_story:
**The Quiet**

You surface from the dream the way a swimmer surfaces from deep water — slowly, then all at once. The room is exactly as you left it. Morning light leans through the blinds. The clock on the nightstand blinks its red numbers. The bed is warm, the ceiling is cracked in the same familiar place, and the world is patiently waiting for you to join it.

There is only one thing missing. You can't name it at first. You lie there, staring at the ceiling, trying to identify the wrongness, and then you realize: there is no sound. None. Not the refrigerator's hum, not the neighbor's dog, not the distant grinding of engines on the highway that has always been the thin bass line of your mornings.

You clap your hands. Nothing. You snap your fingers in front of your face and watch them move, a motion divorced from its consequence. You drag your palm across the sheet and feel the whisper of fabric without hearing it.

In the bathroom, you turn the faucet and watch water strike the porcelain like a silent film. The television shows a news anchor mouthing urgently, and even when you press your thumb against the volume icon and slide it to its limit, her words arrive only as breath. You call your sister. The call connects. Her face appears on the screen, mouth moving, eyes wide. She already knows. Her mouth shapes the same question you've been asking: *Can you hear me?*

You step outside, and the stillness presses against your ears like deep water. A car glides down the street, tires rolling over gravel in perfect silence. A screen door slams — you watch it bounce against its frame — and the blow lands nowhere. Birds hop along the power line, beaks opening and closing on songs you have to imagine.

Downtown, people spill out of shops and stand in clusters on the sidewalk, a whole town performing pantomime. A man in a suit clamps his hands over his ears as if that could change anything. A woman holds her phone up to the crowd, playing something, and everyone leans in anyway, hungry for the idea of sound. Somewhere a dog barks without end, its chest heaving with voiceless effort. You look up and watch a plane cross the sky, leaving behind a white seam of cloud, making no more noise than the cloud itself.

The days that follow have a strange shape. The world does not end; it only turns down. People learn to carry notepads. Traffic lights are repainted and re-timed, because horns no longer exist. Schools teach children to sign with hands and to read the movement of mouths. You learn, too. You learn that a knock on the door is a vibration you feel through the floor if you stand barefoot. You learn that laughter still exists — it lives in the shake of shoulders, in the crinkling around eyes. You learn that a scream is a face, not a noise, and that panic is a language all its own, flung in head-turns and colliding gestures.

You list what you miss: rain on the roof, your mother's voice, the kettle's rising wail, the way a crowded café used to shimmer with overlapping talk. But you also find what the silence has been hiding. Without the engine of the world running all day, you notice things you never heard before: the pulse of your own blood pressed against a pillow, the faint ring inside your skull that might be your brain keeping itself company. Silence, it turns out, has texture. It has weather. It moves through a room like someone you have just begun to understand.

Months later, you stand on the beach at dusk with hundreds of others. It has become a custom, this wordless gathering, everyone facing the water together. The waves come in and come in, and you press one hand flat against your chest and feel their rhythm arrive there, vibration enough. A gull wheels overhead, crying out into the emptiness, and you watch it and find you are smiling.

Then, faintly — so faintly it may be only hope wearing a disguise — a ringing trembles inside your ear. A single, pure thread, like tinnitus learning to become a song. Around you, people touch their ears. Mouths open. A child grabs her mother's sleeve and points upward, and the mother nods, tears shining, and her lips shape a word you already know.

*Listen.*

The gull cries again, and this time, almost, you hear it.
samples.GPT-5.6-Luna_story:
# The Silence

I woke with my cheek pressed against the kitchen table.

For a few seconds, I didn't move. Sunlight spilled through the window in a familiar golden rectangle, warming the wooden floor. The refrigerator stood where it always stood. The clock above the sink showed 8:17. A half-empty mug of coffee sat beside my hand.

Everything was as it should be.

Except there was no sound.

At first, I thought I had gone deaf.

I slapped the table.

Nothing.

I shouted, "Hello?"

My voice vanished the moment it left my mouth. I could feel the vibration in my throat, but there was no echo, no breathy whisper, nothing.

I ran to the front door and threw it open.

The street looked normal. Mrs. Alvarez's blue car was parked beneath the elm tree. A cyclist stood frozen at the intersection, one foot on the ground. Across the road, a dog stared at a mailbox with its mouth open.

I could see the world moving.

I simply couldn't hear it.

A truck rolled past the end of the street. Its tires turned. Its exhaust trembled in the air.

No engine.

I rushed outside.

My phone said 8:18. I called my brother.

The screen showed that it was ringing.

There was no ringing.

I tried again.

Nothing.

Then a message appeared.

**Where are you?**

I typed back:

**Home. Can you hear anything?**

Three dots appeared.

Then disappeared.

Another message came.

**No.**

I stared at the word.

For the first time, I felt afraid.

I spent the next hour walking through town, searching for an explanation. People had come out of their houses, just like me. They moved their mouths, waved their arms, honked car horns that made no noise. Some were crying. Others were laughing hysterically.

At the town square, a crowd had gathered around the fountain.

The water was falling.

Silently.

That was when I noticed something strange.

A little girl was standing at the edge of the fountain, holding a red balloon.

She wasn't crying. She wasn't frightened.

She was listening.

Or trying to.

I walked toward her and knelt.

"Do you know what's happening?"

She shook her head.

Then she pointed upward.

I looked.

The sky was perfectly clear.

Nothing.

She pointed again, more urgently.

Then I noticed it: a tiny ripple moving through the clouds.

It spread across the blue like a stone dropped into invisible water.

Every person in the square looked up.

The ripple reached the horizon.

And suddenly, the world made a sound.

Not a sound exactly.

A feeling.

The pavement trembled beneath my shoes.

Everyone staggered.

Then the silence returned.

The little girl grabbed my sleeve and pointed toward the clock tower.

I followed her gaze.

The clock had stopped at 8:17.

My phone said 9:03.

I looked at the girl.

She whispered something.

This time, I heard it.

"Again."

The clock hand moved.

One minute.

8:18.

And every sound returned at once.

The fountain roared. Cars screamed their tires against pavement. Birds exploded into song. People shouted. Somewhere, an alarm blared. The sheer noise knocked the breath from my lungs.

I covered my ears.

Around me, people laughed and cried in equal measure.

Then I heard my phone ring.

My brother.

I answered.

"Where are you?" he asked.

"I'm in the square."

There was a pause.

"How long were you asleep?"

I frowned.

"What?"

"You called me at 8:17," he said. "You were talking nonsense. You kept saying everything was silent."

I looked toward the clock.

It was still moving.

"What time is it?"

"9:04."

I stared at the girl with the red balloon.

She was gone.

In her place, lying on the fountain's edge, was a small red balloon.

I picked it up.

Something was written on it in black ink.

**NEXT TIME, DON'T WAKE UP.**

I dropped it.

The balloon rose slowly into the bright morning sky.

And somewhere above the town, beyond the clouds, I heard a clock begin to tick backward.
samples.Claude-Sonnet-5-High_story:
I woke up with my cheek pressed against cold linoleum, the kind of cold that seeps into your bones before your brain even catches up to where you are. My kitchen. I was in my kitchen, and the morning light was slanting through the blinds exactly the way it always did at this hour, cutting the room into stripes of gold and shadow.

I sat up slowly, waiting for the ache in my head to announce itself, but there was nothing—just a strange, cottony blankness where a headache should have been. I must have fainted. Low blood sugar, maybe. I hadn't eaten since yesterday.

The refrigerator hummed. No—it didn't. I stared at it, waiting to hear that familiar low drone, the one I'd complained about a hundred times because it kept me up at night. Nothing. I walked over and pressed my palm against the side of it. It was cold, running, the compressor light blinking steady and orange. But silent.

I told myself it was my ears. Maybe I'd hit my head when I fell. I clapped my hands together, hard, right next to my face.

Nothing.

Not a clap, not a sting, not even the small satisfaction of my palms meeting. I did it again, harder, until my hands were red, and the silence sat there in the room with me like a held breath.

I went to the window. Outside, the world looked like a photograph of itself—cars parked along the curb, a bird frozen mid-hop on the telephone wire, leaves trembling slightly in a breeze I couldn't hear. Mrs. Alvarez next door was watering her plants, her mouth moving in what must have been a greeting to someone I couldn't see, her hose spraying a silver arc that made no sound when it hit the pavement.

I ran outside without shoes. The concrete was warm under my feet, at least I could feel that—so some part of the world still reached me. Mrs. Alvarez saw me and waved, said something, her lips shaping words that dissolved into nothing before they reached me. I said her name. I felt my throat move, my tongue press against my teeth, the vibration hum faintly against my collarbone, but no word emerged into the air. It died somewhere between my mouth and the world.

I ran into the street. A car was coming down the road, slow, unhurried, and I stood there and watched its tires roll over gravel that should have crunched, watched its engine that should have rumbled, watched the driver's radio bounce with a beat I couldn't hear even though I could see the dashboard lights pulse to it. The car passed within three feet of me and made no more sound than a held photograph.

I understood, then, standing barefoot in the middle of the street with the sun on my face and the whole hushed world moving around me like a silent film reel. It wasn't that sound had disappeared. It was that I had stepped out of whatever place sound lived in, slipped through some seam in the ordinary, and no one had noticed me go.

I don't know how long I stood there. Long enough to watch the day tilt from morning into afternoon, the shadows shortening and stretching again, all in perfect, dreadful silence. Long enough to accept that shouting would do nothing, that banging on doors would do nothing, that I could scream until my throat tore and the world would simply keep turning, indifferent, deaf to a life it no longer required to make noise.

Eventually I went back inside and sat at my kitchen table, in the stripe of golden light, and waited to see if the silence would ever end, or if I would simply learn, in time, to live inside it.
samples.MiniMax-M3_story:
You wake from a daze that has no edges, and for a moment the bedroom is exactly what it has always been. The morning light comes through the curtain in a soft, dusty stripe. The cup on the nightstand still holds the cold dregs of last night's tea. Your cat is a black comma on the duvet, her eyes half-mast, watching you with the calm expectation that breakfast is imminent.

You say her name. Your lips move.

Nothing comes.

You sit up. The cat does not flinch at your voice, does not flick her ear toward the sound of your hand against the sheet. You swing your legs to the floor and the boards do not creak beneath your feet. You walk down the hallway and your socks make no whisper against the wood. The front door opens without its usual sigh, and you step outside.

The street is dressed for Tuesday. A delivery van idles at the curb. A jogger lifts her knees past the corner. Two men stand outside the corner shop, one gesturing with a sandwich, the other nodding. Everything is as it should be, except for the one thing.

There is no sound.

You stand on the pavement and wait for it, the way you wait for the kettle to click. The world should be giving you something—a horn, a plane overhead, the huff of the jogger, the small clatter of coins on the shop counter. The van's engine ticks. A small bird takes off from a wire. None of it reaches you. The town is moving inside a glass bell jar, and you are inside with it.

You walk. You do not know where you are walking until you reach the park, where an old man is feeding pigeons from a paper bag. He looks up as you approach. He sees you. You see him see you. He extends the bag toward you in a small offering. You reach out and take a handful of the gritty seeds, and the crinkle of the paper between your fingers is a thing that happens in another country.

"I can hear you," the man says, or you think he says, because his mouth shapes the words and you have spent a lifetime knowing how mouths shape words. You cannot hear him. But he is speaking. And the pigeons rise anyway, in a soft explosion of wings, and he watches them with the kind of quiet joy that needs no noise.

You begin to understand, slowly, that you are not the only one who has woken into this. You pass a mother pushing a pram. The pram wheels do not rattle over the paving stones. She sings to the baby inside, and the baby smiles. Two teenagers sit on a wall sharing a set of earbuds, and they laugh at something on the screen, and you can see the laughter more clearly than you have ever seen laughter before—it lives in the lines around their eyes, the way they lean toward each other, the way one of them nudges the other with a shoulder.

By the time you reach the river, the sun has climbed higher and the town is the same town you have lived in all your life, except that every small ordinary noise has been borrowed by something else. You sit on the bench where you sat with your father, years ago, before he went into the hospital and never came out. You used to come here to listen to him. He was a quiet man, but you remember his voice especially. You have been holding it, you realize now, all this time. The sound of him. The shape of it. You thought you might lose it if you did not keep replaying it, the way he said your name, the way he cleared his throat before telling a story.

And now the world has gone quiet in a way that is almost merciful.

You sit with the river. The river is not silent. You can see it moving. You can see the light leaning on it, the way the current folds and unfolds over itself. A heron lifts off from the far bank and the air parts for it, and you watch, and you understand that there are other ways to be heard.

The cat will be hungry. The tea is cold. The day is long. But you sit a moment longer, in the country of the unlost, and you let the silence be the sound of him saying your name.

samples.gpt35_story: Once upon a time in a small town, there lived a young man named Jacob who had a passion for historical grand strategy games. He would spend hours playing these games, delving deep into the intricacies of managing civilizations and leading armies to victory. Jacob had always been fascinated by history, and these games allowed him to immerse himself in different eras and rewrite their fates. <newline>  <newline> One fateful day, Jacob had a particularly intense session with his favorite game. He played well into the night, conquering lands, forging alliances, and altering the course of history. Exhausted, he finally decided to call it a day and went to bed, excited to continue his conquests in the morning. <newline>  <newline> As the sun's first rays peered through Jacob's window, he begrudgingly opened his eyes. But as he looked around, something felt different. The room seemed unfamiliar, as if he had woken up in a different place and time altogether. He quickly realized that something was incredibly wrong. <newline>  <newline> Jacob rushed to his computer, only to find that his game was no longer on the screen. In its place was a strange interface displaying a map of the world, but it was unlike anything he had seen before. It was a map of a different era entirely, one that he had just played through the night before. <newline>  <newline> Confusion and excitement overwhelmed Jacob as he realized the gravity of the situation. He was the only one who knew that the timeline had changed; the world around him was oblivious to the historical events that had been altered. <newline>  <newline> Determined to set things right, Jacob embarked on a journey to mend the timeline he had inadvertently disrupted. Using his knowledge of history and the events he had manipulated in the game, he began strategizing to correct the course of time. <newline>  <newline> With each step, Jacob encountered new challenges and unexpected outcomes. He interacted with remarkable historical figures, many of whom were quite different from their in-game counterparts. Some were delighted to have his assistance, while others regarded him with suspicion, unsure of his true motives. <newline>  <newline> Days turned into weeks, and weeks turned into months, but Jacob persisted, relying on his expertise and adaptability. He soon found himself entangled in the intricate webs of political maneuvering, rivalries, and alliances. The decisions he made had consequences that rippled through the course of history. <newline>  <newline> Ultimately, after countless battles fought and treaties brokered, Jacob succeeded in restoring the timeline to its original state. The world, unaware of the alternate timeline that had once existed, continued its course as if nothing had ever happened. But for Jacob, the experience had been life-altering. He had witnessed firsthand the power of individual actions and the fragility of history. <newline>  <newline> From that day forward, Jacob viewed his passion for historical grand strategy games in a new light. It wasn't just a hobby anymore; it was a window into the past, an opportunity to learn from the past mistakes and triumphs of civilizations long gone. And though he knew he could never truly alter history, he understood the importance of appreciating and honoring the lessons it had to offer.
samples.MiMo-V2.5-Pro_story:
The first thing I noticed was the sunlight. It slanted through my blinds at the wrong angle, painting a stripe across my wall that was too golden, too autumnal for a late May morning. My head throbbed with the pleasant, hollow ache of a marathon gaming session. I’d spent the entire previous day, from dawn until the small hours, guiding the Kingdom of Aragon from a minor Mediterranean power to the undisputed master of the Mediterranean in *Europa Universalis IV*. My dynasty, the House of Montcada, had united Spain, conquered North Africa, and even snatched a personal union over a weakened France. It was my magnum opus.

I groaned, reaching for my phone to check the time. The lock screen image was wrong. It wasn’t my usual photo of my cat, but a detailed, painterly map of Europe. The borders were… familiar, yet alien. A massive, deep-blue blob dominated the Iberian Peninsula and southern France, labeled “The Crown of Aragon.” My stomach did a slow, cold flip.

Shaking my head, I dismissed it as a weird glitch. I stumbled to the kitchen, my mind still half in the 15th century. The news was on the small TV on the counter. The anchor was speaking in crisp, formal Spanish, but the chyron at the bottom read: “His Majesty Felipe VI Montcada Addresses the United Nations on Mediterranean Stability.”

Montcada.

My blood ran cold. I sank onto a stool, my toast forgotten. This wasn’t a glitch. I spent the next hour in a frantic, silent spiral. A quick search online confirmed it. The history I knew—the Habsburgs, the Bourbons, the Spanish Civil War, Franco—was gone. In its place was a timeline where the House of Montcada had ruled an unbroken, globe-spanning empire for over five hundred years. The American colonies had never rebelled, instead becoming a prosperous, autonomous commonwealth. The World Wars, as I knew them, had never happened. The 20th century was defined by a cold war between the Aragonese Empire and a resurgent, technocratic Qing China.

The changes were everywhere, woven into the fabric of reality. The architecture downtown had a distinct Mediterranean flair, all arched courtyards and tiled mosaics. The dominant language was a Catalan-Spanish hybrid. My own name, “Alex,” felt foreign; in this world, I was likely “Alejandro.” My parents, my friends—they all had lived their entire lives in this reality. To them, this was just the way things were.

The weight of it was suffocating. I was the sole possessor of a dead timeline. The billions of lives, the specific tragedies and triumphs of the 20th century I’d learned in school—the Holocaust, the Moon landing, the fall of the Berlin Wall—were now just… footnotes in a history that never was. Had I erased them? Or had I simply tuned into a different frequency?

I spent the day in a daze, walking through a city that was both mine and not. I saw a statue of “Carlos the Great,” my last game ruler, in the central plaza. I heard people casually discussing the “Imperial Diet” in Barcelona. Every confirmation was a small, sharp pain.

That evening, I sat back at my computer. The game was still open on the save file. “The Montcada Hegemony, 1821.” My perfect run. The cursor blinked patiently over the “Continue” button. My hand trembled.

Did I have a responsibility? Could I… fix it? Load an earlier save, make a different choice, and maybe restore the world I knew? But what did that mean for the people here? The billions of souls in this timeline, with their loves and losses, their own history? Was I willing to commit genocide on a cosmic scale to undo my own mistake?

Or was this not a mistake at all, but a discovery? Was every game, every story, every choice imagined, playing out in some parallel reality?

I closed the game without saving. I couldn’t be that god. Not again.

The next morning, the sunlight was still autumnal. The news still spoke of the Montcada Empire. I made my coffee, my hands steady now. The initial panic had subsided into a profound, lonely awe. I was a ghost from a forgotten world, a secret historian. I would live in this timeline, learn its songs, love its people. But I would carry the other one inside me, a silent testament to the fragile, beautiful, and utterly random nature of history. I was the only one who knew that the world was not inevitable, that it was, in fact, a story someone once played through to its very end.
samples.DeepSeek-V4-Flash_story:
You wake with the faint taste of energy drinks and stale victory. For a second, Monday morning is exactly as it should be: cracked ceiling, grey light, the muffled sound of a neighbor’s radio. Then the radio speaks in Greek.

You sit bolt upright. The voice is not a newsreader from the BBC. It is a man intoning, “And the Basileus will address the Synkletos today concerning the grain shipments from Egypt.” You freeze. Egypt? Grain shipments? The radio continues with a weather report: “Temperatures in the Exarchate of Africa . . .” You stumble to the window.

Outside, the skyline is wrong. The familiar glass towers are gone. In their place are domes and columns, ochre stone and red tile roofs. A giant bronze statue stands in the square—not of Nelson, but of a soldier in lamellar armor. The street sign reads “Avenue of the Resurrected Kingdom.” Your mouth goes dry.

You remember the game. Fourteen hours of Europa Universalis, maybe more. You had chosen Byzantium, the broken purple shard, in 1444. You had done everything right—or wrong—depending on which history you believed. You allied with the Serbs, exploited the Ottoman civil war, crossed the Bosporus before the Turks could. You took Gallipoli, then Bursa, then Adrianople. Constantinople never fell; it expanded. You pushed into Anatolia, burned the Sultanate’s banners, and saved Constantine XI’s crown. You played until the clock struck 1821, and by then, the world map belonged to the Roman Empire: all of the Mediterranean, the Black Sea, and the coasts of Gaul, Britannia, everywhere.

You had laughed at the “Perfect Roman Run” achievement. Now you are not laughing.

You grab your phone. It’s not your phone—same interface, but apps named “Misthios” and “Themata” and “Civil Service of the Universal Empire.” The date is the same: the year, month, day. But the “historical” section of your news feed says: “Today in history: Constantinople saved from Ottoman siege, 1453.” You scroll. There are no World Wars. There is no United Nations. Instead an “Imperial Federation” brokers peace. The map in your pocket atlas shows a single massive polity around the Mediterranean, with colonies named “New Athens” and “Roman California.”

You feel a headache building. You know the old timeline. You were born in a world of nation-states, of small and large countries, of a different history. Now everyone else lives as if this has always been true. The coffee shop on the corner is now a thermopolium. You order a flat white, but the barista raises an eyebrow and says, “You mean a latte, strategos?”

You take it outside. On a newsstand, a paperback titled *The Fall of the Ottoman Myth: A Corrected History* catches your eye. A sticker on the cover says “Approved by the Imperial Censor.” You flip to the back. The timeline ends with a note: “The Roman Empire continues to this day.”

You should be terrified. Instead, you feel something else: a strange, unsteady pride. You did this. You, with your fourteen-hour session and your cheese strategy of blockading the Marmara and bankrupting the Turks. You made the world better—or at least different. You think of all the wars and plagues that never happened, all the people who never drowned crossing the Aegean. The old timeline is lost, but you remember it. That is a burden. Maybe it is also a gift.

You finish your latte. A passing legionary salutes you because you are still wearing your pajama shirt with the faded text “Historical Grand Strategy, High Score.” You do not correct him.

You go back inside, close the window, and sit down at your desk. The game is still running on your laptop. A cloud of flag icons hovers over a map of the world—Roman purple from Thames to Tigris. The autosave timestamp shows 11:59 PM. You saved just before the campaign ended.

You stare at the cursor. There is a button: “Start New Game.” But now, for the rest of your life, history will already be in progress. You close the lid and whisper: “No more saves.”
samples.Muse-Spark-1.2-Contributor_story:
You tell yourself you'll just finish one more war.

That's what you said at 2 p.m., when you started as Bohemia in 1444. Just a quick campaign, you thought. You wanted to see if you could actually pull it off this time — survive between the Holy Roman Emperor and Hungary, fend off Austria, build something that wasn't supposed to exist. By 6 p.m. you had taken Silesia. By 9 p.m. you had forced a personal union over Poland. By midnight you were deep in a spreadsheet of ideas and truces and aggressive expansion, three cold cups of coffee on your desk and the blue-white glow of the map painting the whole room.

You remember the exact moment you quit. It was 3:19 a.m. The game clock read January 1, 1821. The map on your laptop was absurd. There was no Germany. There was no Austria. There was a massive, deep-red Slavic Confederation stretching from the Baltic to the Adriatic, from Prague to the Black Sea, with your custom flag flying over Vienna and Budapest and Krakow. Bohemia had not only survived, it had swallowed everything. You had renamed it Greater Moravia for fun. You took a screenshot, saved the game as *moravia_final_FINAL.eu4*, and slammed the laptop shut. Your eyes burned. You stumbled to bed without even brushing your teeth.

You wake up to sunlight and the sound of church bells.

That is strange, because there is no church within bell range of your apartment. You live on the third floor above a laundromat on 5th Street, and the only thing you ever hear in the morning is traffic and the yelling of the guy who runs the bodega downstairs. But now, clear and resonant, bells are ringing. You sit up, confused, and look at your phone to check the time.

The lock screen is wrong.

The date says *12. května 2026*. Not May 12. Května. You frown and swipe it open. The news widgets that normally show you the Yankees score and the weather are showing something else entirely. The top headline from what should be the Associated Press reads: *CONFEDERATION CELEBRATES 200TH ANNIVERSARY OF THE PRAGUE TREATY.*

Your thumb hovers over it. You tap it. The article loads, with a photo of a broad boulevard filled with red-and-white flags — not Czech flags, not Polish flags, but your flag. The flag you designed at 1 a.m. using the in-game designer. A white lion on a red field, crowned, with two tails. You remember agonizing over whether to give it the second tail.

That is your flag.

You get out of bed too fast and your head spins. Your apartment is the same — same chipped paint, same laundry pile on the chair — but on your desk, where your laptop was, there is a small paper flag on a wooden stick. The lion flag. A souvenir. Like from a parade.

"Did you sleep well?" your roommate asks, leaning in your doorway. He is holding two mugs. "You were up so late. I heard you shouting about Silesia."

You have never told your roommate about Silesia. You stare at him.

"What?" he says. "You want to watch the parade? They're broadcasting the King's speech from Prague. He's going to talk about the Confederation's space program."

King. Confederation. Prague.

You take the mug from him because you don't know what else to do. "What king?" you manage.

He laughs. "King Vaclav the Fifth? Come on, man, you literally wrote your thesis on the Moravian Unification. You're not still hungover from the anniversary party last week, are you?"

You did not write a thesis on the Moravian Unification. You majored in accounting. You have never been to Prague.

You go back to your room and open your laptop. It powers on. Your save file is gone. The desktop background, which was a photo of your dog, is now a map. An old, framed-looking map hanging as wallpaper — Europe, but wrong. The Confederation sits in the middle like a heart, massive and unbroken. France is smaller. Russia is called Muscovy and stops at the Urals. Germany is just a phrase — a collection of tiny republics along the Rhine. You open a browser and type *history of Austria*.

The search autocompletes to *history of Austria - did it ever exist?*

The first result is a historical forum. *Why Austria never formed: How Bohemia's victory at the Battle of White Mountain changed European history forever.* White Mountain. That was a battle you won in 1620 in the game, a battle Bohemia historically lost catastrophically. You remember it because you savescummed it three times.

You click it. The article details how Bohemian King Frederick the Victorious crushed the Habsburgs and how the Confederation gradually absorbed its neighbors over the next two hundred years.

Only you know the timeline has changed.

You remember the other timeline perfectly — the one where Austria did exist, where World War I started in Sarajevo, where Germany unified in 1871. You remember looking up Bohemia on Wikipedia last week and reading that it had ceased to be a kingdom in 1918. Now Wikipedia says the Greater Moravian Confederation has a population of 82 million and a GDP larger than France.

You sit on the edge of your bed with the bells still ringing outside, and you understand with a cold, quiet certainty that you did not just dream the campaign. You played it, and the world listened. Somehow, the long, obsessive hours you poured into moving little armies and clicking diplomatic options bled through.

Your phone buzzes. A push notification: *LIVE: King Vaclav V addresses the Confederation from Prague Castle.*

You could tell people. You could try to explain that none of this was supposed to happen, that this whole empire is just the result of you not wanting to go to bed at 3 a.m. No one would believe you.

Instead, you tap the notification. The King's face appears, older, bearded, wearing a crown you recognize from the game's heraldry designer. Behind him, the flag you made ripples in the wind.

You watch the speech, and you finally let yourself exhale.
samples.Gemini-3.6-Flash_story:
I woke up at seven in the morning with a blinding headache, a desk cluttered with empty energy drink cans, and the phantom sensation of a glowing mouse beneath my palm. I had spent fourteen straight hours playing *Europaean Hegemony IV*, guiding the obscure Medieval Kingdom of Navarre from a tiny Pyrenean buffer state into a global maritime empire. Through ruthless trade embargoes, absurd royal marriages, and aggressive culture-shifting, I had painted the world map in Navarre’s rich shade of purple. It was a classic, irresponsible grand-strategy binge.

I groaned and reached for my smartphone to turn off the morning alarm.

The lock screen flickered to life, but the interface looked entirely wrong. The carrier logo didn't say Verizon or AT&T; it displayed a golden crest of a Basque mountain peak. A news notification popped up across the glass: *President Errotaberea signs new transatlantic trade accord with the Republic of Nov-Vasconia.*

I blinked, rubbing the sleep from my eyes. *Nov-Vasconia?* That was the ridiculous, custom name I had given to my colonial subject in North America at two in the morning.

I sat up, cold sweat pricking my neck. I unlocked the phone and opened a web browser. Instead of my usual search engine, the portal read *Bilbo Search*. I typed in "United States of America."

*Did you mean: The United Republics of Euskal Herria West?*

A surreal panic seized my chest. I scrambled out of bed and threw open the blinds. The familiar suburban skyline of my North Carolina neighborhood had vanished. In its place stood sleek, terra-cotta-roofed apartments framed by sweeping Pyrenean archways. Spanish moss hung from the live oaks, but the street signs were written in a language dense with unfamiliar letter combinations.

I rushed to my desktop computer. The saved games folder was completely empty. The game files had vanished entirely. But the internet was very real, and it was a living, breathing monument to my late-night gaming session.

I spent the next hour staring at online historical archives in absolute horror and fascination. History had been entirely rewritten by my mouse clicks. France hadn't existed since 1542, when I had systematically dismantled the Valois dynasty before exiling them to Madagascar—an island currently listed as *Ile de Valois*, a tiny, obscure French-speaking principality in the Indian Ocean.

Great Britain had never united. After my navies blockaded the English Channel in the seventeenth century, I had balkanized the island, dividing it into Basque-managed administrative zones. English was a dead language, preserved only by a few hundred linguistics scholars. Every absurd, min-maxed exploit I had executed in my dimly lit bedroom was now undisputed historical truth. The global economy ran on the Biscay Standard, and global diplomacy was conducted in Euskara.

Then, a terrible realization washed over me.

I sat frozen, remembering the final ten minutes of my gaming session right before I shut my computer down at 3:00 AM.

I had grown bored. The campaign was won, my empire had achieved total global dominance, and I had accumulated infinite gold. So, just to see what would happen before going to bed, I had deliberately broken every alliance, declared war on a massive coalition of rival powers, and tanked my nation’s internal stability to negative three by revoking every noble privilege simultaneously.

I had saved and quit right as three dozen massive rebel armies spawned across five continents, and an unstoppable world war was declared against my purple empire.

Suddenly, a low, deafening siren began to wail over the rooftops outside my window.

My phone buzzed violently with an emergency broadcast alert in bold crimson text. Even without knowing Euskara, the flashing icons of crosshairs and incoming missile trajectories were unmistakable.

I looked out the window as supersonic fighter jets screeched across the morning sky. Only I knew the awful reality: the world wasn't ending because of a tragic diplomatic failure. It was ending because I had decided to finish my playthrough with a chaotic rage-quit.
samples.Kimi-K3_story:
By three in the morning, I'd done it. Ulm — the tiny one-province duchy every *Europa Universalis IV* player jokes about — controlled the entire world. Eighteen hours of warm Mountain Dew, save-scumming, and abusing the dumbest AI exploits known to man had finally paid off. The victory screen read GREATER ULM — WORLD CONQUEST COMPLETE above a map painted the hideous neon pink I'd chosen at the start. I posted the screenshot to Discord (three people online, none awake), shut my laptop, and passed out fully clothed.

When I woke up, the flag flying over city hall across the street was neon pink with a black stag — the exact flag I'd designed while half-delirious. The corner store sold "traditional Ulmer pretzel twists." On television, a German-accented anchor reported on the Emperor's birthday celebrations.

At school, my history teacher clicked through slides of a world map matching my campaign borders exactly — including the shameful mid-game border gore, where my territory snaked across Europe in ugly tentacles because I'd been too lazy to consolidate. "As everyone knows," she said, "Jeff the Magnificent unified the world in 1748." I'd renamed my heir "Jeff" as a joke in year one of the run, and apparently he'd gone down in history. So had the capital, which I'd renamed "Buttstadt" at four in the morning, and which was now, apparently, a UNESCO World Heritage Site. My classmate whispered, "Jeff's encirclement at Vienna — textbook genius." I had stack-wiped an Austrian army there by abusing the enemy AI's pathing. Genius.

Over lunch I tested it with encyclopedias, library books, and my grandfather, who'd always rambled about the Habsburgs. Grandpa now rambled about the glorious Ulm dynasty. Only I remembered the old timeline — the one where Austria mattered, the Habsburgs existed, and "Ulm" was just a German market town. I briefly considered telling someone. Then I imagined explaining to a doctor that reality had been overwritten by my save file, and decided against it.

Here's the strange part: the knowledge turned out to be worth something. Because I'd personally conquered every province on that map, I knew this world with absurd intimacy — its trade routes, its capitals, its stupid pink banners. I was the only student who could recite the whole Stag Dynasty from memory. By spring I was county history-bee champion, and no one could figure out why I refused to cite sources.

But that night, alone, I sat with the unease. Every war I'd simulated for fun was archived in this world's museums as real. Every army I'd sacrificed clicking through battles had been real sons. I opened the laptop. The game was still installed, but my save file was gone — replaced by one named REALITY_SAVE.DO_NOT_DELETE.

I stared at it a long time. Then I clicked New Game. The world pulsed under my cursor like a heart. This time, I told myself, I'd play small. I'd trade instead of conquer. Build markets, not armies.

The difficulty slider blinked. I chose EASY — for everyone's sake.
samples.GPT-5.6-Luna_story:
# The Save File

I woke to the sound of church bells.

That was the first thing I noticed.

The second was that they were coming from outside my bedroom window, and the third was that there was no church anywhere near my apartment.

I sat up slowly, still half-asleep, staring at the gray morning light leaking through the curtains. My head felt heavy. The last thing I remembered was sitting at my computer at two in the morning, playing *Crown and Powder*, a historical grand strategy game I'd bought on a whim.

I'd spent the entire day on it.

In my campaign, I'd taken a minor German duchy in 1444 and somehow turned it into a European superpower. I'd avoided the usual wars, married my way into half the continent, crushed France after a disastrous succession crisis, and—most importantly—prevented the Ottoman conquest of Constantinople.

By the time I finally stopped playing, the map looked nothing like history.

I laughed about it before going to bed.

Then I heard the bells.

My phone said **August 29, 2026**, exactly as it should.

I reached for it.

There were dozens of notifications.

At first, I assumed I'd slept through some major news event. Then I opened the browser.

The headline made my stomach tighten.

**EUROPEAN UNION CELEBRATES 575 YEARS OF CONTINUED IMPERIAL SUCCESSION**

I blinked.

"What?"

I searched for France.

The country existed, but its flag was different. Its capital was Lyon.

I searched for Germany.

There was no Germany.

Instead, there was the **Holy Roman Empire**, still apparently functioning as a constitutional monarchy.

I laughed once, nervously.

Then I searched for Constantinople.

The results were worse.

The city was officially called Constantinople. It was the capital of the Byzantine Empire.

I stopped breathing.

I opened an online encyclopedia.

The Byzantine Empire had survived the fifteenth century because, according to every source I could find, a German prince named Matthias von Falken had intervened during the Ottoman siege of 1453. The victory triggered a chain of alliances that kept the empire alive.

Matthias von Falken.

My character's name.

The name I'd chosen because it sounded vaguely medieval.

I stared at the screen.

There were portraits of him. Paintings. Statues.

One showed him standing beside the Byzantine emperor.

I knew that pose.

I'd watched the game generate it yesterday.

My hands began to shake.

I ran outside.

The street looked familiar, but not quite. Cars drove on the right. People carried smartphones. Modern buildings stood where they belonged.

But above the bank was a golden imperial eagle.

A bus passed me bearing the words:

**IMPERIAL TRANSIT AUTHORITY**

I hurried back upstairs.

My computer was still on.

The game was open.

Except it wasn't displaying my campaign.

The screen showed a black map covered in red lines.

A message appeared in the center.

**HISTORICAL DIVERGENCE CONFIRMED.**

I froze.

Then another line appeared.

**PLAYER INTERVENTION: 1,842,937 EVENTS**

The cursor moved by itself.

A final message appeared.

**CURRENT TIMELINE: STABLE**

I unplugged the computer.

The screen stayed on.

I pulled the power cable from the wall.

It stayed on.

Then the game began displaying photographs.

Not game images.

Real photographs.

Soldiers marching beneath Byzantine banners. Schoolchildren learning imperial history. Rockets launching from an imperial spaceport. A modern Constantinopolitan skyline stretching across the Bosporus.

Then came one photograph that made my blood run cold.

It showed me.

Not as I was now, but as an old man, standing beside Matthias von Falken's statue.

Underneath was a date.

**2049.**

I stumbled backward.

"No."

The image changed.

This time it showed a newspaper.

The headline read:

**MYSTERIOUS HISTORIAN CLAIMS RESPONSIBILITY FOR THE RESTORATION OF THE WORLD'S ORIGINAL TIMELINE**

Below it was a photograph of me.

Older.

Much older.

I realized then that I had misunderstood what had happened.

The game hadn't changed history because I played it.

It had changed history because someone had played it before.

Someone had been given the same impossible choice.

Someone had seen a different world and tried to restore their own.

And now the process had reached me.

The screen went black.

A single question appeared.

**DO YOU WISH TO RESTORE ORIGINAL HISTORY?**

Two buttons appeared beneath it.

**YES.**

**NO.**

I thought about everything I'd seen.

The wars that never happened.

The nations that never existed.

The millions of people who had been born into this world instead of mine.

For me, this was a strange timeline.

For them, it was home.

My hand hovered over the mouse.

Then I closed my eyes.

I clicked **NO**.

The screen went dark.

Outside, the church bells began ringing again.

This time, I smiled.

History had changed.

And for the first time, I decided that didn't necessarily mean it was wrong.
samples.Claude-Sonnet-5-High_story:
The Roman Empire never fell.

I sat up in bed, and the wrongness of that thought hit me like cold water before I even understood why I knew it. I'd fallen asleep at my desk sometime around 3 AM, my eyes burning from fourteen straight hours of *Imperium Aeternum*, the grand strategy game I'd bought on a whim. I remembered the last thing I'd done: reformed the tax code of the Western Roman Empire in 476 AD, the exact year it was supposed to collapse. I'd saved it. Laughed about it. Gone to bed proud of myself for keeping a dying empire alive in a video game.

Now I was standing in my kitchen, and the calendar on my wall said it was the 1,548th year of the Pax Romana.

My roommate Dana was making coffee like nothing was strange. "You look like hell," she said. "Pull another all-nighter with the Consul's Assembly readings?"

"The what?"

She gave me a look. "For Civics? The vote on the Gallic provinces? Ben, you've been talking about this for weeks."

I hadn't. I'd been talking about deadlines for a job that, I was slowly realizing, might not exist anymore in whatever this was. I turned on the television instead of answering. The news anchor was discussing trade tariffs between the Empire and the Han Successor States. There was no United States. There was no Christianity, not the way I understood it — some analyst mentioned "the Old Faiths" in passing, gods with names I recognized from history books, still worshipped, still official.

I went back to my room and my computer was there, same as always, except the game wasn't installed. I searched for it. Nothing. Not on Steam, not in my downloads, not in my memory of purchase confirmations. But I remembered playing it. I remembered the little icon, the tutorial voice, the satisfaction of watching my empire's borders creep outward on the map like spilled ink.

I spent that whole day in a fog, nodding along to conversations I didn't understand, googling things that gave me answers too complete, too settled, like a history that had never had room for doubt. Emperor Aurelian IX had apparently died last spring. I remembered naming him. I remembered choosing his heir in a succession crisis event, clicking through dialogue options at two in the morning with a bag of chips in my lap.

By evening I'd stopped trying to convince Dana or anyone else. Who would believe me? That I'd sat in a chair and made choices that rewrote two thousand years of human history, one decision box at a time? That somewhere in a save file that no longer existed, I'd once decided not to let the Visigoths sack Rome because it seemed like the efficient move, the number-optimizing move, without any weight of what it meant?

I sat on the back steps as the sun went down over a skyline that had never known a Renaissance in the way I'd learned it, never known a Reformation, never split into the nations I used to trace on paper maps in grade school. The city was still beautiful. People still laughed in the streets below, ordering food, arguing about small things, living lives that felt whole and real to them because this was simply the only world they had ever known.

I thought about trying to fix it. Find the game again, reload an old save, undo whatever I'd done. But there was no game to find, no menu to open, no undo button anywhere in sight. Whatever choices I'd made were no longer choices. They were just history now.

So I did the only thing left to do. I went back inside, sat down at Dana's kitchen table, and asked her to tell me everything I apparently already knew.
samples.MiniMax-M3_story:
I blinked awake to sunlight that felt wrong. Not the color — gold, ordinary, sliding between the venetian blinds the way it always does — but the angle. Too low. Too sharp. I had gone to bed in late autumn and now the world outside my window looked like early June.

I grabbed my phone. 8:47 AM. June 14th.

I sat up so fast I nearly headbutted the headboard.

Yesterday was October 12th. I knew this with the certainty only a person who has lost ten hours to a grand strategy game can have. I had been playing since one in the afternoon. It was four in the morning when I finally saved and quit, my eyes burning, my tiny Balkan nation having absorbed the Ottomans, half of Austria, and a worrying stretch of coastline. I had started as the Kingdom of Serbia in 1444. By the time I closed the laptop it was 1922 in-game, and I had not lost a war in eighty years.

I laughed, at first. I thought I had lost my mind. I went downstairs and my mother was making coffee, humming something, and I almost asked her what year it was — except that would have been unhinged — so instead I asked how she had slept and she said, "Fine, love. You're up early."

But then the news came on.

The presenter mentioned a new coalition forming in Belgrade. *Belgrade.* I leaned forward. The map behind her showed borders I had drawn myself, two days ago in my bedroom, clicking and unclicking provinces like they meant nothing. They had been rectangles on a screen. Now they were lines on a map that real people lived inside.

I called in sick to work. I sat in front of the television for four hours.

The Byzantines had held Constantinople. Of course they had — I had rushed to save them in 1453 with a desperate crusade, even though historically the city had fallen centuries ago. Now there were reports out of Istanbul about a Patriarch consecrating a new cathedral on the site of the old one. There were video clips. I recognized one of the men in the front row of the congregation. He was a portrait I had dismissed as a generic clergyman in 1470, when I had clicked "send diplomat" and moved on with my conquest of Wallachia.

The strangest part was how *normal* everyone was. The barista at the coffee shop, when I finally went out for air, asked how my day was going. I wanted to shake her. I wanted to say: do you know that Hungary is a vassal of a man named Stefan Nemanjić? Do you know that there is no Austria-Hungary? Do you know that there is no Germany?

But she didn't know. Nobody knew. The borders on the maps in her phone, the history in her textbooks, the country she lived in — all of it was *my* doing. Yesterday's whim. Yesterday's "eh, I'll release this as a client state."

I went home and opened my laptop. The save file was still there. I scrolled through the timeline. 1870: Serbia declares war on the ERE. 1881: Serbian victory. 1890: Stefan VII crowned Emperor of the Romans in Hagia Sophia.

I closed the laptop slowly.

Here is the thing about grand strategy games. They give you a god's-eye view of history. You can see every province, every leader, every tiny modifier on every war. You feel, for a moment, that the world is a thing you can rearrange.

I had rearranged the world.

And now it was Tuesday, and nobody knew it was Tuesday the way I knew it was Tuesday — because Tuesday existed in a world I had rebuilt in my sleep. My mother still made coffee on Tuesday. The buses still ran on Tuesday. Somewhere in Belgrade, a parliament convened that would not have convened without me, and the men in that parliament had childhoods and grandchildren and lunch plans, and they did not know that they owed any of it to a tired guy in Manchester who hadn't slept.

I sat on the sofa for a long time.

Then I went and made myself a sandwich, and ate it slowly, and looked out the window at a street that looked the same as yesterday, except that everything underneath it had been rearranged by me. I thought: I should not save-scum anymore. I thought: I should be very, very careful what I click.

I did not turn on the laptop.

Not today.
