You wake up to the beeping.

It's steady and too loud, and it takes you a second to realize the sound is synched to something inside your chest. The light above you is white and fluorescent and it hurts to look at. Your mouth is dry as paper and tastes faintly like blood. When you try to move, a sharp pain lances up your left side and your arm doesn't want to cooperate — it's wrapped, heavy, in a sling and a cast.

A woman in scrubs leans into your field of vision. "Hey there, you're awake. That's good. Try not to move too much, honey."

You try to ask where you are, but your voice comes out as a rasp. Before you can try again, you notice the two other people in the room. They are not doctors. They stand at the foot of your bed in dark uniforms, notebooks already open.

The taller one steps forward. "Mr. Ellis? I'm Officer Chen, this is Officer Reyes. Do you know why you're here?"

You shake your head, and immediately regret it. The room swims.

"You were in an accident last night. On Route 9, about eleven forty. Your car went off the road and hit the guardrail. You were lucky. A passing driver called it in," Chen says. His voice is calm, practiced. "We just need to ask you a few questions about what happened before that. Can you tell us where you were headed?"

You stare at him. Your mind is a flat, white blank. You try to reach back past the beeping, past waking up, and there is nothing. No last night. No yesterday. Just a vague, familiar panic that you should know.

"I... I don't remember," you say.

Reyes exchanges a glance with Chen. "You don't remember being at the Riverside warehouse? The party?"

That means nothing to you. The name fizzles. "I don't remember anything."

Chen's expression doesn't change. "We found your phone in the car. You're welcome to look. Sometimes it helps jog the memory. We'll be right outside if you want to talk."

The nurse gives you a pitying look as they step out into the hall, leaving the door cracked just enough that you can see their shoulders.

Your phone is on the rolling tray beside the bed, plugged in, its screen cracked in the corner. Your left hand is useless, so you fumble with your right, your fingers clumsy from the IV. You type in your passcode on muscle memory alone and it unlocks.

The first thing you see is a flood of notifications. 12 missed calls. 23 new texts. The most recent is from 8:47 this morning. It's from MOM.

*MOM 8:47 AM: Honey please call me when you wake up. The police called us. We love you.*

You scroll past it. You need last night.

You open your conversation with JESS.

*YOU 7:12 PM: u sure u want me to pick up the cake??? im already late for daniels thing*
*JESS 7:13 PM: yes please!! ur the best. daniel will kill me if i forget again*
*JESS 7:15 PM: bakery closes at 7:30!!*

Then a gap. Then:

*YOU 8:31 PM: dude where r u*
*DANIEL 8:33 PM: warehouse. where r u???*
*YOU 8:34 PM: stuck at bakery line is insane*
*DANIEL 8:34 PM: hurry*

Then, at 9:02 PM, the tone shifts. It's not you texting Daniel. It's you texting MIA.

*YOU 9:02 PM: Mia pls don't do this*
*MIA 9:03 PM: I told him I'm not going to lie for you anymore*
*YOU 9:03 PM: If you tell him I swear everything is ruined*
*MIA 9:05 PM: You should have thought about that before you drove there drunk. I'm done covering.*

Your stomach drops. You don't remember typing any of this.

Below that, at 9:18 PM, from MIA again: *Where are you?? Daniel says you never showed?? Are you okay?*

And then a flurry from DANIEL between 9:40 and 10:15 PM:
*DANIEL 9:40 PM: where tf are u*
*DANIEL 9:55 PM: bro pick up*
*DANIEL 10:15 PM: Jess called me crying, she said u left her on read. what is going on*

And then, the last message YOU sent, at 10:51 PM, to JESS:

*YOU 10:51 PM: I got the cake. I'm on my way now. Tell Daniel I'm sorry I messed up. Don't let Mia tell him*

You read that last line three times. The timestamp burns. 10:51 PM. The accident was at 11:40 PM. Route 9 is the road between the bakery and the Riverside warehouse. You weren't going to the party. You were trying to get back with a cake before anyone realized you'd spent the whole night driving to see Mia.

You remember now, in a sickening flash that isn't a memory but a reconstruction: you and Mia. The affair. Daniel is your best friend. Mia is his girlfriend. Jess is his sister. You had begged Mia not to confess. You had driven after drinking at a bar near her apartment, panicked, trying to make it back in time to pretend you'd just been running an errand.

Your door creaks. Officer Chen is back. He must have seen something change in your face.

"Remember something?" he asks quietly.

You look down at the phone, then at your casted arm, at the beeping monitor. Your throat is still dry, but your voice is clearer now.

"Yeah," you say. "I remember. I was drunk. I shouldn't have been driving."

Reyes steps forward, pen ready. "Do you want to tell us what happened on Route 9?"

You take a breath. The beeping is still steady, but it no longer feels like it's just keeping time for you. It feels like a countdown you get to walk back from.

"I was trying to get back before anyone noticed I'd left," you say, and you hand him the phone, open to the messages, ready to finally tell the whole truth.
samples.Gemini-3.6-Flash_story:
You wake up to the sharp, chemical stench of antiseptic and the harsh glare of fluorescent lighting. A rhythmic *beep-beep-beep* echoes in your ears, pulsing in sync with the dull throbbing behind your eyes.

Standing at the foot of your hospital bed are two police officers. The older one, Detective Vance, has tired eyes and a grim, lined face. Beside him stands Officer Miller, younger and restless, shifting his weight from foot to foot.

"Glad to see you're finally awake," Vance says, his voice heavy. "Care to tell us what happened at Pier 4 last night? Where’s the package, and where is Leo?"

You open your mouth, but your mind is a sterile, white void. No memories of Pier 4. No memories of a package. Even the name 'Leo' feels like a word from a language you used to speak but have long forgotten.

"I... I don't know," you croak, your throat raw. "I don't remember anything."

Officer Miller scoffs under his breath, but Vance merely sighs and pulls a ziplock evidence bag from his coat pocket. Inside rests your smartphone, its glass screen shattered into a spiderweb of fracture lines.

"We unlocked it," Vance says, placing the bagged phone on your bedside tray. "Maybe your text messages will jog your memory. Walk us through what you were doing before someone cracked your skull."

With trembling hands, you slide the phone out of the plastic. Your fingers move on instinct, tapping the messaging app. The top thread is with *Leo*. You open it and scroll back to last night.

*10:15 PM – Leo:* "Meet me at Pier 4. Don't tell anyone. I found out who killed Sarah."

A sudden chill grips your chest. Sarah. A vague shadow of a face flickers in your mind, accompanied by a hollow ache in your chest.

*10:30 PM – You:* "Leo, drop it. It's too dangerous. Let the police handle it."  
*10:42 PM – Leo:* "The police *are* the problem. The lead detective on Sarah's case was paid off. I'm taking the evidence tonight."

Your breath hitches. You glance up from the screen. Vance is staring down at you, his face an unreadable mask. "Finding anything?" he asks smoothly.

"Just... confusion," you lie, forcing your voice to remain steady while praying the heart monitor doesn't betray your accelerating pulse. You scroll further down.

*11:15 PM – You:* "I'm on my way. Who's the detective?"  
*11:20 PM – Leo:* "Vance. It's Vance. Don't trust anyone at the precinct."

Cold sweat breaks out across your neck. You keep your head down, desperate not to give away the terror flooding your veins. You scroll to the final messages, sent just after midnight.

*11:55 PM – Leo:* "Someone's outside the warehouse. It's not Vance. It's his partner, Miller."  
*11:58 PM – You:* "Hide! I'm pulling up now!"  
*12:02 AM – You:* "I see Miller. Sending our live GPS location and the audio files to the District Attorney's office right now."

The final message was an automated system response: *Message delivered to DA_Internal_Taskforce@citygov.org.*

The puzzle pieces snap together with agonizing clarity. You weren't an accomplice. You were the witness who came to save Leo, carrying the digital evidence that could bring down both officers in this room. You were ambushed from behind before you could reach him.

You slowly let the phone rest on your lap, keeping your face a mask of dim-witted frustration.

Miller steps forward, leaning over the guardrail of your bed. "Well? Does any of it make sense to you?"

You look back and forth between them—Vance with his hands buried in his coat, Miller blocking the only exit. You are trapped in a small room with two corrupt officers who don't yet realize you know the truth, but who are waiting for an excuse to ensure your memory never returns.

You squeeze your eyes shut and rub your temples, letting out a weak, confused sigh.

"It's just a bunch of random numbers and wrong turns," you say, letting your voice quiver slightly. "I think... I think I was just lost trying to find a late-night diner. I don't even know who this Leo guy is."

Vance relaxes his shoulders slightly, exchanging a quick, subtle glance with Miller.

"Alright," Vance says, taking the phone back. "Get some rest. We'll be right outside if you remember anything else."

They turn and exit, the heavy wooden door clicking shut behind them.

The moment the latch catches, you open your eyes, reach up with a steady hand, and press the red call button above your pillow. As the nurse's station chimes, you prepare to tell her to get hospital security, knowing the District Attorney's task force is already on its way.
samples.Kimi-K3_story:
**Forty-Seven Missed Calls**

The ceiling was water-stained and too bright. A nurse kept saying my name, and behind her, at the foot of the bed, stood two police officers—one in uniform, one in a suit the color of dishwater.

"Mr. Bell? Do you know where you are?"

"Hospital," I said. My head felt like a bell that had just been rung.

"Do you remember Friday night?"

I tried. Nothing came. "No."

The suited one—Detective Rios—stepped closer. "A cyclist was hit by your car on County Line Road around eleven. We need to know your movements."

"My car hit somebody?" The room tilted. "I don't—I was home. Maybe. I don't know."

They kept asking. I kept saying I didn't know. The doctor finally shooed them out, explaining that memory loss came standard with a concussion. It might return in pieces, he said. Or not at all.

Once they'd gone, I asked for my phone. It was in the plastic belongings bag, the screen cracked like lake ice. Forty-seven missed calls. I opened my texts and started rebuilding myself.

Thursday, to Marcus: *You can borrow the car, but I need it back Friday. Lydia's flight gets in at 8.*

Marcus: *You're the best, bro. I owe you.*

My stomach dropped. Marcus Torres. Twenty years my friend, three months unemployed, one ex-wife.

Friday, 6:42 p.m., me: *Lyd's flight got cancelled. Keep it till Saturday. What are you even doing?*

Marcus: *Interview was trash. Grabbing a drink with Rick.*

So there was time to kill. That tracked; my sister flew standby and missed flights the way other people missed buses.

Friday, 11:03 p.m., Marcus: *Hey, can I keep it till Tuesday? I'll explain later.*

Me: *Everything ok?*

Marcus: *Yeah.*

Rios returned Saturday at noon, polite as a collections agent. "The cyclist, Mr. Abernathy, is stable. What I can't figure out is why you were out there at all. You weren't in your car when it hit him. Your left shoe was on the shoulder, sixty feet from the crash. So what were you doing, Ray?"

I looked at the cracked phone. "What time was I brought in?"

"Call came in at 11:19 p.m."

I scrolled down.

11:06, me: *Where are you?*

11:09, Marcus: *Bell. Oh God. I hit him. The bike guy. I hit him and I panicked. I'm parked at the VFW. I didn't know what to—"

11:11, me: *Stay there. I'm walking over. Did you call 911?*

11:13, Marcus: *I didn't. I know. I messed up. I'm sorry. I'll tell them everything.*

I read it aloud to Rios. My chest hurt in a way that had nothing to do with the bruise blooming across my ribs. "He texted me the whole thing," I said. "I must have gone out to find him. Or the man he hit."

A fragment surfaced then, like something bobbing up through black water: gravel under my cheek, the orange hum of a work light, headlights swinging wide. Maybe Marcus kneeling over me. Maybe not. The police figure it was a pickup that caught me on the shoulder and never stopped, while Marcus, panicking in the VFW lot, had no idea I was lying in the ditch.

By Sunday, Marcus showed up with flowers and eyes scrubbed raw. He'd confessed to Rios already. "You walked out to check the guy," he said. "You were always walking into stuff for me."

"I don't remember," I told him.

"I know." He squeezed my hand. "So let me. Some of this you get to remember through other people."

The funny thing is, I believe him. The phone says I chose the right side of that road. I just have to trust the evidence—the cracked screen, the timestamps, a friend who finally told the truth—that whoever I was on Friday night, I'd be him again.
samples.GPT-5.6-Luna_story:
# The Last Message

I woke to the smell of antiseptic and the steady beep of a machine beside my bed.

For a few seconds, I stared at the ceiling and tried to remember where I was.

Nothing.

Then I noticed the two police officers sitting in the corner.

“Mr. Carter?” the older officer asked.

I swallowed. My throat felt like sandpaper. “What happened?”

The officers exchanged a look.

“That’s what we’re trying to find out,” the younger one said. “Do you remember anything from last night?”

I closed my eyes.

Nothing.

Not the evening. Not where I had been. Not how I had ended up in a hospital bed with stitches above my eyebrow and bruises covering both hands.

The older officer leaned forward. “There was a serious accident on Blackwood Road. A car went through a guardrail and landed in a ravine. Your car.”

“My car?”

“You were found unconscious inside it.”

I looked at my hands.

“What about anyone else?”

Neither officer answered immediately.

Finally, the older man said, “Your friend Daniel was with you.”

A cold feeling spread through my chest.

“Is he—?”

“He survived,” the officer said. “He’s in surgery.”

Relief came first. Then confusion.

“Why can't I remember?”

The younger officer placed a plastic evidence bag on the table. Inside was my phone.

“You were conscious briefly at the scene,” he said. “You apparently made several phone calls, but you haven't told us what happened. We need to know where you were before the crash and why you were driving so fast.”

“I don't know.”

The older officer nodded toward my phone.

“Then perhaps your messages can tell us.”

They unlocked it using the emergency access code I'd given the paramedics.

At first, the messages seemed ordinary.

Daniel: **Still coming tonight?**

Me: **Of course. I owe you one.**

Daniel: **You really don't want to know what I found.**

I frowned.

“What did he find?”

The officer shook his head. “That's what we'd like you to tell us.”

I kept scrolling.

At 9:47 p.m., I had sent Daniel a message.

**Don't tell anyone yet. I'm coming over.**

Then, twelve minutes later:

**Bring the box.**

I stared at the screen.

“What box?”

No answer came.

There were dozens of messages after that, but many were strange fragments.

**He's watching us.**

**Don't use the front door.**

**Delete everything.**

Then, at 10:31:

**Daniel, if I don't make it, check the blue folder.**

I felt my heartbeat quicken.

“What blue folder?”

The younger officer leaned closer. “You tell us.”

I scrolled further.

At 10:42, Daniel had replied.

**I knew you wouldn't believe me. The files are real.**

Then another message from me:

**I'm going to the police.**

The officers looked at each other.

I suddenly remembered something.

Not an event, exactly. A feeling.

Fear.

I had been sitting in my car. Daniel was beside me. Someone was following us.

I kept scrolling.

At 10:48, Daniel wrote:

**They're behind us. Don't stop.**

My next message was only three words.

**Call Officer Reed.**

The older officer went completely still.

“What's wrong?” I asked.

He didn't answer.

I looked at his name tag.

**Reed.**

My stomach dropped.

I turned the phone toward him.

“You're Officer Reed.”

His face had gone pale.

The younger officer immediately reached for his radio.

Officer Reed stood.

“Give me the phone.”

“No.”

“Mr. Carter, you don't understand what you're looking at.”

“Yes, I do.”

My memory came back in pieces.

Daniel had discovered financial records hidden inside the company where we worked. Money had been disappearing for years. He had copied the files and planned to expose the people responsible.

But someone had discovered us.

We had been followed.

And before the crash, Daniel had sent one final message.

I hadn't noticed it because it was buried beneath the others.

**Reed is one of them.**

The hospital door opened.

Two more officers entered.

Reed froze.

The younger officer drew his weapon.

“Step away from the patient,” he ordered.

For the first time since waking up, I felt certain about something.

I hadn't forgotten everything.

My mind had simply buried the truth to protect me.

Later, after Reed was arrested, I was told that Daniel had survived his surgery. The blue folder was found in my apartment, exactly where my messages said it would be.

Inside were enough documents to bring down the entire operation.

The last thing I remembered was lying in my hospital bed, staring at my phone.

There was one unsent message in the drafts.

I had written it before the crash.

**If I forget, the phone will remember.**

I smiled.

For once, I was glad I had been too scared to delete anything.
samples.Claude-Sonnet-5-High_story:
The lights were too white. That was the first thing I noticed—the fluorescent hum pressing against my skull like a second headache stacked on top of the first one. The second thing I noticed was the two officers standing at the foot of my bed, one with a notepad, the other with his thumbs hooked into his belt like he was waiting for something.

"Ms. Hale, can you tell us what happened last night?"

I opened my mouth. Nothing came out because there was nothing there. No memory, no thread to pull. Just static where Tuesday night should have been.

"I don't—I don't know," I said. My throat felt like sandpaper. "What happened? Am I in trouble?"

The officer with the notepad exchanged a look with his partner. "There was an accident. A car was found wrapped around a light pole on Ferris Street. You were in the passenger seat. The driver's still in surgery."

Driver. I didn't even know who had been driving.

"We need to know what you remember," he said again, gentler this time, like patience might jog something loose.

"I don't remember anything after work yesterday," I admitted. "I left the office around six. That's it. That's where it stops."

They asked me to think harder, but hard thinking doesn't work like that. Memory isn't a drawer you can force open. Eventually they left, saying they'd be back once I was more "stable," which felt like a polite way of saying *once you're not so obviously useless.*

A nurse brought my phone in a plastic bag, my personal effects from the crash. The screen was cracked, spiderwebbed in the corner, but it turned on. Forty-three unread messages. My hands were shaking as I opened them, like I was about to read a stranger's diary.

**6:12 PM, from Jordan:** *You still coming tonight? Marcus is being weird about it but whatever, just show up.*

**6:45 PM, from me, to Jordan:** *On my way. Traffic is insane.*

**7:30 PM, from Marcus:** *Where are you guys. This isn't funny.*

Marcus. The name meant nothing and everything at once, a shape without a face.

**8:02 PM, from Jordan:** *She's here. We're gonna get food after, don't wait up.*

**9:15 PM, from unknown number:** *I really think you should let me drive.*

I stared at that one for a long time. Unknown number. Not saved. I scrolled further, my chest tightening with each swipe, piecing together a night I'd lived through but couldn't access, like reading a police report of my own life.

**9:47 PM, from me, to unknown number:** *I'm fine. Stop asking.*

**9:48 PM, from unknown number:** *You've had four drinks. I'm serious.*

**9:52 PM, from me, to unknown number:** *Fine. You drive. Happy?*

My stomach dropped. So I hadn't been driving. Someone else had, someone who'd tried to stop me from getting behind the wheel and ended up behind it instead. Someone in surgery right now because I hadn't listened the first time.

**10:03 PM, from Jordan:** *Where'd you guys go? Marcus wants to leave.*

**10:04 PM, from me, to Jordan:** *Heading back now. Ben's driving.*

Ben. The name settled into the empty space like a key into a lock. Not Marcus, not Jordan. Ben—the one who'd argued with me, the one who'd taken my keys, the one now unconscious two floors below me because I'd had four drinks and still almost driven anyway.

I called Jordan the second I found the courage. She picked up on the first ring, voice already breaking.

"You're awake," she said. "God, you're awake. Ben's still in surgery, they don't know—" She stopped herself. "Do you remember any of it?"

"No," I said, and it felt like the truest thing I'd said all day. "Just what's on my phone."

"That's more than nothing," she said quietly.

When the officers came back an hour later, I handed them my phone without being asked. I couldn't tell them what happened. But the messages could. And maybe that was enough to start piecing together not just the accident, but who I needed to become afterward—someone who listened the first time.
samples.MiniMax-M3_story:
You wake to the hum of fluorescent lights and the dull ache of bandages wrapped tight around your ribs. The ceiling is institutional white. The smell is bleach and plastic and something metallic underneath. Your tongue feels like sandpaper.

"Sir? Can you hear me?"

A woman in a navy blazer sits beside your bed, notepad balanced on her knee. A man in a matching blazer stands by the door with his arms crossed. Both wear badges clipped to their belts. The woman watches you the way people watch stray dogs — cautious, ready to move.

"You're at St. Catherine's," she says. "You're safe. Do you know your name?"

You do. Marcus Adelhardt. That much, at least, is still in there.

"Do you know what happened to you last night?"

You don't.

She sighs, exchanges a look with the man by the door, and sets your phone on the bed beside your hand. The screen is cracked in two places. There's something dark and dried in the grooves around the camera lens.

"When you're ready, we'd like you to walk us through the last twenty-four hours."

You pick up the phone. Forty-seven unread messages.

The most recent are from your sister, Lila. *Call me.* *Please call me.* *Marcus, where are you.* *I'm coming over.* *Answer your phone.* Then nothing since 3 a.m.

Before those, a name you haven't thought about in years: Danny. Your brother. The one who left for Portland eight years ago and stopped returning calls. His messages start civil.

*Hey. It's me. Back in town for a bit.*
*You around?*
*I know things got weird between us. I'd like to talk.*

Then less civil: *I need to talk to you, Marcus. It's important. Don't ignore me.*
*Warehouse off Henderson. Tomorrow. 11pm.*

You scroll up. Between Danny's messages and Lila's panic, there's a name you don't recognize: Sloane. The texts are warm in a way that makes your stomach drop. *I miss you already.* *Wish you hadn't left so fast.* A photo you don't open, not with the officers watching — but the preview shows a bare shoulder, a coffee cup on a side table.

The detective watches you scroll. "Recognize any of those names?"

"No," you say, and it's mostly true.

She taps her pen against the notepad. "Mr. Adelhardt, a man was pulled from the river this morning. He's alive, barely. He's asking for you by name."

You look at the phone again. Danny's last message, sent at 10:47 p.m.:

*She's not who you think she is. Don't come to the warehouse.*

You scroll back through Sloane's messages. There, between a joke about burnt coffee and a heart emoji, something that doesn't fit:

*End it tonight and we're done. You won't have to worry about him anymore.*

Your hands are shaking. The detective is watching. She knows, you realize, what this looks like from the outside. A man who went to meet his brother. A woman who wanted someone "ended." A body in the river.

"Can you tell me," she says carefully, "who Sloane is?"

You want to say: *I don't know. I woke up an hour ago and I am reading my own messages like they belong to a stranger, and I am scared of what I'm going to find next.*

But you keep scrolling. There's a voicemail from Lila you missed at 2 a.m. You press play, low, the phone tilted away.

"Marcus. Danny's in the hospital. Someone attacked him. The police want to talk to you. Call me the second you get this."

You look up. The detective's face hasn't changed, but something behind her eyes has.

"I need to tell you about Sloane," you say.

You don't know yet whether what comes out will save you or bury you. You only know the story your phone is telling is not the one she came expecting to hear.

Dr. Malice — known to the world as the architect of the Volcano Fortress Incident, the man who once held the entire Eastern Seaboard hostage with a weather machine — stood on the doorstep of a modest yellow house in Dayton, Ohio, holding a bouquet of carnations and feeling genuinely terrified.

He checked his watch. 11:47 a.m. He was thirteen minutes early, which meant his mother would comment on it. If he'd been thirteen minutes late, she would have commented on that too. There was no winning. There was never any winning with Margaret Holloway.

He rang the doorbell.

The door swung open, and there she was — four foot eleven, silver-haired, wearing a floral apron dusted with flour. She looked him up and down, taking in the black cape, the obsidian gauntlets, the skull-shaped belt buckle.

She took the carnations, sniffed them, and frowned. "You remembered I like lilies."

"I — the florist was closed. There was a hero battle on Fifth Street and —"

"There's always a hero battle. You'd think with all that genius you brag about on the news, you could find a florist that stays open past ten." She stepped aside. "Well, come in before the neighbors see you. Mrs. Patterson already thinks I raised a delinquent."

Dr. Malice ducked through the doorframe — he was six foot four, a fact his mother attributed to "all that radiation you exposed yourself to, as if vitamins weren't enough" — and was immediately hit by the smell of pot roast. His pot roast. The one she only made on holidays and his birthday, because she knew it was his favorite, though she would die before admitting she still cooked for him with love.

The dining room was exactly as he remembered. The same oak table with the wobbly leg he'd promised to fix in 2003. The same curtains with the little blue flowers. The same framed photos on the wall — his school portraits, his graduation photo, and, inexplicably, a newspaper clipping of his first major arrest with the headline SUPERVILLAIN TERRORIZES CITY. She'd circled his face in red pen and written *that's my boy* in the margin.

"Sit down," she commanded, disappearing into the kitchen. "And take off those ridiculous gloves. This is a house, not a lair."

He sat. He removed the gauntlets. Underneath, his hands were pale and ordinary — the hands of a man who had once been a little boy who built volcanoes out of papier-mâché for the science fair. His mother had helped him with that project. She'd been so proud when he won first place. He sometimes wondered if she regretted that.

She returned with the pot roast, mashed potatoes, green beans, and a glass of sweet tea. She set his plate down with the precision of a surgeon, then sat across from him, watching.

"Eat," she said. "You look thin. Do they not feed you in that volcano?"

"It's a fortress, Mom. And yes, I have a full kitchen staff."

"Restaurant food." She waved her hand dismissively. "You need a home-cooked meal. You need a wife."

"We've talked about this."

"I'm just saying. Even that flying man — Superman, whatever — he has a girlfriend. You're telling me the world's most dangerous mind can't find one nice girl?"

He ate the pot roast. It was perfect, as always. The silence between them was comfortable in the way that only decades of the same argument could make it.

"I brought you something," he said, reaching into his cape. He produced a small velvet box and slid it across the table.

She opened it. Inside was a bracelet — delicate, silver, with a tiny charm shaped like a volcano. It was, of course, also a miniature force-field generator that would protect her from any threat on Earth, but she didn't need to know that.

Her eyes softened for just a moment. Then she snapped the box shut.

"It's beautiful," she said quietly. Then, louder: "You should visit more often. Not just holidays. I'm not going to live forever, you know."

"Yes, you will," he said. "I've already made sure of that."

She stared at him. He stared at his potatoes.

"What did you do?"

"Nothing illegal." A pause. "Mostly."

She sighed the sigh of a woman who had been sighing at this particular man for over forty years. "You are the worst son in the world."

"I know, Mom."

"Next time, bring lilies."

"Yes, Mom."

She reached across the table and squeezed his hand — just briefly, just once — and Dr. Malice, the most feared villain on the planet, felt something dangerously close to peace.

**Visiting Hours**

Every spring, the second Sunday of May confronts me with a problem no death ray can solve: Mother's Day.

My minions don't understand. "But Lord Vex," they say, "you were going to hold the city's water supply hostage this weekend." I tell them the ransom can wait twenty-four hours. My mother made me, quite literally—it says so right on the birth certificate she keeps framed in the hallway—and a man doesn't become one of the most feared villains on the eastern seaboard without honoring the woman who packed his school lunches.

So I set the orbital laser to "standby," put a minion in a necktie (presentation matters), and climb into my least conspicuous vehicle—the hearse, monogrammed, but relatively subtle—and drive to Maple Grove Assisted Living, where my mother, Maureen Vex (she kept the name; says it sounds "dynamic"), occupies a one-bedroom with a view of the koi pond.

The front desk knows me by now. "He's my son," she tells the receptionist without looking up from her crossword, the way she has every year since the nursing staff got jumpy about the cape. "He's in the arts." Mother has never once called me a supervillain, and I have never once corrected her. There are some classifications a mother dismisses at the door.

The gifts this year: a bouquet of genetically modified irises from my own horticulture lab (they hum a soft G when happy, and Mother says they brighten the room), a box of butter pastries from the shop on Route 9 (acquired legally—I've learned to send a minion with actual cash since The Incident), and a card with a cocker spaniel on the front that says "You're the best, Mom." I've stolen the crown jewels of three nations, but picking out a Mother's Day card remains the hardest decision of my year.

"You're thin," she says, hugging me around the breastplate. "Are you eating?"

"We have a cafeteria, Ma."

"A cafeteria." She says it the way other women say "a hostage situation."

Then we settle into ritual. She shows me photographs from the cruise she took with her friend Doreen, who has a doctorate and therefore, Mother reminds me gently, "options." She asks about my work in the careful way she always does, as if it might explode—which, to be fair, it often does. I tell her I've been working on a big project, that the mayor has been "difficult" again, that it'll be in the papers soon. She nods. "Your father always said you had focus. Terrifying, but focus."

Lunch is in the dining hall: chicken, gravy, Jell-O, and Mrs. Finklestein from across the hall, who I have twice frozen solid (temporarily) and who nevertheless whispers to Mother, "Your son has such nice manners, Maureen."

Afterward we walk the grounds, my boots clicking on the garden path, her hand resting on my gauntlet. At the koi pond she says—like she does every year—that I don't have to visit, that I'm busy, and like every year I say the world can burn a day later. She pats my hand. The irises hum.

Back at the door, she presses Tupperware into my arms. "Pot roast," she says. "For your caf-ay-ter-ria." I promise to call Sundays. I promise not to vaporize the governor before her book-club weekend (a long-standing request). I promise, secretly, that one day the city will kneel, and when it does, it'll be because she taught a boy that manners matter, attention matters, and if you're going to do something—anything—you do it to completion.

"Be safe, sweetheart," she says. "And wear a scarf. It's damp out."

And that, every year, is when the dreaded Lord Vex—conqueror, scourge, the man who once turned the moon slightly mauve—gets back in his hearse and cries just a little on Route 9, because there is no force on this earth stronger than a woman who once made you wear a scarf and still makes you want to deserve one.

Happy Mother's Day, Ma. The ransom's extended by a day.

# The Villain Who Came Home

Every year on Mother’s Day, the citizens of Blackstone City locked their doors a little earlier than usual.

They knew that Dr. Malice might attack.

Dr. Malice was the city’s most feared super villain. He had once threatened to freeze the ocean, steal the moon, and replace every traffic light in the city with his own face. His underground laboratory was filled with dangerous machines, mysterious chemicals, and enough explosives to make the police nervous.

But there was one day when Dr. Malice never caused trouble.

Mother’s Day.

At exactly eight o’clock that morning, he put away his black cape, removed his metal gloves, and looked at himself in the mirror.

“Today,” he announced, “I am simply a son.”

He climbed into his black flying car and headed toward the small village where his mother lived.

The village was completely different from Blackstone City. There were no skyscrapers, police sirens, or superhero battles. There were only green hills, little houses, and birds singing in the trees.

Dr. Malice stopped his car outside a tiny blue house.

Before he could knock, the door opened.

“There you are!” cried his mother.

She was a short, cheerful woman named Margaret. She wore a pink sweater and an apron covered with flour.

“Happy Mother’s Day, Mum,” Dr. Malice said.

He handed her an enormous bouquet of black roses.

Margaret stared at them.

“Oh, dear. Are these poisonous?”

“No,” he said proudly. “I had them genetically modified so they can survive nuclear explosions.”

His mother sighed.

“Malcolm, normal flowers would have been fine.”

Dr. Malice frowned. “I am Dr. Malice.”

“You’re Malcolm when you’re in my house.”

“Yes, Mum.”

She smiled and hugged him.

For a moment, the most dangerous man in the city looked like an ordinary little boy.

Inside, Margaret had prepared his favorite meal: roast chicken, potatoes, carrots, and apple pie.

Dr. Malice sat at the kitchen table and looked around. There were photographs everywhere. One showed him as a baby wearing a ridiculous yellow hat. Another showed him at age ten holding a science project. In yet another, he stood beside his mother at his school graduation.

“You kept all these?” he asked.

“Of course,” Margaret replied.

Dr. Malice looked away.

“I suppose I was always destined for greatness.”

“You were always destined to be troublesome,” his mother corrected.

After lunch, they washed the dishes together.

Then Margaret asked, “So, Malcolm, what have you been doing lately?”

“Nothing much.”

“Really?”

“Well…” He hesitated. “I did threaten to destroy the city last Tuesday.”

“Did anyone get hurt?”

“No.”

“Good.”

“I also built a giant laser.”

“Did you use it?”

“No.”

“Good.”

She patted his hand.

“Whatever you become, Malcolm, just remember that being powerful isn’t the same as being important.”

Dr. Malice stared at her.

Those words followed him everywhere. They followed him into his laboratory and into every evil plan he created. He had spent years trying to prove that he was the most powerful person in the world.

But his mother had never cared about any of that.

To her, he was simply her son.

Suddenly, the front door burst open.

“Dr. Malice!” shouted a voice.

A superhero in a silver suit stood outside.

“Captain Courage!” Dr. Malice exclaimed.

The hero raised his fists. “I have tracked you to your secret hideout!”

“My mother’s house is not a secret hideout!”

Captain Courage looked confused.

Margaret walked into the room carrying a tray of tea.

“Would you like some tea?”

The superhero lowered his fists.

“Uh… yes, please.”

“This is excellent,” he said.

“Thank you,” Margaret replied.

Dr. Malice whispered, “You’re supposed to arrest me.”

“After dessert,” Captain Courage whispered back.

Margaret smiled.

“You boys always were too dramatic.”

Captain Courage expected another battle the next day.

The crowd cheered.

Captain Courage stared at him.

“Why?”

Dr. Malice smiled.

“Because I have to call my mother.”

And for the first time in many years, the city’s greatest villain did something that made everyone happy.

He went home.

"You wore the mantle to my house on Mother's Day."

"I wore it because I was coming straight from—"

"You're not getting cat hair on my good armchair."

He sighed, a sound that rattled the wind chimes on the porch. Edith was already turning, already walking, already pulling him into the house by the sleeve of his enchanted battle-mail. Vor allowed himself to be pulled. He always allowed himself to be pulled. Somewhere in his fortress, a legion of dreadbound warriors were polishing the obsidian throne in his absence. He hoped they were. He'd told them twice.

"You look thin," Edith said, over her shoulder, already in the kitchen.

"Mom."

"I'm just saying. Do they not feed you in that— what do you call it—"

"The Citadel of Eternal Gloom."

"The Citadel. Do they not feed you there? Is there a *cafeteria*?"

"There's a dining hall. We mostly dine on the suffering of—"

"Pot roast, Morty."

He sat at the kitchen table. The kitchen smelled like rosemary and onion and the particular warmth of a home that had decided, decades ago, to be a home and had never gone back on the decision. Edith poured him a glass of iced tea without asking. He removed one gauntlet to drink it. She frowned at the other.

"Both," she said.

"Mom."

"*Both.*"

He removed the other gauntlet. She nodded and disappeared into the dining room to fuss with a vase.

Vor looked around. On the fridge, a school photo of himself at nine, missing his two front teeth. Beside it, a magnet from the Grand Canyon. Beside *that,* a card he had sent her last Mother's Day: *To the world's greatest mother. May your enemies tremble.* Edith had framed it.

He had written it on a Tuesday after losing three lieutenants and a fortress to the Radiant Seven. He'd thought it sounded strong.

"Mortimer."

"Yes, Mom."

"Come taste this."

He rose. He went.

They ate at the small table in the breakfast nook. Edith did not ask about the cape. She asked about the weather. She asked about his sister, Janet, who had become a dentist and was, in Edith's view, the only Ashworth child with sense. She told him his father would have been proud, though she did not specify of what.

After, she made him wash the dishes. He washed the dishes. His gauntlets sat on the counter like two defeated birds.

At the door, she hugged him.

He was careful. He was always careful. The cape bunched. His chin fit awkwardly on top of her head.

"You could come more than once a year," she said into his chest.

"I'll try, Mom."

"You said that last year."

"I know."

"And the year before."

"I know, Mom."

"And—"

"I know."

She released him. He reassembled his gauntlets. The faint violet crackle returned, obedient. Edith looked at it, and at him, and did not flinch.

"You were a beautiful baby," she said.

"I know, Mom."

"It won't be enough, when they come for you."

He paused. "What?"

"It won't be enough," she repeated, "that you were a beautiful baby. You have to be a good man, Mortimer. I mean it."

He opened his mouth. Closed it.

"Goodbye, Mom."

"Goodbye, sweetie."

The door closed. The cape settled.

Vor stood on the porch for a long moment. The suburbs were quiet. A sprinkler ticked somewhere. A dog barked. Somewhere across the city, a great horn sounded from his citadel—his second-in-command, probably, summoning him to a war council concerning the Sphere of Nocturne.

He walked to the car.

He did not put on the gauntlets again until he was three blocks away, and even then, only because the crossing guard was looking.

The words of the old courtier, Sir Alaric, echoed in my mind as I stood in the shadowed alcove of the Queen’s private library. “Don’t be a fool, the Queen can’t die.” He’d said it with such finality, a dismissal of my whispered concern over her recent pallor, the way she’d faltered on the steps of the throne. To him, and to most of the kingdom, Queen Elara was not a woman but an institution, a living monument as eternal as the mountains that ringed our valley.

I, however, was her personal archivist. I saw the tremor in her hand as she signed decrees, the faint blue veins at her temples that seemed more pronounced each season. I catalogued her life, and in doing so, I saw the relentless march of time that others willfully ignored. The legend was simple: a blessing from the First Tree at her coronation had granted her a lifespan tied to the realm itself. As long as the kingdom stood, so would she. It was a beautiful, comforting lie.

My suspicion became an obsession. I began to research not the Queen’s public deeds, but the private logs of her physicians, the cryptic notes in the margins of alchemical texts she’d studied in her youth. One night, hidden in a folio of celestial charts, I found it: a loose page in her own hand, a formula. It was not a blessing, but a complex, grueling regimen. Elixirs brewed from the sap of the very tree that had “blessed” her, combined with rare minerals and a ritual of renewal performed every decade during the lunar eclipse. The next eclipse was in a fortnight.

The truth was staggering. She wasn’t immortal; she was meticulously, arduously maintaining a facade. The stability of the kingdom, the unbroken line of succession, the sheer psychological power of an undying monarch—it all depended on this secret. To reveal it would be to invite chaos, to make her vulnerable to every ambitious lord who saw only a throne, not a tired woman.

I confronted her in the solar, the damning page in my hand. She didn’t feign surprise. Her eyes, ancient and weary, met mine. “So, the archivist has found the final entry,” she said softly. “You think me a fraud?”

“I think you are human,” I whispered, the words feeling like a betrayal. “And the weight of this lie must be crushing.”

She smiled, a sad, thin thing. “The lie is the crown I wear, Leo. It is heavier than any metal. But it keeps the wolves at bay. It keeps the harvests coming and the borders peaceful. My death, when it comes, must be a sudden, tragic event—not the slow decay of a mortal. It must be a story, not a statistic.”

The night of the eclipse arrived. I stood guard outside the hidden chamber beneath the royal gardens, my heart a frantic drum. The ritual was not one of dark magic, but of profound sacrifice. It required a willing participant to share the burden, to take a portion of the life-force channeled from the tree. The Queen had always performed it alone, bearing the full cost.

When I entered, she was pale, slumped against the stone altar. The vial of shimmering sap was empty. “It… it is not enough,” she gasped. “The tree is old. The blessing wanes.” Her eyes found mine, filled not with fear, but with a desperate, silent plea. The fool’s choice was clear: obey the legend and let her die, or become part of the lie.

I knelt, took her hand, and placed it over the vial’s residue. “Then share it,” I said, my voice steady despite my terror. “Let the archivist bear some of the history.”

A light, warm and golden, flowed from the altar, through her, and into me. It was not a transfer of life, but of *responsibility*. I felt the roots of the kingdom in my bones, the weight of its past and the fragile hope for its future. The Queen’s color returned, her breathing eased. The lie was now ours.

The next morning, Queen Elara appeared on the balcony, radiant. The people cheered, their faith reaffirmed. Sir Alaric clapped me on the shoulder. “You see, boy? I told you. She can’t die.”

I smiled, the secret a warm, heavy stone in my chest. “No,” I agreed, my gaze meeting the Queen’s across the courtyard. “She can’t.” And I, the fool who knew the truth, would spend the rest of my days ensuring the legend lived on.
samples.DeepSeek-V4-Flash_story:
The blade trembled in Aldric’s hand. I caught his wrist before he could lunge. “Don’t be a fool,” I said. “The Queen can’t die.”

He sneered. “Everything dies. I’ve seen horses die, dogs, men. Even kings. The Queen is a woman of flesh and blood.”

I released him and stepped back. The Queen sat on the throne, watching us through half-lidded eyes. She did not call for the guards. She never did. “Tell him,” she said. “Tell him what happened to the last one who tried.”

I didn’t want to. But the boy deserved the truth before he threw his life away. “I was the last one,” I said.

That shut him up.

Fifty years ago, I was a young man in the service of a different rebellion. Queen Elara had ruled too long, they said. Her taxes were cruel, her justice crueler. We all believed the realm would breathe free once she was dead. I volunteered to kill her.

I stole into her bedchamber at midnight with a poisoned dagger. She was awake, sitting by the fire, not a guard in sight. She looked up at me and smiled. “You’re early,” she said. “The others came at dawn.”

I lunged. The blade sank into her chest. She didn’t scream, didn’t bleed. She simply sighed, as if I’d made a bad joke. Then the flames in the hearth roared up and swallowed her. I stumbled backward, but the fire did not touch me. When it died down, she was standing there again, whole, wearing the same white gown.

“You see?” she said. “I can’t die. I’ve been trying for a hundred years.”

I learned later that she had been cursed by a god who loved her. Every time she died, fire remade her. She had drowned, hanged, been beheaded, stabbed, poisoned. Always, the fire brought her back. The rebellion withered. The other conspirators were executed. I alone survived, because she found my foolishness amusing. She made me her knight—her jailer, really.

Aldric’s hand was shaking. “Then how do we end her reign?”

“You don’t end it,” I said. “You wait. You hope. You pray that one day the god grows tired of her and lets her go. But she doesn’t die, boy. And neither will you if you try.”

The Queen rose from her throne, gliding down the steps. She stopped before Aldric, close enough to kiss. She touched his cheek, and her fingers were cold. “Your grandfather,” she said, “was just like you. He tried to drown me in the lake. I walked out three days later with reeds in my hair.” She smiled. “I miss him. He was a good man.”

Aldric’s face went pale. He dropped the knife. It clattered on the marble floor.

“I’m sorry,” he whispered.

“Don’t be,” the Queen said. “I would have killed you too. But you’re too young to die.” She turned to me. “Take him to the kitchens. Feed him. Send him home. Another fool will come soon enough.”

I took Aldric’s arm and led him out. At the door, I looked back. The Queen was standing by the window, staring at the setting sun, her face unreadable. Fifty years ago, I had wanted to save the realm. Now I just wanted to save her. But I couldn’t. The god who loved her had also cursed her with an endless life, and my love was not strong enough to break it.

“Does she ever cry?” Aldric asked in a small voice.

“Every night,” I said. “But the fire dries her eyes before morning.”

We walked on. Behind us, the throne room was silent. The Queen did not die that day, or the next, or any day after. But I kept my vigil. It was the only gift I could give her—someone who remembered that she was not a monster, but a woman who had been loved too much.
samples.Muse-Spark-1.2-Contributor_story:
You hear the bells before you see the body.

They are not the bright, brassy bells for a coronation or a wedding. These are the low bells, the ones they keep muffled with cloth for funerals, and they make the stone of the palace feel like a throat trying not to cough. You are pressed behind the tapestry in the north hall, the one with the stag hunt woven into it, and the dust is getting in your nose and making your eyes water. You are seventeen and you are supposed to be in the kitchens peeling turnips, not here.

Old Miri finds you there. Her hand closes around your wrist, thin and hot as a bird's claw.

"Don't be a fool, the Queen can't die," she hisses at you, and she says it the way she says everything, like she's scolding you for leaving the cellar door open again.

You stare at her. You want to say, *but she is dead, listen*, but Miri pulls you out from behind the tapestry and drags you back down the servants' stair before you can answer. Her grip doesn't loosen until you are both back in the steam and the clatter of the kitchens.

That is how it has always been. For your whole life the Queen has been there. Not the woman — you have seen her, of course, a small woman with a lined face and hands that shake a little when she lifts her teacup on the balcony — but the fact of her. THE Queen. The coins have her profile on them, worn smooth at the cheek from so many thumbs. The oaths you swore when you were tall enough to hold a broom were to her. When the northern lords tried to rebel when you were nine, they were beheaded in her name. When the river flooded the low quarter, it was her granaries that opened. She doesn't just rule the kingdom. In your mind, she *is* the kingdom.

And now the low bells are ringing and the maids at the washbasins are crying and the steward is walking the halls with his black armband on, and none of it makes sense with what Miri said.

You don't stay in the kitchen. You tell Miri you need to fetch water and instead you slip back up the stairs. You need to see it for yourself. You are not a fool, you tell yourself, you are just someone who needs to see.

The palace is strange when it is in mourning. No one stops you. The guards at the royal apartments stand with their halberds reversed, their eyes fixed forward, tears cutting clean lines through the dust on their faces. The doors to her bedchamber are open. You have never seen them open before.

You step inside. You shouldn't be there. The air smells of lavender and something else, something sharp and medicinal that makes your stomach turn. The physicians are standing by the windows, murmuring. The priests are kneeling. And on the great bed, under the heavy velvet coverlet, the Queen lies very still.

She looks smaller than she did on the balcony. Her mouth is open a little. Her chest does not move. One of her hands rests outside the covers, and you can see the blue veins through the paper-thin skin. She looks, terribly and finally, dead.

A sob escapes you before you can stop it. One of the priests looks up, sees you in your stained kitchen apron, and doesn't even have the energy to chase you out.

It is then that you hear Miri's voice behind you again. She has followed you, of course she has.

"Oh, child," she says, softer this time. She comes to stand beside you and takes your hand. You expect her to pull you away, but she doesn't. She just looks down at the bed too. "Don't you understand what I meant?"

You shake your head. Your eyes are full.

Miri sighs. "That woman there, Elena? She was born in a farmhouse with six other girls. She married a prince because her father had wheat to offer. She will die, as we all do. She is dying now."

She squeezes your hand.

"But the Queen?" Miri nods at the priests, at the guards outside, at the bells that are still tolling low and steady enough to rattle the glass in the windows. "The Queen was never Elena. The Queen is the promise that when the river floods, someone will open the granary. The Queen is why those boys out there stand still instead of looting the silver. Elena dies. The Queen can't die. If she did, what would we be?"

You look at the still face on the pillow, and then past it, to the window. Outside, in the courtyard below, you can see the crowd growing. They are not rioting. They are kneeling. A new standard is already being raised over the gate — the same stag, the same crown. Somewhere a herald is clearing his throat to announce the Princess.

You finally understand that the bells are not just mourning one old woman's stopped heart. They are making room for the next one.

Miri tugs your hand again, and this time you go with her willingly back toward the kitchens, back toward the turnips and the steam, where work still needs to be done.
samples.Gemini-3.6-Flash_story:
The silence in the royal chamber was heavy enough to drown in. I dropped to my knees beside the velvet canopy bed, my fingers trembling as I pressed them against her throat. Nothing. No fluttering pulse, no faint whisper of breath against my knuckles. Her skin, usually glowing with that strange, ethereal warmth, was as cold as iron in midwinter.

"She’s gone," I whispered, my voice breaking under the weight of a kingdom’s ruin. "The poison... it worked. Lord Vane, we have failed."

Behind me, the old advisor didn't hurry to her side. He didn't tear his robes or call for the guard. He merely swirled the wine in his goblet, the ruby liquid catching the dim light of the tallow candles.

"Don't be a fool, the Queen can't die."

I snapped my head around, my eyes burning with tears and fury. "Look at her! Her heart has stopped! The shadow-blade pierced her ribs not an hour ago! I watched the life leave her eyes, Vane!"

Vane sighed, setting his glass upon the mahogany desk with a dull click. He stepped forward, his leather boots echoing hollowly on the stone floor. He didn't look at the corpse with grief, but with the weary patience of a clockmaker looking at a stopped pendulum.

"You have served her for three years, Julian," he said quietly, reaching out to peel back the embroidered blankets. "You believed you were guarding a woman. A beautiful, fragile sovereign who wore a crown of white gold."

"She *is* a woman," I rasped.

"She is the anchor," Vane corrected.

He reached down, but instead of pulling her eyelids closed, he pressed his thumb firmly against the center of her collarbone. A faint click echoed through the room.

I staggered back, drawing my sword halfway from its scabbard. "What are you doing to her?"

Before he could answer, the room grew cold—colder than her skin, colder than death itself. The air thrummed with a low, vibrating hum that made my teeth ache. Beneath the pale, dead flesh of her neck, thin veins of iridescent gold began to ignite.

The black blood that had pooled beneath her chest didn't dry; it bubbled, evaporating into thin, sweet-smelling purple smoke. Her skin began to spiderweb with fractures, glowing from within like light shining through cracked porcelain.

"What is this magic?" I gasped, paralyzed by the sight.

"It is no spell, Julian," Vane said, stepping back beside me, placing a heavy hand on my trembling shoulder. "It is a contract made three hundred years ago, when the first king bled out on the barren fields of Oakhaven. The land demanded a living heart to bleed for it, forever."

The porcelain shell of her cheek shattered with a soft sound, like fine glass underfoot. It dissolved into dust, revealing not bone or muscle beneath, but a swirling, radiant core of raw energy. The fractures spread quickly down her arms, her torso, her legs, until the dead shell crumbled entirely into gray ash.

Floating inches above the bed, the golden core pulsed once. Twice.

Then, it expanded. Light flooded the bedchamber, so bright I had to shield my eyes. The blinding glow spun into silk-like threads, weaving together in midair. I watched in horrific wonder as bone formed from light, muscle from shadow, and skin from the fading illumination.

Within moments, the light collapsed with a soft sigh of wind.

On the bed lay a young woman. Her dark hair cascaded over the pillows, her chest rising and falling in deep, rhythmic breaths. Her face was different—younger, her nose slightly softer, her lips fuller—yet when her eyelids fluttered open, those same ancient, violet eyes locked onto mine.

She looked down at her new hands, then up at the ash resting on the blankets. A single tear slipped down her cheek.

"It hurts every time," she whispered, her voice bearing the eerie, resonant echo of a dozen forgotten queens.

Vane bowed deeply, his head almost touching the floor. "Welcome back, Your Majesty."

I slowly lowered my sword, the metal clicking softly back into its sheath. I looked at the advisor, then at the eternal creature sitting on the bed, realizing the true terror of our realm. Enemies could breach our walls, armies could fall, and dynasties could crumble into obscurity, but we were bound forever to a ruler who could never escape her crown.

When the Queen collapsed at the harvest feast, goblet clattering across the marble, I did what any young physician would do: I panicked, and then I reached for my purge kit. The poison was thick在她的 wine—corval, judging by the blue veins spidering up her wrist. Corval kills in minutes. Everyone in the hall knew it. The guests froze mid-scream when old Odile, who had served three generations of the crown, seized my sleeve and hissed in my ear.

"Don't be a fool, the Queen can't die."

I stared at her. Behind her, Her Majesty lay rigid on the stones, lips darkening, and still Odile blocked my path with the serenity of a woman guarding garden gate. Around us the court held its breath, waiting, not for a miracle, but for something they already understood. Then, before my eyes, the blue in the Queen's veins receded. The color returned to her face. She sat up, straightened her circlet, and asked for another glass of wine.

The court applauded. I vomited into a decorative urn.

That night Odile found me cataloguing poisons in the dispensary, my hands still shaking.

"Corval should have emptied her," I said. "I've seen it stop a draft horse."

"Three hundred years ago," Odile replied, "the first Queen of our line knelt beneath the old chapel and caught a falling star. It was a heart, still beating. She bound it to her blood with promises no one remembers properly, and so long as that heart beats under the flagstones, the crown cannot be killed by poison, blade, or time." She hesitated. "It passes to each Queen. The kingdom calls it a blessing."

"And the Queen?" I asked. "What does she call it?"

Odile did not answer. That was answer enough.

I should have left it alone. Instead, I began meeting Her Majesty in the dispensary after midnight, officially to check the scar tissue along her ribs, where an assassin's pike had once closed like a clasp. She was, by decades, older than any portrait admitted. She had buried a daughter sixty winters ago, and a granddaughter, and every friend she had not had the discipline to avoid making.

"I have read your father's notes," she told me one night, turning a vial of corval in her fingers. "He suspected the truth and burned the page. You won't."

"That's slander."

"It's permission."

For a year we experimented with the careful cowardice of two people committing treason against biology. Distillation, dosage, venoms that were technically prayers. Nothing held; the star-heart thumped on far beneath our feet, resetting her body to some untouchable template, night by night. She began to tell me which child had had her laugh, and which the hard jaw. She told me the coronation had frightened her because it measured eternity against a girl's courage. The longer we failed together, the less professional our hours became, and the more the kingdom seemed, to both of us, a theater with one actress who had never been allowed to leave the stage.

On the last night we went down to the chapel with a mason's hammer and my sister's ringed hand, because the court had begun to whisper and whispers grow teeth. The star-heart hung in a reliquary of root and wire, pulsing like a coal. I lifted the hammer. I confess I lifted it slowly, giving her time to forbid me.

Instead she placed her palm over mine, warm and ordinary, a hand that had signed treaties and once, briefly, dried my tears.

"Don't be a fool," she said softly, and the words had changed since Odile first spoke them. "I *can* die. You're only making it take longer."

I struck. The light under the chapel went out like a held breath finally let go.

Her Majesty died that winter in her bed, at the age she chose to tell the history books, with the windows open to whatever snow was falling that year. The kingdom mourned, then learned, slowly, the ordinary difficulty of mortal queens, which I attend now from the dispensary Odile gave me. On the last page of my father's burned notebook there is one surviving line, which I have taken as my oath and occasionally my warning: a long life is not a promise; it is only more time in which to choose what it is for. She chose. I was permitted, at the end, to be a witness instead of a fool.

“Don’t be a fool, the Queen can’t die.”

Edwin whispered the words as if speaking them too loudly might make them untrue.

I stared at him across the candlelit chamber. Beyond the tall windows, rain battered the palace roofs, and thunder rolled over the city. Every bell in the capital had been silent since midnight.

That was how we knew something was wrong.

The Queen had ruled for seventy-three years. She had survived wars, rebellions, poisonings, fires, and three assassination attempts. She had become less a woman and more a fact of nature. Children were born, grew old, and died while the Queen remained exactly as she had always been.

Until tonight.

“I saw her,” I said. “She was lying in the Hall of Mirrors. The physician declared her dead.”

Edwin shook his head.

“The physician is a fool.”

“He checked her pulse.”

“Then he checked the wrong wrist.”

Despite myself, I almost laughed. Edwin had been the Queen’s servant since childhood. He knew every secret passage in the palace, every hidden drawer, every mood that crossed her face. If the Queen had been poisoned, he would have known the smell. If she had been stabbed, he would have seen the wound.

But I had seen her body.

“She was cold,” I said.

Edwin’s expression changed.

“Cold?”

“Yes.”

He stepped closer and lowered his voice.

“Then we have very little time.”

He led me through a narrow door behind a tapestry of the royal hunting party. We descended a spiral staircase I had never known existed. At the bottom stood an iron door.

Edwin produced a key.

Inside was a room filled with books, clocks, and strange instruments. At its center stood a stone table.

On the table lay a small silver box.

“The Queen showed me this twenty years ago,” Edwin said. “She made me swear never to speak of it.”

He opened the box.

Inside was a black crystal no larger than a walnut.

“What is it?”

“The reason she cannot die.”

I reached toward it.

“Don’t touch it.”

Too late.

The crystal flashed.

Suddenly, memories flooded my mind—not mine, but hers.

I saw the Queen as a young girl, standing beside an ancient lake. I saw a pale figure rise from the water and place the crystal in her hand.

*You may live as long as the kingdom needs you,* the figure had said.

Then I saw the cost.

The Queen could not die while the crown remained in her possession.

Not from age.

Not from illness.

Not even by murder.

But the kingdom had grown desperate. Its people were starving. Nobles fought in secret. The army was preparing to rebel. The Queen had become the single thing holding everything together.

And now she wanted to leave.

“She asked me to help her,” Edwin said.

“Help her die?”

“No. Help her choose a successor.”

Footsteps echoed above us.

Edwin’s face went pale.

“The council.”

We hurried back upstairs.

The Hall of Mirrors was crowded when we returned. Ministers stood around the Queen’s body, arguing about who should take the throne. Outside, soldiers gathered in the rain.

Then one of the ministers shouted, “The kingdom must have a ruler by sunrise!”

A hand moved beneath the white cloth covering the Queen.

Everyone froze.

The cloth fell away.

The Queen sat upright.

She looked at us with tired eyes.

“I heard you were having trouble deciding what to do with me,” she said.

Someone screamed.

Edwin laughed.

I could only stare.

The Queen rose slowly from the table.

“For seventy-three years,” she said, “I have believed that immortality was a blessing.”

She looked toward the windows.

“Tonight I discovered it was a prison.”

She removed the crown from her head.

The moment it touched the floor, every bell in the city began to ring.

The Queen smiled.

Then, for the first time in her life, she looked old.

Not weak. Not frightened.

Simply human.

She turned to me.

“Come here, child.”

I stepped forward.

“Tomorrow,” she said, “you will help me choose a king.”

“And what happens to you?”

She glanced at Edwin.

He was crying.

“I suppose,” she said softly, “I finally get to find out what everyone else already knows.”

She walked toward the open doors.

Behind her, dawn began to brighten the sky.

And for the first time in seventy-three years, the Queen was afraid of tomorrow.

She was also smiling.

That was how I knew she was free.
samples.Claude-Sonnet-5-High_story:
"Don't be a fool, the Queen can't die."

Marta said it the way she said everything—flat, certain, like she was reading from a book only she could see. I had run three miles through the frost-hardened fields to bring her the news, and this was what I got. Not shock. Not grief. Just that maddening calm.

"I saw the body," I said, still catching my breath. "I saw them carry her out of the east wing myself."

"You saw *a* body." Marta didn't look up from the herbs she was sorting, her fingers moving with the same unhurried rhythm as always. "The Queen has not died in three hundred years, Josia. Not once. Do you understand what that means?"

I didn't, not really. I was nineteen and had grown up on stories—the Queen who never aged, who had ruled since before my grandmother's grandmother was born, who some said was not entirely a woman anymore but something older wearing a woman's shape. I had always assumed these were just stories, the kind told to children to make the world feel steadier than it was.

"The physicians pronounced her dead an hour ago," I said. "The bells have already started."

Marta finally looked up. Her eyes, pale as winter sky, held something I hadn't seen in her before—not fear, exactly, but a kind of tired recognition. "Then we don't have much time. Come."

She led me down through the cellar of her cottage, past shelves of jarred roots and dried flowers, to a door I had never noticed before, hidden behind a curtain of hanging garlic. Beyond it, stone steps spiraled down into darkness that smelled of earth and something else—something like the inside of a church, all incense and old stone.

"What is this place?"

"Insurance," Marta said. "Every physician who has served the crown for the last three centuries has known this passage. Every one of them has sworn to use it, should the day ever come." She produced a small brass key from beneath her collar, one I'd seen a hundred times and never asked about. "The Queen does not simply die, Josia. When her body fails, there is a passage. A transfer. The soul does not end—it moves."

I stared at her, this woman who had bandaged my knee when I was six, who had taught me which mushrooms would kill a man and which would only make him sleep. "You're saying she's some kind of—"

"I'm saying the crown requires continuity, and continuity requires more than one body can give." Marta's voice was steady, but her hands, I noticed, were not. "There is a girl. Sixteen years old, living three villages over, who has no idea what she is about to become. I was supposed to fetch her before the old Queen's heart stopped. I miscalculated the time she had left."

The stairs ended in a chamber lit by candles that seemed to have been burning for years without diminishing. In the center stood a mirror, tall as a door, its surface rippling like water though nothing touched it.

"You're going through that."

"We both are." Marta held out her hand. "You wanted to know why I wasn't afraid, Josia. This is why. The Queen can't die because the Queen was never meant to be one woman. She is an office. A vessel. And vessels can be replaced, refilled, carried forward." She smiled, and for the first time it didn't look like her at all. "I have done this eleven times now. It does not get easier. But it is necessary."

I took her hand because I did not know what else to do, because the bells above us were still ringing, mourning a death that apparently was not one, and because some part of me understood that whatever waited on the other side of that mirror, I could not face it alone.

We stepped through together, into whatever came next.
samples.MiniMax-M3_story:
``don't be a fool, the Queen can't die.''

Master Toma said it without looking up from the parsnips he was peeling, his knife moving in long, steady strokes. The skin fell away in pale ribbons, curling at his feet like the shed skins of small pale snakes. I stood in the doorway of the kitchen, still holding the sack of onions I had been sent to fetch, my arms aching, the morning light from the scullery behind me making my shadow stretch long across the flagstones.

``But everyone says—'' I began.

``Everyone says a great many things.'' He set the knife down and looked at me then, his eyes the color of old tea, and very tired. ``Everyone said the eastern wall would hold. Everyone said the Duke of Verren was our friend. You know how everyone ended.''

I did. Everyone ended in the long cold of last winter, when the snow came early and the grain did not, and the great bells of the cathedral rang for forty days and did not stop. I was nine years old then. I am twelve now, and thin, and I know how to skin a rabbit and how to tell a good potato from a bad one by feel alone.

``Her Majesty has ruled for sixty years,'' I said. ``She will rule for sixty more.''

Master Toma was quiet for a long moment. Then he picked up his knife again. ``Sixty years,'' he said softly, almost to himself. ``Yes. That is a long time to be the only mother half the kingdom remembers.''

I had not thought of it that way. I had only ever thought of the Queen as the Queen — a name spoken in whispers, a portrait in the great hall, a seal pressed into red wax on proclamations I could not read. My mother had died in the winter too, of the cough that took so many. When I think of mothers now, I think only of the Queen, and how she must be very old, and very tired, and how she must surely wish for rest.

``Set down those onions, boy,'' Master Toma said. ``And listen to me.''

I set them down. He wiped his hands on his apron and leaned against the great oak table where the day's bread was rising in its cloths.

``The Queen is a woman,'' he said. ``She was a girl once, and then a young woman, and then a woman, and now she is an old woman. Her heart is no different from yours or mine. It can be broken. It can be stopped.''

I stared at him. I had never heard anyone speak of the Queen so.

``There are those who wish it stopped,'' he went on. ``There are always such. And there are those who would tell you the Queen cannot die because it is convenient for them that she lives. Do you understand? The crown must pass to someone. The crown always passes to someone. And when it does, the world will not end, but it will change, and the ones who profit from the changing will be ready, and the ones who do not will weep in the dark.''

I thought of the man who had come to our village last spring, with his fine coat and his soft hands and his questions about the old Queen and her habits and her health. I had answered some of them. I had not known I should not.

``What do I do?'' I asked.

Master Toma looked at me for a long moment. ``You peel the onions,'' he said at last. ``You do not speak to strangers. You do not repeat what you hear in this kitchen. And you pray, if you pray, for a gentle end, whether it comes this year or in twenty.''

He turned back to his parsnips. The skin fell away. Outside, somewhere beyond the high walls of the kitchen garden, a bell began to toll — not the mourning bell, not yet, but the small bell of the palace, calling the Council to session.

I picked up the sack of onions. My arms ached. The light had shifted, and my shadow was no longer long but small and dark at my feet, as though I had grown smaller in the speaking.

``Master Toma,'' I said, and my voice sounded strange to me, very young and very old at once. ``Do you think she knows?''

He did not turn around. ``I think,'' he said, ``that she has known for a very long time. And I think she is tired. And I think that when the end comes — as it must come for all of us, fool or king, queen or kitchen boy — we should be glad she had such a long and such a stubborn run of it.''

The parsnip peeled clean in his hand. I carried the onions to the table and began to cry, though I could not have said why.

The first sign was the silence. Not the quiet of a winter morning, but a profound, muffling stillness that swallowed sound whole. Commander Elara Vasquez watched from the observation deck of Artemis Base as Earth, her brilliant blue marble, slowly turned a uniform, sterile white. The communications feeds had died three days prior, one by one, like stars winking out. The last coherent message from Houston was a choked, static-laced farewell: “The ice… it’s everywhere. Godspeed, Artemis. You’re the seed now.”

The seed. That’s what they were. One hundred and twelve souls in a pressurized can on the Moon, the last flickering candle of humanity. The initial shock gave way to a grim, methodical routine. Every gram of water was recycled with fanatical efficiency. The hydroponic bays, glowing with purple light, became their temples, the tender green shoots of lettuce and soy more precious than gold. Elara instituted strict rationing, her voice steady over the intercom even as her own stomach knotted with hunger. They were a closed system, a tiny, fragile biosphere hurtling through the void.

The middle was a long, cold grind. Morale was a resource as critical as oxygen. Dr. Aris Thorne, the base’s psychologist, organized “Earth Remembrances” in the common module. Crew members would share stories—of rain on skin, of the smell of pine forests, of the chaotic, beautiful noise of a city. Engineer Jin would describe the taste of his grandmother’s spicy noodles, his eyes closed, and for a moment, the recycled air would seem to carry a ghost of ginger and chili. These moments were both a comfort and a torture, a reminder of all they had lost.

Their salvation, ironically, came from the very thing that had doomed their home. The lunar regolith, the powdery dust that coated everything, was rich in helium-3. With Earth’s supply chains gone, their small experimental fusion reactor became their lifeline. Jin and his team worked miracles, coaxing more power from the aging system, patching leaks with ingenuity and desperation. The reactor’s hum became the heartbeat of the base, a constant, low vibration that promised another day of light, of heat, of life.

But the seed needed to grow. Elara convened the council. “We can’t just survive,” she said, her gaze sweeping over the tired faces. “We have to build. We have to become a civilization.” They began with the domes. Using sintered regolith and polymer composites, they expanded, creating new spaces not just for living, but for *becoming*. A school module was established, where the base’s seven children learned physics from astronauts and poetry from botanists. A small observatory was built, not for studying the dead Earth, but for charting the stars, for dreaming of other worlds.

Years bled into one another. Elara’s hair turned silver. The children grew into teenagers, then young adults who had never felt wind or seen an ocean. They were the Lunars, a new generation with a different perspective. They didn’t mourn Earth with the same raw ache; they revered it as a sacred, lost origin. Their hope was not to return, but to go forward.

The breakthrough came from the school. A young woman named Kaelen, analyzing deep-core ice samples from a permanently shadowed crater, found something unexpected: preserved microbial life, dormant for eons. It wasn’t a complex organism, but it was *life*, resilient and patient. The discovery electrified the base. If life could persist here, in the frozen, airless dark, then the universe was not so hostile. The seed wasn’t just preserving a memory; it was discovering a new truth.

On the twentieth anniversary of the Freeze, Elara, now elderly, stood before the assembled base in the newly completed Atrium—a vast dome where a single, genetically engineered oak tree grew under a simulated sun. She looked at the faces before her: the original crew, lined and weary; the Lunars, strong and clear-eyed; the children, squirming with restless energy.

“They called us the last hope,” Elara said, her voice thin but clear. “But hope isn’t a static thing you guard. It’s a direction. We are not a museum of humanity. We are its next chapter. We have learned to live with less, to cherish more, and to look outward. Earth gave us our past. The Moon has given us our future. And now, we must give that future to the stars.”

A new ship, the *Odyssey*, was taking shape in the orbital dock, its destination a promising exoplanet detected by their observatory. It would carry a crew of Lunars, embryos, and the sum of their knowledge. The seed was preparing to scatter. As Elara watched the construction lights twinkle against the black sky, she felt a profound peace. The Earth was a frozen tomb, a beautiful, heartbreaking monument. But here, in the dust and silence of the Moon, humanity had not just survived. It had learned to plant a garden in the stars.
