The fluorescent lights above the fry station have been flickering for three weeks. I've reported it twice. Nobody's fixed it. In my old life, a flicker like that would have been a warning, a crack of divine displeasure that sent mortals running to their temples. Now it just gives me a headache by hour six.

My name is Kael. I used to be the god of storms. I held dominion over thunder and lightning, the wild winds that toppled empires, the gentle rains that fed the fields. Twelve thousand years of worship, of temples and sacrifices and prayers answered in flashes of light. Then one day, the prayers stopped. The temples crumbled. The new gods with their bright ideas and better marketing took over, and I was... retired. Not by choice. The universe simply moved on.

That was eighty-seven years ago. I learned to live without the power. Learned to sleep through the night without dreaming of hurricanes. Learned to flip burgers without a hint of divine fire. I work the 6 a.m. to 2 p.m. shift at a McDonald's in a strip mall in Akron, Ohio. My manager, a woman named Denise who has never once suspected I once controlled the weather, calls me reliable. I have a 401k and a small apartment with a cat named Thunder.

I was mopping the floor at 1:47 p.m. when the door chimed.

A man walked in. Tall, silver-haired, wearing a coat that looked like it had been stitched together from clouds and starlight. He moved through the lobby as if he owned the air in it. And I knew him. Of course I knew him.

"Mithras," I said, leaning on the mop.

"Kael." He smiled, but it didn't reach his eyes. "You look... mortal."

"Working on it," I said. "What are you doing here?"

He glanced around the restaurant. A teenager in the corner was attempting to eat a McFlurry with a knife and fork. A toddler was screaming about Chicken McNuggets. The ice cream machine was, as always, broken. Mithras seemed to find the whole thing deeply, cosmically amusing.

"I have a proposition for you," he said. "A real one, this time. Not one of those half-measures we've seen over the millennia."

I set the mop against the wall. "I'm listening."

"The Pantheon is being restructured. The old order is gone—most of us scattered, diminished, or pretending to be investment bankers. But there's a vacancy. A big one. The god of storms and ruin needs a new occupant, and the Council has decided to offer it to you."

I stared at him. The air in the restaurant seemed to hold its breath, though that might have been the broken thermostat.

"You're serious," I said.

"I'm always serious. I was the god of solemn oaths, remember? I can't joke about contracts." He pulled out a chair from a booth, sat down, and gestured for me to sit across from him. I hesitated, then untied my apron and joined him.

"If I accept," I said slowly, "I'd be a god again. Full power. Full domain."

"Full power," he confirmed. "Storms. Lightning. The rains. The floods. The hurricanes. All of it. Your temples would be rebuilt. Your name spoken in millions of households. You'd be Kael the Storm-Bearer again, instead of... whatever your name tag says."

I looked down. The tag read KARL. Denise had spelled it wrong on my first day. I never corrected her.

"Give me one reason," I said.

"Because the world needs you," he said. "Because the storms are restless. Because we are, all of us, more than the small lives we've been living."

I thought about my apartment. About Thunder, who would miss the scheduled dinner time. About Denise, who would have to find another reliable employee. About the regulars who came in at 7 a.m. and ordered the same thing every day, and how they waved at me now, and how that had started to feel like something that mattered.

"You can give me a week to think about it," I said.

Mithras nodded, unsurprised. "A week," he said. "But Kael—don't wait too long. The old world is waking up. And I think it needs you more than Akron does."

He stood, tipped an invisible hat, and walked out the door. The bell above the door chimed twice, and somewhere in the distance, just for a moment, I could have sworn I heard thunder.

I retied my apron. The lights above the fry station flickered once more, and this time, on a whim I couldn't quite explain, I waved at them. The flicker stopped.

Denise poked her head out of the office. "Karl? You heading out?"

"Yeah," I said. "Just finishing up."

I picked up the mop again. Outside, the sky was the color of a clean slate, and I had a week to decide what kind of god I wanted to be—if I wanted to be one at all.

# The House at the End of Maple Street

Have you ever gone back to a place you swore you'd never return to? Did you ever stand at the edge of a town you once called home and feel your stomach twist into a knot so tight you thought you might be sick right there on the cracked sidewalk? Isn't that what brought Clara back to Millhaven on that gray October morning, twenty years after she'd left with nothing but a duffel bag and a bus ticket?

Hadn't she told herself a thousand times that she was done with this place? Didn't she build an entire life in Portland — a career, a small apartment with tall windows, a cat named Hemingway — precisely so she'd never have to come back? So why did the phone call from her brother change everything? Could three words — "Mom is dying" — really unravel two decades of careful distance?

Wasn't the house on Maple Street exactly as she remembered it, only smaller somehow, as though it had shrunk in her absence? Didn't the porch sag in the same place where she'd once sat reading comic books while her father drank himself into oblivion inside? Hadn't the oak tree in the front yard grown enormous, its roots buckling the walkway like the bones of something trying to break free from underground? Could a tree hold memories the way a person did?

Did her brother, Thomas, look older than his forty-two years when he opened the front door? Wasn't there a weariness in his eyes that she recognized, because hadn't she seen it in her own reflection every morning? Did they stand there for a long moment, neither of them moving, before he finally pulled her into a hug that smelled like coffee and the same cheap detergent their mother had always used?

Wasn't her mother lying in the back bedroom, propped up on pillows that had gone yellow with age? Could Clara reconcile this frail, papery woman with the fierce, sharp-tongued woman who had once thrown a ceramic plate at the wall hard enough to leave a crater in the plaster? Did her mother's eyes — still that startling shade of green — find Clara's face and fill immediately with tears? Was "I'm sorry" enough, after everything? Could two words carry the weight of a lifetime of damage?

Didn't they talk for hours that first evening? Didn't her mother tell stories Clara had never heard — about her own mother, about a childhood in rural Georgia, about a girl who had dreams of painting but married too young and lost herself in the ordinary machinery of raising children? Could Clara feel something shifting inside her chest, some old wall beginning to crack? Wasn't forgiveness less like a single dramatic moment and more like water slowly wearing down stone?

Did the days that followed blur together in a rhythm of hospital visits and long walks through streets Clara thought she'd forgotten? Didn't she find herself noticing things she'd overlooked as a child — the way the light hit the church steeple at sunset, the sound of Mrs. Gutierrez's laughter carrying over the fence, the smell of bread from the bakery on Third Street that had somehow survived every recession? Could a place you'd hated become, almost against your will, a place you understood?

Wasn't her mother gone by the end of the second week? Didn't Clara hold her hand at the very end, and didn't Thomas hold the other, and wasn't the room unbearably quiet afterward? Could grief and relief exist in the same breath, tangled together like two vines growing around the same post?

Didn't Clara stay for the funeral, and then another week after that? Didn't she help Thomas sort through boxes of old photographs, discovering images of their mother as a young woman — radiant, unburdened, smiling at something just outside the frame? Could Clara carry those photographs back to Portland and set them on her windowsill, where the morning light would touch them every day?

And wasn't that, perhaps, the beginning of something she didn't yet have a name for — a peace that didn't erase the past but made room for it, the way a river makes room for stones?

Did I ever think I would return to a place I swore I would never see again? Wasn't that why I hesitated at the gate, with my hand on the rusted latch? Did I really expect the house to look smaller than it had in my memory? Why did the windows seem darker, as if they were closed like eyes? Who had let the garden grow so wild, with brambles reaching for the porch like thin arms? Had she stopped caring after I left, or had she simply grown too tired to keep up the pretense? Did I have the right to ask those questions now? Didn't the key still fit the lock, turning with the same reluctant click I remembered? Was that a good sign, or a bad omen? Why did I step inside instead, closing the door behind me as if I belonged there? Hadn't the hallway always smelled of beeswax and bread? Where was the old coat rack with its crooked mirror? Did the floorboards creak in the same places, as if they remembered my footsteps? Wasn't it strange that I still ducked under the doorframe? Did I call out “Mother?” and hear only the clock ticking? Was the clock still ticking? Who had wound it since she died? Could a clock keep going out of pure habit, like a heart that refuses to stop?

Didn't I find myself at her bedroom door without remembering the climb? Was the door open a crack, and didn't a cold draft slip through? Did I push it open, or did it move on its own, as if inviting me in? Didn't I see the white envelope on her pillow, with my name written in her shaky hand? Why was there no dust on the pillow, as if she had just lain down? Wasn't her brush still on the vanity, with a few gray hairs caught in the bristles? How could a letter be heavier than the whole house?

Did I sit on the edge of her bed, or did my knees simply give way? Didn't the paper crackle like dry leaves when I unfolded it? What was the first line that blurred before my eyes? Did she write, “To my daughter, who taught me that love can be silence”? Or did she write, “I have saved every newspaper clipping about you”? Did she ask why I had stopped calling, or did she answer her own question by saying that she had learned to wait without expectation? Wasn't that the saddest phrase I had ever read? Did the letter end with an instruction to water the plants, or with a plea to forgive her? Did it matter if the words were an apology or a blessing?

Hadn't I noticed the date at the top of the letter? Wasn't it written three days after my mother died? Who could have placed it on her pillow if not her? Did I believe in ghosts now, or was it just my own longing that made the ink look wet? Wasn't the truth simpler: that she had written it in advance, folding her love like a secret she knew I would need? Didn't I finally understand that she had always been preparing for this moment? Had she not left the lamp by the bed, with a new bulb in it, so I would never be in the dark? Could there be a more perfect farewell than a question?

Was I crying now, and didn't the tears make the words blur into a single gray river? Did I hear a voice, or was it only the wind in the eaves? “Is that you, my love?” Would I answer with a question, as I always did, or would I give her the answer I had withheld for twenty years? Did I say, “Yes, Mother, it's me”? Was that not the only answer that mattered? Hadn't I come home at last? Could I stay now and let the house ask me no more questions? Would I water the roses, wind the clock, and open the windows to the sun? Didn't I know that grief was not a question to be solved but a door to be walked through? Wasn't every breath from now on a question I would answer with my life? Can I begin to ask myself what I want for tomorrow? Will I finally be brave enough to say, “Yes”?

Had she not already read that book four times anyway?
Did she then sit beside him and did they start trading books every week as if they were trading secrets?
Had that bench at the station not become the only place he wanted to be?
Had waiting ever felt so much like arriving before she entered his life?
Did she not tell him one rainy afternoon that she was leaving the city for graduate school in Seattle?
Did the announcement board not flicker that afternoon as if it knew something was ending?
Did she promise she would write, and did he promise he would wait for her letters at that very station?
Had he ever made a promise he knew would be impossible to keep but made it anyway because saying goodbye forever was unthinkable?
Did the first letter arrive exactly two weeks later, folded neatly and smelling faintly of rain?
Did he carry that letter in his pocket until the paper softened at the edges?
Did the second and third letters come just as faithfully, and did he answer each one the night he received it?
When did the letters start to come less often, and when did he start to check the mailbox with dread rather than hope?
Was it his fault for writing too much or too little, or was distance simply doing what distance always does?
Did he not stand at that station long after the line was officially closed, holding a letter that had been returned unopened?
Had he ever stared at a stamp marked Return to Sender and felt as if he himself were being returned?
Did he tell himself he had finally stopped going to the station, or did he merely pretend he had stopped?
Was it not true that he still walked by there every Thursday out of habit, or was it out of something he refused to name?
Would anyone believe that last Thursday the station was not empty at all?
Did he not see a fresh coat of paint on the benches and a new schedule flickering on the board?
Had they reopened the old line without announcement, or had he simply not been paying attention?
Was she not sitting on their old bench, wearing a yellow scarf that was faded but unmistakably the same?
Did his heart not stop when she looked up and smiled as if no time had passed at all?
Could anyone imagine how many questions flooded his mind at once, all of them fighting to be asked first?
Did she ask him if he had kept his promise, and did he ask her why her letters had stopped?
Did she laugh and pull out a bundle of letters tied with twine, all addressed to him and all marked with the wrong address?
Had such a simple mistake not caused three years of silence?
Did she explain that she had moved apartments in her first month and the forwarding order had failed without either of them knowing?
Did he show her the returned letter he had kept in his drawer like some absurd relic?
Did they sit there on that bench and read each other's lost years in a single afternoon, laughing at the misunderstandings that had kept them apart?
Did she ask him when the new 7:15 train finally pulled in, hissing and bright, whether he wanted to finally take that train somewhere together instead of just waiting for it?
Did he hesitate even for a second before saying yes, or did his answer come out before she had even finished asking?
Had an ending and a beginning ever happened at the exact same moment before that?
Would waiting be called wasted time, or would it be called the only thing that kept him in the right place?
Did they board that train together, and did they finally leave that station side by side?
Will the bench they left behind remain empty, or will another lonely soul find it tomorrow and begin a new story?

Did I just open my eyes, or is this suffocating darkness merely playing tricks on my exhausted mind? Why does the stale, stagnant air taste so heavily of ozone, burnt copper, and damp earth? Can you hear that faint, rhythmic thrumming vibrating endlessly beneath the smooth, ice-cold floor? How did I end up trapped in this strange place without a single memory of arriving? Wasn't I just walking home through the pouring rain, watching the amber streetlights bleed across the wet asphalt? Where are my comfortable shoes, my heavy autumn coat, and the silver watch my father gave me? Is this windowless room a forgotten medical ward, a hidden cellar, or something far more sinister? 

When I extend my trembling hands into the void, why do my fingertips collide with a smooth, seamless wall of freezing glass? Am I enclosed inside some kind of transparent cylinder? Is that a faint, flickering light suddenly blooming in the darkness beyond my glass wall? Could that dim glow be coming from a digital monitor mounted high on the opposite stone wall? Why are there small, precise surgical incisions neatly lined along the insides of both my forearms? Did someone drag me here against my will, or did I somehow walk into this nightmare of my own volition? 

As the screen brightens, isn't that a tall, motionless silhouette standing in the shadows just past the glass? Why won't that silent figure answer when I slam my open palms against the enclosure and scream for help? Can't they hear the rising panic in my voice, or is this thick box completely soundproof? What is that glowing red timer in the corner of the room counting down toward? Do we really only have two minutes left before those glowing red numbers reach zero? 

Is that a soft, ominous hiss of gas beginning to seep from the narrow vents near my bare feet? Why does my chest suddenly feel so terribly constricted, as if an invisible iron band is tightening around my lungs? Should I yield to the overwhelming urge to faint, or is there still a tiny chance of escape? What if that spiderweb of faint hairline cracks near the base of the left glass panel is my only salvation? If I draw back my shoulder and hurl my entire body weight against that structural flaw, will the barrier shatter, or will it merely break my bones? Isn't a fractured shoulder far preferable to suffocating in this toxic fog? 

Did the glass just yield with a deep, satisfying groan under the force of my initial blow? Can I manage to strike it again, even harder this time, before the sweet-smelling vapor fills the cylinder entirely? Why is the watcher in the shadows suddenly taking a step back in obvious surprise? Did that arrogant observer truly believe I would just lie down and let the gas take me without a fight? With one final, desperate surge of adrenaline, doesn't the entire transparent wall burst outward into a brilliant shower of glittering shards? 

How impossibly sweet does the cool, dusty air of the outer room feel as I collapse onto the concrete floor? Can I force my trembling legs to stand up before the stunned captor reaches into his heavy coat for a weapon? Is that a heavy iron ring of security keys swinging from his leather belt? What if I rush him before he finishes unholstering whatever metal device he is pulling from his pocket? Isn't that the heavy steel emergency exit door directly behind him, illuminated by the reassuring green glow of an exit sign? 

As I tackle the man into the shadow of the door and snatch the key ring from his waist, don't the missing pieces of my memory suddenly fall into place? Wasn't I the lead architect of this very security vault, locked inside my own experimental chamber by a traitorous research assistant? Didn't my traitor forget that the creator of a maze always knows where the secret maintenance hatches are built? As I jam the master key into the hidden floor lock and slide into the dark safety of the escape chute, can't I help but laugh at the sudden reversal of our roles? Who is the helpless test subject now?
samples.Kimi-K3_story:
Did you wake before dawn with the taste of salt on your tongue? Had the sea been calling your name all night through the cracked window? Why did the floorboards lead you toward the cellar instead of the kettle? Was it strange that the door below the stairs had never been there before? Did its brass knob turn cold in your palm? Could you hear breathing behind it, or was that only your own? When you opened it, did the stairs descend farther than the house allowed? Were the walls lined with bottles, each holding a small blue flame? Did every flame whisper a question as you passed?

Had you taken the lantern because the dark asked you to? Did the first step creak like an old dog dreaming? Were you already too far from morning to turn back? When the tunnel split into three, did you choose the path that smelled of rain? Why did the other two sigh when you left them? Did the stones underfoot remember every traveler who had doubted? Could a map drawn on your wrist by no hand be trusted? Was the ink moving because your pulse was moving? Did you follow it anyway?

Who left a coat on the hook shaped exactly like your shoulders? Whose boots waited beside it, still warm? Did you put them on because they fit, or because they asked to be worn? When the mirror at the bend showed you older, did you bow to yourself? Why did your reflection mouth a word you could not hear? Was it “run,” or was it “stay”? Did the mirror crack when you refused to choose? Could a question break glass if spoken kindly? Did you step through the silver rain without bleeding?

Had the garden beyond the mirror been growing inside you all along? Were the flowers opening only when you wondered what they were? Did the trees lean closer to eavesdrop on your fear? Why did the path keep asking where you had buried your name? Had you lost it in a schoolroom, a hospital, a letter never sent? When the well offered water black as ink, did you drink? Could you taste every answer you had ever swallowed? Did they rise in you like fish toward light? Were you thirsty still?

Who was the keeper waiting beside the gate of thorns? Did she wear your mother’s voice and your enemy’s eyes? Why did she ask what you would give to know one true thing? Did you offer your shadow first, then your laughter, then the key to your house? When she refused them all, did you understand what remained? Could you give the question itself? Would the gate open if you admitted you did not know? Did the thorns bloom when your certainty fell away? Was that the first door you had ever truly unlocked?

Beyond the gate, did the sea stand upright like a wall? Were ships sailing across its face without sinking? Did gulls spell your name and then erase it? Why did the tide bring back the bottle you had thrown away as a child? Was the message inside still blank because you had never dared to write it? When you uncorked it, did the blue flame leap into your chest? Could you feel it asking to be carried home? Did the wall of water become a road when you stopped demanding it move? Were you walking on the sea, or was the sea walking through you?

Had dawn been waiting on the cellar stairs the whole time? Did the house look smaller when you returned? Why did the kettle whistle as if nothing had happened? Were your boots muddy with stars? Did the mirror above the sink show you younger now, or only braver? When someone upstairs called your name, did you answer with a question? Could love be a door held open by not knowing? Would you leave the cellar unlocked for the next frightened traveler? Did you finally understand that every answer had only been another door?

# The Last Question

Could anyone remember when the rain had begun?

Had it started before Mara left the village, or had the first cold drops fallen only after she crossed the old stone bridge?

Why had she ignored the villagers who told her that the forest path disappeared whenever the river rose?

Wasn’t she supposed to be home before sunset?

And why, now that the trees had swallowed the road behind her, could she no longer hear the river at all?

Could the silence mean that she had wandered farther than she realized?

Had she really been walking for three hours?

Why did the forest seem unchanged, with the same crooked oak appearing again and again beside the path?

Was that oak actually the same tree?

Could she have been walking in a circle?

Would anyone in the village come looking for her before nightfall?

What if they had already searched the path and decided she was gone?

Why had she brought the old brass compass if its needle refused to point north?

Could the strange trembling of the needle have something to do with the low humming she now heard beneath the rain?

Was someone singing?

Or was the forest itself making that sound?

Why did the humming stop whenever Mara stopped walking?

Could there be someone following her?

Should she turn around?

Wouldn’t turning around be more dangerous than continuing?

Why, then, did the narrow trail ahead suddenly appear brighter?

Was that moonlight?

But how could there be moonlight when the storm clouds covered the sky?

Could the clearing beyond the trees be the way home?

Why was there a small house standing in the middle of it?

Had that house always been there?

Could a house have appeared without leaving a single footprint in the mud?

Why was its door already open?

Was someone waiting for her?

Should she knock anyway?

What if the house belonged to the person who had been humming?

Could the warm yellow light inside really be more comforting than the darkness outside?

Why did Mara step across the threshold?

Why did the door close behind her?

Was that a candle burning on the table?

And why was there another brass compass beside it?

Could that compass be identical to hers?

Why did both needles suddenly point toward the same locked door at the back of the room?

What was behind that door?

Could the humming be coming from there?

Why did Mara's hands become cold when she touched the handle?

Was she afraid because she already knew what she would find?

Could she possibly have forgotten something important?

Why did the door open so easily?

Was that her own bedroom on the other side?

How could her bedroom be standing inside a house she had never seen?

Why was her younger self sitting beside the window?

Could that little girl really be Mara, eight years old and waiting for her mother to return from the river?

Why was the child holding the same brass compass?

Had Mara's mother given it to her before she disappeared?

Could the compass have been waiting all these years for Mara to come back?

Why did the little girl look up and smile?

Was she asking Mara a question without speaking?

Could Mara hear her own childhood voice whispering, “Will you come home this time?”

Why had she never remembered making that promise?

Had she spent all these years believing her mother had vanished when perhaps it was Mara who had refused to follow?

Could the forest have been keeping the memory until Mara was brave enough to face it?

Why did the rain suddenly become louder?

Was the house beginning to shake?

Could the walls disappear like mist?

Why was the little girl reaching toward her?

Should Mara take her hand?

What would happen if she did?

Could she finally change what had happened?

Why was the compass needle spinning faster?

Was time running out?

Could one question truly change a life?

Why had Mara been so certain that she needed an answer?

What if the answer had always been another question?

Would she forgive her mother if she learned that her mother had not abandoned her but had drowned trying to save Mara from the river?

Could Mara forgive herself for surviving?

Why did the little girl suddenly disappear?

Was the bedroom collapsing into darkness?

Could Mara still hear the child asking whether she would come home?

Why did Mara run toward the voice instead of away from it?

Was the floor becoming water beneath her feet?

Could she swim?

Why did she reach for the compass as it floated past?

Did she hear someone shouting her name?

Was it the village bell?

Could morning already be breaking?

Why did Mara open her eyes beside the old stone bridge?

Were the villagers gathered around her?

Had she been missing only one night?

Why was the brass compass still clenched in her hand?

Could anyone explain where she had found it?

Why did the compass needle now point steadily toward home?

Would Mara ever tell anyone what had happened in the forest?

Could she explain it without sounding like a dream?

Why did she begin walking toward the village?

Was it because, after all those years, she finally understood what her mother had wanted?

Could coming home sometimes mean accepting that the past could not be changed?

And if forgiveness was not an answer, could it be the question she was finally willing to live with?
samples.Claude-Sonnet-5-High_story:
Have you ever noticed how a house sounds different at three in the morning?

Wasn't it strange, the way the floorboards seemed to breathe when I finally got out of bed that night?

Why else would I have walked downstairs in the dark, barefoot, heart thudding, if not because I heard something scrape against the kitchen window?

Could it have been a branch, or was it something else entirely, something with intention?

Isn't it funny how the mind invents monsters the moment the lights go out?

But what was I supposed to think when I saw the back door standing open, swinging gently on its hinges, though I was certain I had locked it before bed?

Wasn't Mrs. Alvarez, my neighbor, always warning me about the raccoons that got into everyone's trash on this street?

Could a raccoon really have unlatched a deadbolt, though?

What kind of person, or creature, leaves a door open just enough to invite someone out into the night?

Didn't I know, even as I stepped onto the cold porch, that I should have called for help instead of walking out there alone?

Why do we always ignore the voice that tells us to turn back?

Was it curiosity, or something more foolish, that made me follow the faint trail of footprints leading toward the old shed at the edge of the yard?

Hadn't that shed been locked for years, ever since my father passed and left it full of tools nobody used anymore?

So why was there a sliver of light glowing beneath its door?

Could it be that someone had been living out there, hidden from the world, all this time?

Wasn't my hand shaking as I reached for the handle, half hoping it would be locked after all?

What would you have done, if the door creaked open on its own before you even touched it?

Was I imagining the shape hunched in the corner, or was it real, breathing, alive?

Didn't its eyes catch the moonlight in a way that made my stomach twist?

Could I have run, should I have run, instead of whispering, "Who's there?"

Wasn't it my father's voice that answered, low and rasping, as though it had traveled through years just to reach me?

How could that be possible, when I had watched them lower his casket into the ground three years ago?

Wasn't grief supposed to fade, not manifest as a shape in a dusty shed at midnight?

Did I dream it, or did he really say my name, the way he used to when I was small and scared of the dark?

Why did I feel such an unbearable pull toward that voice, even as every rational thought screamed at me to step back?

Could love outlast death enough to leave an echo like this?

Wasn't I crying by the time I knelt down in front of him, even though I couldn't be sure it was really him at all?

What do you do when the impossible looks you straight in the eye and calls you "sweetheart"?

Didn't I want, more than anything, to believe it was true?

But wasn't there also a small, aching part of me that knew grief could conjure ghosts out of longing alone?

Could I let myself hope, knowing hope like that might break me all over again?

Wasn't it easier, in the end, to reach out and touch the shape, to see if it was real?

And when my fingers passed through nothing but cold air and settled dust, wasn't that answer enough?

Didn't the shape dissolve like breath on a winter morning, leaving only silence and the smell of my father's old pipe tobacco?

Wasn't I sitting there afterward, alone in the shed, wondering if I had imagined the whole thing?

But wasn't there also a strange peace settling over me, as though some final goodbye had finally been said?

Isn't it strange how we spend our lives searching for signs, and how sometimes, just once, in the middle of the night, we find them?

And isn't it enough, in the end, just to have been reminded that love doesn't have to make sense to be real?

Have you ever woken up and felt certain something was wrong before you even opened your eyes? Did I really believe that the morning would be ordinary as I swung my legs over the side of the bed? Why was the air in the apartment so quiet, when I usually woke to the sounds of traffic and the neighbor's dog? Should I have noticed sooner that the sunlight coming through my window had the wrong color, that pale yellow of late autumn rather than the bright gold of June? Was this the first sign that the world I knew had quietly ended while I slept?

Did I hesitate at the bedroom door because part of me already knew what waited on the other side? Could the photograph on the wall really have shown my mother's face if she had been alive, when I had buried her only seven months ago? Did the empty hook in the hallway mean that my father had finally taken his coat and left, the way he had threatened to do for years? Why did the kitchen smell of fresh coffee when no one else had a key, and when had I last remembered to buy any grounds? Was I the kind of person who brewed coffee in his sleep and forgot, or was someone else entirely moving through my home while I lay dreaming?

Should I have called out then, instead of padding barefoot down the hall toward the front door? Did I really think I would find an answer in the street, when all the answers I needed were inside? Was the snow on the doorstep in June an omen, or simply a trick of memory and the wrong season bleeding through the glass? Why was the newspaper lying in the bushes, dated three days from now, and what did it mean that my own name was printed in the obituaries? Had I died without noticing, and was this the strange country the dead were sent to when their work on earth was not yet finished?

Could I have stopped at any moment and chosen to sit down, to wait, to refuse the strange gravity pulling me out into the world? Would the street have looked any different if I had paid attention to where I was going instead of where I had been? Did the man sitting on the park bench know my name before I spoke it, and how long had he been waiting there for someone exactly like me? Was his smile a welcome or a warning, and should I have read the meaning of it before he opened his mouth to ask the questions I had been asking myself all morning?

Why did his voice sound so much like mine, only slower, the way a record plays when the battery is dying? Did he offer me a cup of something warm, and was I foolish enough to take it from a stranger on a day when even the light was lying? What did he mean when he said that every question carries its own answer inside it, like a seed carries the whole tree? Could it really be true that I had not been searching for what had happened to me, but for what I had been avoiding for years? Had I built this strange June snow and this impossible future obituary so that someone would finally make me stop and sit down on a bench and listen?

Should I have believed him when he told me my mother was waiting at home, alive and young again the way she had been before I was born? Did he really say that I could walk back into my apartment and find everything the way it had been, or had I invented that part in the hope of making the morning bearable? Why was the snow under my feet turning to rain, and why was the man on the bench beginning to fade at the edges like a photograph held too close to a candle? Was I waking up, or was I finally letting myself sleep, and which of these two states had I been afraid of all along?

Did I open my eyes in the right world, or had I simply traded one question for another, and would the next morning bring more snow, more silence, more answers I had not yet earned?

# The Last Verse

It started the Tuesday after Marcus's twenty-sixth birthday. One moment we were sitting in our usual booth at Sal's Diner, arguing about whether a hot dog qualifies as a sandwich, and the next moment Marcus opened his mouth and said, "A hot dog in a bun, I think, is not a sandwich, not a wink." He froze. I stared at him. He stared at me. Then he tried again: "I mean to say, this isn't right, my words have taken sudden flight."

We both laughed at first. We figured it was some kind of nervous tic, a one-time glitch. But by Wednesday morning, Marcus couldn't order coffee without saying, "One cup of black, if you don't mind, the darkest roast that I can find." By Friday, he'd been fired from his accounting firm for telling a client, "Your taxes are a tangled mess, your deductions cause me great distress."

That was when the laughing stopped.

I dragged Marcus to Dr. Pham, a neurologist who'd once fixed my migraines. She ran every scan and test imaginable. Her conclusion was delivered with a furrowed brow and a shrug: "I've never seen anything like it. His brain is perfectly healthy. There's no tumor, no lesion, no electrical anomaly. It's as if his language center has simply... rewired itself."

"Can you fix it?" I asked.

She hesitated. "I don't even know what *it* is."

Marcus, sitting on the exam table in his paper gown, looked at me with those brown eyes that always reminded me of a confused puppy. "The doctor cannot find the key, to unlock the words inside of me," he said softly. Then he buried his face in his hands.

I refused to accept that. Marcus had been my best friend since the third grade, when he'd shared his fruit snacks with me on the playground. He'd talked me through my parents' divorce, helped me move three times, and once drove four hours in a snowstorm because I'd called him crying after a breakup. I owed him everything. I would not let him become a permanent nursery rhyme.

I started researching obsessively. I read about aphasia, about Tourette's, about every neurological condition that could affect speech. I found a case study from 1987 about a woman in Prague who'd spoken exclusively in haiku after a car accident. She'd been cured through a combination of cognitive behavioral therapy and targeted electrical stimulation. It was a long shot, but it was a shot.

I found Dr. Elara Voss at Johns Hopkins, a neurolinguist who specialized in speech pattern disorders. I called her office fourteen times before she agreed to see Marcus. We flew to Baltimore on a rainy Thursday in March.

Dr. Voss was different from Dr. Pham. Where Pham had shrugged, Voss leaned forward with hungry eyes. "Fascinating," she murmured as Marcus described his symptoms in couplets. She mapped his brain activity while he spoke, while he tried to suppress the rhyming, while he sang, while he whispered. After three hours, she pulled me aside.

"I think I understand what's happening," she said. "His Broca's area — the speech production center — has formed a feedback loop with his auditory cortex. Every word he plans to say gets filtered through a pattern-recognition process. His brain is essentially autocorrecting his speech into rhyme, the way yours might autocorrect a misspelled word."

"Can you break the loop?"

"I want to try something unconventional. Music therapy, combined with rhythmic disruption exercises. We'll teach his brain to recognize rhyme as a *choice* rather than a *compulsion*."

The treatment took six weeks. Marcus spent hours each day with Dr. Voss's team, learning to speak in deliberately arrhythmic patterns, reciting prose passages while listening to discordant music, training his brain to separate sound from meaning. There were setbacks — days when he could barely get a sentence out at all, when the conflict between his compulsion and his training left him stuttering and frustrated.

But slowly, beautifully, it began to work.

On the morning of the sixth week, Marcus called me. I answered with my heart in my throat.

"Hey," he said. Just that. One word. No rhyme. No meter. Just my best friend's voice, plain and imperfect and free.

"Hey," I whispered back, and I felt tears rolling down my cheeks.

"I want a hot dog," he said, and we both burst out laughing — the kind of laughter that shakes something loose inside you, the kind that feels like coming home.

Marcus still rhymes sometimes, but only when he wants to. Usually to make me laugh. Usually at Sal's Diner, in our usual booth, over a hot dog that is definitely not a sandwich.

You first noticed it at the coffee shop on a Tuesday. Alex ordered a latte and said, “A warm brown sea in a cup, please, / with foam like a cloud and a hint of a breeze.” You laughed because it sounded like a joke. Alex didn’t. And that was when the ice started forming in your stomach.

By Thursday, it was undeniable. “Where are my keys? I’m in a daze, / I swear I left them in the maze.” The cashier stared. You paid quickly and led Alex out. Your best friend—the one who had taught you to parallel park, who held your hair back at parties, who never missed a birthday—could no longer say a sentence unless it rhymed.

The doctor called it “acquired rhyming speech disorder.” The MRI was clear. There was no tumor, no stroke, no obvious damage. “It’s as if her language center rewired itself overnight,” the neurologist said. “Her brain is doing this for a reason. We don’t always know what that reason is.”

You decided to find the reason. You were a fixer by nature, the friend with a first-aid kit in your glovebox and a list of emergency contacts in your phone. Rhyming Alex was a puzzle you could solve.

So you tried everything. Speech therapy exercises—slow breathing, counting to ten before speaking, reading newspaper headlines aloud. Alex read with heroic effort, flat and colorless, and for one shining moment she sounded like herself. Then you asked what she wanted for lunch and she said, “I could eat soup with a spoon, / or a sandwich and fly to the moon.” You made flashcards. She answered each one in a couplet. You tried a metronome, thinking a steady beat would disrupt her rhythm. She synced to it perfectly.

You tried aversion therapy with a small beep. She rhymed “beep” with “leap,” “weep,” and “sheep.” You tried having her write in a journal. She filled three pages with a ballad about unlocking the front door.

One night, you sat across from her in silence. “We’re going to beat this,” you said. “Just think before you speak.”

Alex stared at you. Then she said, “The thinker thinks and the speaker speaks, / but neither one fixes the hole in the week.”

You slammed your hand on the table. “I’m trying to help you! Don’t you want to be normal?”

Her face crumpled. “Normal is a coat that’s small; / it only fits when you’re not tall.” She left.

You spent three days replaying that moment. The answer, you realized, was not in the flashcards or the metronome. The answer was in the hole in the week. Alex’s mother had died in March. You had sent flowers and gone to the funeral and made casseroles, and then you had both pretended to move on. You never asked her about it. You never asked her what she was afraid of.

You showed up at her apartment with a pineapple upside-down cake, the kind her grandmother used to make. She opened the door with swollen eyes. “You came back with cake and a frown, / did you finally figure out how to tear me down?”

“No,” you said. “I came to listen.”

She blinked. “Listen to what? The rhymes are a wall, / a rhythm I built—”

“Stop,” you said softly. “Tell me what you’re really afraid of.”

And then it happened. Alex’s mouth opened and closed. She looked like someone at the edge of a high dive. When the words came, they were not shaped by rhyme.

“I’m afraid you’ll stop trying. I’m afraid I’ll be this person who talks like a song and everyone will laugh and you’ll get tired and leave me, and I’ll be alone with the music that won’t stop.”

It was prose. It was raw. It was the truest thing she’d said in weeks.

You hugged her. The cake squished between you. You felt her sob. “I’m not going anywhere,” you said. “And I’m sorry I tried to change you. I was scared too.”

She pulled back and sniffled. “You’re messy,” she said. “But you’re my mess.” The last word wobbled, almost rhymed with “guess”—but she smiled. “I think that one was free.”

You laughed. She laughed. The cake was ruined, and the rhymes weren’t gone, but they didn’t need to be. The cure, you finally understood, had never been about the words. It was about showing up—and asking the question she needed to hear.

You first notice it on the Tuesday after the lightning struck the old oak behind Mara's house.

You and Mara are sitting on your porch steps, splitting a bag of stale pretzels the way you have since you were twelve. You ask her if she wants the last one, and she opens her mouth and says, "I would love a bite, for my delight, it feels so right tonight!"

You laugh. She doesn't.

She claps a hand over her mouth, eyes wide. You think she's doing a bit. Mara has always done bits. But then she tries again to say thank you and what comes out is, "Thank you dear, for being near, please do not fear."

That is eight months ago.

The doctors call it post-traumatic palilalia with compulsive rhyming, a rare neurological misfire. The lightning had been close. Too close. It didn't hit her, but it hit the tree while she was standing under it with her phone to her ear, talking to you. She fell backward and hit her head on the garden wall. When she woke up in the ER, every sentence came out coupled and cadenced, whether she wanted it to or not. She can't stop. She can't speak normally. If she tries to force plain speech, she goes silent entirely, her throat working, her face turning red with effort, until the rhyme forces its way out anyway.

At first you try to make it fun. You rhyme back at her. You bring her notebooks full of rhyming dictionaries. But you see how tired she is. How ordering coffee takes five minutes because she has to build a couplet around "oat milk latte." How she stopped answering the phone. How she writes you notes in plain text instead of speaking, just to give her jaw a rest.

So you decide to cure her.

You start the way you start everything: with research. You stay up late at your kitchen table, your laptop burning your thighs, scrolling through medical journals and obscure forums while Mara sleeps on your couch. You print out articles about melodic intonation therapy. You book an appointment with a speech neurologist two towns over, a woman who speaks to you in a calm, clinical voice while Mara sits beside you, twisting her hands.

The neurologist asks Mara how she feels, and Mara says, "I feel so stuck inside a rhyme, I’m running out of time."

The neurologist nods and prescribes exercises, breathing techniques, a drug that is supposed to calm the overactive language loop. For three weeks you sit with Mara every evening and run through the exercises. You hold flashcards. You time her silences. You watch her swallow the small white pill with water. Nothing changes, except now her rhymes sound tired.

You try the other route. Mara's grandmother, who still lives in the house with the scarred oak in the yard, tells you the lightning put a rhythm in her. She tells you to take Mara back to the tree at dusk and wash her hands in the rainwater that collects in its hollow. You think it's ridiculous, but you love Mara enough to be ridiculous for her.

So you take her back there. The tree is blackened on one side, split to its heart. The air smells like wet earth and ozone even though it hasn't rained in days. You bring a little glass jar. Your friend stands before the tree looking small in her oversized jacket.

You say, "Ready?"

And she looks at you and says, "I am scared to hope, I cannot cope, I’m at the end of my rope."

You unscrew the jar and tip the water over her hands. She shivers. Nothing happens. She wipes her hands on her jeans and says, "The water’s cold, the story’s old, the tree does what it’s told."

On the drive home you grip the steering wheel so hard your knuckles ache, because you feel the failure like a stone in your chest.

The worst attempt comes a month later. You read a post from a man who claims he cured his own compulsive speech by enforcing total silence for seventy-two hours. A hard reset. You bring the idea to Mara, carefully, on paper so she doesn't have to answer in rhyme. She reads it and writes back one word: *Okay.*

For three days you don't speak either. You communicate in notes, in gestures. You make her soup and leave it on the counter. You watch movies with subtitles. By the second night, her eyes are bright with something like hope. On the morning of the third day, you sit across from her at your tiny table and nod. She takes a deep breath.

She opens her mouth. Nothing comes out. She tries again. Her lips tremble. You lean forward. You want so badly to hear her plain, flat, familiar voice say "hey."

What comes out, cracked and small, is, "I tried to be free, but the rhyme won’t let me be."

And you break.

You start to cry before you can stop yourself, and you reach across the table and grab her hands. You say, "I am so sorry. I am so sorry I kept trying to fix you like you were a broken radio."

She cries too, and through her tears she says, "Don’t be sorry, you are still my dear, you’ve always kept me near."

In that moment you understand what you have been doing wrong. You have been treating her rhyme as a disease to be cut out, instead of a new shape her mind has taken to keep her safe after the shock. You have been listening for what you wanted to hear, not for what she is actually saying.

You stop trying to cure her.

You learn to listen inside the rhyme. You hear that she is still funny, still sharp, still Mara, just translated. You buy her a cheap poetry slam trophy from the thrift store and you crown her the queen of couplets. She laughs until her shoulders shake and says, "Long live the queen, in denim and green, the best friend I’ve ever seen."

You haven't heard Mara speak normally in eight months. You probably never will again. But last night, when you asked if she was happy, she didn't hesitate. She looked you right in the eye and said, "With you I’m fine, you’re my sunshine, my whole design." And you knew exactly what she meant.

Julian sat across from me, his fingers nervously drumming against the armrests of the leather chair. The metallic electrodes taped to his temples glinted under the harsh fluorescent lights of my home laboratory.

"I do not think this rig will work," Julian said, his voice trembling slightly. "It feels as though my brain will pop."

I sighed, adjusting the dial on the neural-auditory feedback loop I had spent three months building. "It *will* work, Julian. We just need to interrupt the meter before your brain completes the stanza."

Six months ago, a mild traumatic brain injury left Julian with a condition the neurologists called Compulsive Cadence Syndrome. To the outside world, it sounded whimsical, like living with a rhyming fairy-tale character. But for Julian, it was a waking nightmare. He had lost his job at the bank because he couldn't explain loan terms without resorting to strict AABB rhyme schemes. Last month, he tried to report a gas leak to emergency services, but the operator hung up, assuming it was a prank call because Julian reported that "the cellar smells of rotten eggs, it makes me shaky in the legs."

He was exhausted. I was his best friend, and as a cognitive neuroscientist, I was his last hope.

"Remember the protocol," I said, placing a pair of heavy noise-canceling headphones over his ears. "I’m going to display words on the screen. Most of them are non-rhymable nouns in the English language—words like *orange*, *silver*, *purple*, and *month*. The headset will send a gentle micro-pulse to your auditory cortex every time it detects the rhythmic brainwaves associated with poetic meter. Your job is to say the word on screen and stop. Do not complete the couplet."

Julian nodded solemnly. Through the clear visor, I saw his throat tighten.

"Let's begin," I said, hitting the start switch. The monitor flashed red, then displayed a single word: **ORANGE**.

Julian stared at the screen. His mouth opened. His jaw muscles quivered as his brain fought its own pathological compulsion.

"The... orange..." he rasped out. I watched the brainwave monitor spike as his mind scrambled for a forced rhyme. "...is sitting on the door hinge!"

A sharp tone hummed through his headphones, and Julian winced, clutching his head.

"No," I urged softly. "Don't force a rhyme that isn't naturally there. Break the chain, Julian. Suppress the second line."

The monitor refreshed: **SILVER**.

"I wear a ring of silver bright..." Julian began, his voice rising in panic.

A feedback pulse interrupted him.

"Stop!" I called out, leaning over the console. "Look at me, Julian. Don't look at the screen. Look at me. You don't have to be clever. You don't have to be poetic. Just give me plain, boring, broken thoughts."

Sweat beaded on his forehead. He was breathing heavily, his chest heaving under the strain of battling his own neural pathways. The sheer cognitive load of resisting the rhyme was physically draining him.

The screen flashed the next word: **MONTH**.

Julian squeezed his eyes shut. His fists clenched so tightly his knuckles turned white. I could see the battle raging inside his skull—the natural human desire to speak normally clashing against the corrupted circuit demanding symmetry and song.

"Month," Julian whispered.

He stopped.

The room fell dead silent. The brainwave monitor hummed, its green line flattening into irregular, non-rhythmic ripples.

I held my breath, afraid that if I spoke, I would shatter the spell. "Julian?" I whispered. "Say something else. Anything."

He slowly opened his eyes. He looked at the window, then down at his hands, then up at me. He swallowed hard, testing the silence in his mouth.

"The weather is pretty bad today," he said.

No rhyme. No meter. Just plain, flat, beautiful prose.

A slow smile broke across his face, followed immediately by a sob of overwhelming relief. He pulled off the headphones and collapsed forward, resting his forehead against my shoulder.

"It worked," I laughed, tears pricking my own eyes as I patted his back. "You sound completely boring."

"Thank God," Julian choked out, laughing through his tears. "You have no idea how hard that was."

The first time Daniel rhymed in front of me, I thought he was joking.

We were sitting on the roof of our old apartment building, watching rain crawl down the windows of the city below. Daniel had just told me that he had failed his driving test for the third time.

“Apparently I turned too wide,” he said with a sigh, “and now my driving dreams have gone up in smoke and flame.”

I laughed.

He didn’t.

“Don’t laugh, Ben. I’m afraid this isn’t a game. Every word that I speak comes out sounding the same.”

That was when I realized something was seriously wrong.

The doctors called it a rare linguistic disorder. Daniel called it “a terrible curse that has ruined my world and made every conversation absurd.” He could understand everything perfectly, but whenever he tried to speak, his brain automatically arranged his words into rhyme.

At first, we tried to laugh about it. Then we tried everything else.

Daniel went to speech therapists. He practiced reading newspapers aloud. He carried a notebook so he could communicate without speaking. Nothing worked. Worse, people began avoiding him because they found his condition strange.

So I decided I would cure him myself.

I spent three weeks researching his condition. I filled notebooks with theories and possible treatments. Eventually, I noticed something unusual: Daniel’s rhyming became stronger whenever he was nervous.

That gave me an idea.

“If fear is causing the rhymes,” I told him, “then maybe we can teach your brain not to be afraid.”

“And how will we do that?” he asked. “Please tell me your plan, if you possibly can.”

I took him to an abandoned theater on the edge of town.

The stage was covered in dust, and the red curtains hung in tatters. I had prepared a series of exercises. First, Daniel had to say random words without thinking about what came next.

“Tree,” I said.

“Free,” he answered.

“Chair.”

“Bear.”

“Window.”

“Shadow.”

I threw a shoe at him.

“Potato!”

He stared at me.

Then he burst out laughing.

“Potato,” he said, “doesn’t rhyme with that.”

For the first time in months, he had spoken a sentence without forcing it into a rhyme.

We stared at each other.

“Do it again,” I whispered.

“Potato.”

No rhyme.

Daniel’s eyes filled with tears.

But the improvement didn’t last.

The next day, when he tried talking to his mother, the rhymes returned. At work, they became worse. Every attempt to resist them made him more frightened, and every frightened thought seemed to tighten the invisible knot inside his mind.

I realized I had been thinking about the problem all wrong.

Daniel didn’t need to be forced out of his condition.

He needed to stop being ashamed of it.

A week later, I brought him back to the theater. This time, I invited twenty people: his family, coworkers, neighbors, and friends.

Daniel looked horrified.

“What are you doing?” he demanded. “This plan is cruel. This audience will make me a fool.”

“Maybe,” I said. “Or maybe they’ll finally hear you.”

I walked onto the stage and told the audience about Daniel. Then I handed him a microphone.

He stood frozen.

Finally, he spoke.

“I wish I could talk like everyone else,” he said. “I wish my words didn’t twist themselves into something strange and embarrassing.”

Nobody laughed.

Daniel swallowed.

“But perhaps I have spent too long fighting what my mind has made.”

His voice trembled.

“So if my words must dance and rhyme tonight, then let them dance. Let them shine.”

The audience applauded.

Daniel smiled.

For the next hour, he told jokes, stories, and memories entirely in rhyme. People laughed when he wanted them to laugh. They cried when the story became sad. Nobody treated him like he was broken.

When he finished, he stepped off the stage.

“You didn’t cure me,” he said.

“No,” I replied.

He smiled.

“But you helped me see,” he continued, “that maybe being different doesn’t mean there’s something wrong with me.”

Months passed.

Daniel still rhymed. Some days were better than others, and he continued seeing his doctors. But something had changed. He no longer whispered his words into notebooks or avoided strangers.

Then one morning, he called me.

“Ben,” he said, “I have news for you.”

“What?”

He paused.

“I passed my driving test.”

There was silence.

Then I heard him laugh.

“And this time,” he added, “I only hit one tree.”

I laughed so hard that I nearly dropped the phone.

Daniel laughed too.

Maybe I had never cured him.

Maybe friendship was never supposed to be about curing people.

Maybe it was about standing beside them until they could see that they were worth accepting exactly as they were.

And, if necessary, laughing with them when they accidentally drove into a tree.

Maya started rhyming on a Tuesday in October, right after she fell off her bike and hit her head on the curb. At first I thought she was joking.

"You okay?" I asked, pulling her up by the arm.

"I'm fine, don't worry, my dear old friend, this bump will surely mend."

I laughed. She didn't.

That was three weeks ago. Since then, every single word out of Maya's mouth has rhymed. Not occasionally—always. Ordering coffee, arguing with her mom, crying during a sad movie. All of it, perfect meter, like she'd swallowed a poetry textbook and it rearranged her vocal cords on the way down.

The doctors ran every test they had. CT scans, blood work, a neurologist who specialized in speech disorders and looked personally offended that he couldn't explain it. "Sometimes the brain does strange things after trauma," he said, shrugging like that was an actual diagnosis. "It may resolve on its own. It may not."

Maya, to her credit, tried to stay positive. "It's kind of fun," she said the first week, "like living inside a Dr. Seuss book, hun." But by week two, the fun had worn thin. She'd missed two shifts at work because her manager thought she was mocking him. Her boyfriend broke up with her over text because, in her words, "explaining feelings in rhyme makes everything sound like a nursery crime." She'd started crying more, and even her tears came out sounding like a greeting card.

So I decided I would fix this myself, because apparently modern medicine had given up, and I refused to watch my best friend since third grade get slowly erased by her own mouth.

I researched everything. Speech therapy techniques, hypnosis videos, an article about a woman in Ohio who'd developed a foreign accent after a dental surgery and how her doctors had helped retrain her speech patterns through repetition. I bought flashcards. I made her do vocal exercises where she had to say sentences without rhyming, timing her with a stopwatch like some kind of deranged coach.

"Say 'the sky is blue,'" I'd tell her.

"The sky is blue, and so are you—wait. Damn it." She'd throw her head back and groan.

We tried distraction techniques next. I'd ask her sudden questions, hoping to catch her brain off guard before it could load its rhyming dictionary. "What's seven times eight?"

"Fifty-six, that's my fix." Still rhymed.

I tried making her angry, thinking maybe raw emotion would override whatever glitch was happening in her brain. I brought up her ex. I brought up the time she failed her driver's test twice. Nothing worked—if anything, her rhymes just got angrier and more elaborate, which honestly was almost impressive.

Three weeks of failed cures. Three weeks of watching her go quieter and quieter, not because she couldn't speak, but because she'd started to hate the sound of her own voice.

It was late on a Thursday when she called me, crying, saying she wanted to stop talking altogether. I drove to her apartment right away. She opened the door with red eyes.

"I hate this so much, I really do, I miss just talking normal, without rhyming through and through."

And something about the exhaustion in her voice, the sheer unfairness of it, made me start laughing. Not at her—at the absurdity of everything we'd tried, the flashcards, the stopwatch, the pop quizzes about multiplication tables.

"What's so funny?" she asked—and stopped.

No rhyme. Just four flat, ordinary words.

We both froze. She said it again, slower. "What is so funny?" Still nothing. It turned out the cure hadn't been a technique or a trick at all. It was just watching me lose it laughing on her doorstep, some emotional short-circuit resetting whatever her brain had rewired.

She never rhymed again after that night, though sometimes, when she's really tired, a stray couplet slips out by accident. We just laugh about it now. Turns out the best medicine wasn't science. It was just showing up, and being a little ridiculous, together.

The doctor called it a rare neurological condition, something to do with a misfiring in the language centers of his brain. I called it annoying at first. Then I called it terrifying. Now, three years later, I call it Eli.

It started on a Tuesday in March. We'd been best friends since third grade, when I'd moved into the yellow house next door and he'd offered me half his peanut butter sandwich for helping me retrieve a baseball from the Hendersons' yard. We grew up together, traded secrets, survived high school with our combined wits and his older brother's ID. So when I got the call that Eli had collapsed at work, I dropped everything.

He woke up in the hospital speaking in rhyme. Not a little rhyme. Not the occasional poetic flourish. Every sentence, every grocery list, every awkward bit of small talk had to come out in couplets. The neurologist said it might pass. The specialist said it might not. Eli took it in stride.

"Can't say it's grand," he said from the hospital bed, "but at least I always have the last word."

I laughed, because that's what you do when your best friend is being charming. But over the next few weeks the humor wore thin. Eli couldn't hold a regular job. His girlfriend left him. His parents cried in the kitchen when they thought he couldn't hear. And I watched him turn into a prisoner of his own head, his thoughts trapped in iambic pentameter like some Shakespearean curse.

I became determined to cure him.

I started with the obvious routes: doctors, then more doctors, then a string of specialists so long I lost track of their last names. There was the hypnotist in Albany who made Eli speak in rhyming German for an entire afternoon. The energy healer who told us to drink celery juice at the new moon. The speech therapist who cried during our third session and admitted she wasn't qualified.

Then I tried the less obvious routes. I read books on brain plasticity until I dreamed in synapses. I played recordings of his pre-condition voice at night, hoping to trigger something. I even flew us to a monastery in Nepal where a monk swore he could lift the curse with a chant and a strict diet of brown rice.

Nothing worked.

One evening, after the brown rice had failed spectacularly and Eli was working his way through his third bowl of plain pasta ("my comfort's a bowl, it feeds my soul"), I sat across from him at the kitchen table and finally broke.

"I just want you back," I said. "I want to talk to you like we used to. I want you to be okay."

Eli set down his fork. He looked at me for a long moment, his green eyes—still the same green eyes from third grade—soft and thoughtful.

"You have me back," he said. "I'm still your friend. Just one with a rhyme at the end."

"That's not—" I started.

"It is," he said. "I love you, I do. I see you trying. I see this through and through. But the doctors are gone. So is the monk. And so is the celery juice. Time to let go of this funk."

I wanted to argue. I wanted to pull out my notebook of cures, my list of specialists, my folder of promising clinical trials. But I looked at him—really looked at him—and saw what I'd been missing for three years. He was still Eli. He still made terrible jokes. He still borrowed my shirts. He still showed up when I needed him, sometimes in the middle of the night, sometimes with nothing more than a rhyming couplet and a hug.

"Okay," I said. "Okay."

"Good," he said. "Movie night, what a treat. You pick the film; I'll grab snacks you can't beat."

I laughed. I cried a little, too. And somewhere between the couch and the credits, I realized the cure I had been looking for was never going to come in a pill or a chant or a special diet. It was going to come from me, in the simple act of loving my friend exactly as he was.

Eli has been speaking in rhyme for three years now. The doctors have stopped returning my calls. The monk has blocked my number. But Eli still calls me every Sunday, and we still talk for hours about nothing and everything, and I still laugh at his jokes—even when they rhyme.

That's enough. That's more than enough.

You first notice it at the bus stop, when Maren drops her coffee and says, “Oh no, my cup, my luck, please let this not be the start of things gone wrong.”

You laugh because Maren has always been quick, always been able to turn a spilled morning into a little stage. Then the light changes, and she steps off the curb still rhyming: “Cars pass, hearts drum, hold your breath, here they come.” A cyclist swerves. A horn splits the wet air. You grab her sleeve hard enough to wrinkle it, and she looks at you with eyes that are frightened of their own music.

By winter, the doctors have names for it: compulsive rhyming, prosodic intrusion, a rare storm in the language centers after the fever that nearly took her in October. They give you pamphlets. They give Maren pills that make her mouth taste like pennies and do nothing for the couplets that leap out whenever she is startled, tired, or afraid.

You decide to cure her yourself because you are twenty-three and arrogant with love.

You try a metronome, setting it slow on the kitchen table while Maren grips the edges and sweats through simple sentences. “The toast is—burning, yearning—no.” You snap the little arm still and hold her hands. You try bitter tea from an herbalist who smells like cedar and charges too much. You try a speech therapist with kind eyes who teaches Maren to breathe in for four, out for six, to place words like stones rather than toss them like bright coins. You try silence, whole weekends in your apartment with the phones dead and labeled pictures covering every object: DOOR. BREAD. SORRY.

For one miraculous April morning, it works. Maren wakes before you, makes oatmeal, and says, plain as rain, “I think the raisins are old.” You nearly weep into the sink. Then downstairs neighbor slams a door, and Maren blurts, “Old, cold, bold—don’t fold,” and presses both palms to her mouth as if she can push the music back in.

The breaking comes at her mother’s funeral. You are there in the second row, holding the program she cannot read aloud. When the minister asks if anyone wants to speak, Maren rises because she loved her mother fiercely and because grief has made her brave in the exact way that makes the condition worst. At the podium she opens her mouth and out comes, terrible and shining: “She taught me thread, she taught me bread, she held my head—” A cousin laughs once, shocked. Someone else coughs. Maren freezes, and you are halfway down the aisle before you know you’ve moved.

That night, sitting on the bathroom floor while she runs the faucet so no one hears her cry, you finally understand what all your cures have missed: the rhyme is not the enemy. It is the bridge her mind builds when the ordinary road washes out. You have been trying to burn the bridge while she was still standing on the far shore.

So you stop.

Not all at once. You still drive her to the clinical trial across town, where Dr. Bell offers a new drug that may “reduce compulsive patterning” with a list of side effects longer than Maren’s arm. You sit outside while she decides alone, because it is her voice, her weather, her right. When she comes out, she is not carrying the prescription bag. Your heart lifts, then falls, because she says, “I’ll take it if the bad days get bigger. I won’t take it just to make rooms quieter.” Plain words. No music. Both of you flinch at how much they cost.

On the train home, a baby cries, brakes scream, the lights flicker out. Maren’s hand finds yours in the dark. “Black, track, don’t look back,” she whispers, and you feel the old panic rise in you anyway. Then she breathes in for four, out for six, and adds, quieter, “Stay.”

You do.

The rhymes never leave completely. Some mornings they are sparrows; some nights, knives. But Maren learns to say, “Give me a minute,” and you learn to give it. You learn that cure is not always absence. Sometimes it is a door you build together, and on the other side, your friend—still singing, still herself—choosing when to walk through.
