The first thing I noticed wasn’t the light, or the clouds, or the pearlescent sheen of the gates. It was the sound. A soft, persistent rustling, like a thousand accountants turning pages in a vast, celestial library. I was standing on a floor of polished marble that reflected a sky I’d never seen before—a soft, perpetual dawn. Before me, the gates shimmered, not with gold, but with a light that felt like a memory of kindness.

A figure in a simple, grey robe approached. He didn’t have a clipboard or a book. He held a single, shimmering ledger that seemed to hum with a low, anxious energy.

“Name?” he asked, his voice the sound of turning parchment.

I told him.

He didn’t flip through pages. He simply opened the ledger, and the pages fanned out on their own, stopping at a section that glowed with a frantic, pulsing light. He frowned, a gentle crease forming between his brows.

“Ah,” he said. “A hoarder.”

“A what?”

He turned the ledger towards me. It wasn’t a list of deeds, good or bad. It was a list of… concerns. Worries. Anxieties. And at the top of the page, in bold, celestial script, was the heading: **FUCKS GIVEN.**

My entire life was there, quantified not in years, but in units of emotional expenditure. *Fretted for 3.2 hours over a coworker’s ambiguous email (2021).* *Allocated 14% of mental bandwidth to a perceived slight from a barista (2019).* *Spent 47 consecutive minutes worrying if the oven was left on, despite having checked it twice (last Tuesday).* The list was endless, a monument to my own internal noise.

“You have a surplus,” the attendant explained, his tone clinical. “A lifetime’s worth, meticulously collected and stored. You gave a fuck about everything, and therefore, effectively, about nothing. The ledger is… overfull. It’s causing a bureaucratic imbalance.”

“So I’m… rejected?” The word felt hollow.

“Not rejected. Recycled.” He gestured with a hand that seemed to hold the weight of the ledger. “You are granted a dispensation. You will relive your last twenty-four hours. Your task is simple: empty the ledger. Give them all away. Spend every last fuck you have on something, or someone, that warrants it. Return with the ledger balanced, and the gates will open.”

The world dissolved into a nauseating swirl of light and sound, and then I was back. In my apartment. The digital clock on the microwave read 7:01 AM. Yesterday morning. The day of the accident—a stupid, freak thing with a loose balcony railing and a moment of distraction.

The first hour was chaos. My mind, a habitual worrier, tried to resume its old programming. *Did I leave the stove on? What did my boss mean in that meeting? Is that person judging my grocery cart?* But now, I could feel the ledger, a phantom weight in my chest, pulsing with each wasted thought. I had to consciously, physically, *let go*.

I started small. The barista got my order wrong. My old self would have stewed, replaying the interaction, crafting a passive-aggressive complaint in my head. This time, I looked at the flustered young man, took the wrong drink, and said, “No worries. It’s a beautiful day. Keep the change.” The ledger in my chest felt a fraction lighter. A tiny, glowing mote of light drifted from it and vanished.

The day became a mission of radical release. I called my sister, not to complain, but to tell her I loved her, to listen to her talk about her garden for twenty minutes. I spent an hour helping a neighbor carry groceries up the stairs, not out of obligation, but because her smile felt like sunlight. At work, when a project went sideways, I didn’t spiral into blame. I took a breath, said, “Okay, let’s fix it,” and meant it. Each act of genuine, un-anxious engagement was a release. The ledger grew lighter, the pulsing light softening from frantic to a warm, steady glow.

The final hours were the hardest. I knew the accident was coming. The balcony. The loose railing. My old self would have been consumed by a thousand petty worries in that moment. But as I stepped out, the evening air crisp, I felt the ledger, almost empty now. I saw the railing, noticed the slight give, and instead of a cascade of panic, a single, clear thought emerged: *This is it. This is the only fuck that matters now.*

I didn’t give a fuck about the fall. I didn’t give a fuck about the pain. I gave the last of my fucks to the view—the sunset painting the city in hues of orange and purple. I gave a fuck about the profound, simple beauty of being alive for one more second. I gave a fuck about the peace that came with finally, truly, letting go.

I opened my eyes. The pearlescent gates were before me. The attendant stood there, the ledger in his hands. It was no longer pulsing. It was calm, its light a soft, contented hum. He opened it. The pages were blank.

“Balanced,” he said, a hint of a smile in his voice. He stepped aside.

As I walked through the gates, I realized the truth. Heaven wasn’t a reward for hoarding your worries or your kindness. It was the space you created when you finally stopped giving a fuck about the wrong things, and learned to spend your heart on the right ones.
samples.DeepSeek-V4-Flash_story:
One minute you were in the produce aisle, squeezing a mango with unreasonable confidence. The next, a rogue avocado—launched by a distracted teenager on a motorized shopping cart—pinged off a display of canned beans, ricocheted off a ceiling fan, and struck you squarely in the temple. You died instantly. The last thing you heard was an announcement: “Cleanup needed in produce.”

When you opened your eyes, you were standing on a cloud. Before you stood a gate made of something that looked suspiciously like mother-of-pearl and a very tired-looking angel holding a clipboard.

“Name?” he said.

You gave it.

“Right,” he said, flipping through pages. “Well, we’ve got your records here. But before we get into deeds and misdeeds, we have a little… situation.” He gestured, and the pearly gates swung open to reveal not a heavenly city, but a vast subterranean warehouse. It was filled, wall to wall, with dusty glass jars. Inside each jar was a small, glowing, writhing thing—a fuck.

“These are all the fucks you’ve ever given,” the angel said.

“That’s… a lot,” you said.

“Yes,” he said. “You’re a hoarder.”

“But I gave those fucks! I cared about things!”

“You cared about things the way a dragon cares about gold. You collected them. You never spent them. You never gave a single fuck to anyone else. You just hoarded fucks about your own career, your own comfort, your own opinions. Every time you said ‘I give a fuck about the environment’ or ‘I give a fuck about my health,’ you stored that fuck in your jar. But did you ever actually give one away? No.” He sighed. “You’re branded a hoarder. Entrance denied.”

Your stomach dropped. “So what happens now?”

“Second chance,” he said. “We’re going to send you back to relive your last twenty-four hours. You have until midnight. If you can give away all the fucks you have—actually give them, to people, to causes, to moments that need them—you get in. If not…” He pointed downward.

You woke up in your bed, heart pounding. Phone buzzing. Mom texted: “Call me when you can. Just thinking of you.”

Normally, you’d ignored that. You had fucks to preserve. But now you reached inside your chest and felt a warm, wriggling orb. It slid up your throat and out your mouth like a glowing marble. You grabbed it, looked at your phone, and whispered, “I give a fuck about you, Mom.” The orb dissolved into the text. The reply came instantly: “That means the world to me, honey.”

At work, your coworker Dave pitched a terrible idea. Normally you’d roll your eyes and hoard a magnificent fuck about how stupid it was. Instead, you pulled out another orb and pressed it into his hand. “Dave, I give a fuck about this idea. Let’s make it work.” Dave blinked as the orb vanished into his chest.

At noon, a barista spilled coffee on your shoes. You gave a fuck about her apology. At 3 p.m., a homeless man asked for change. You didn’t have any, so you gave him a fuck. He smiled like he’d been given a warm blanket.

The day went on. You gave fucks to your neighbor’s barking dog, to your boss’s email, to the kid crying in the grocery store, to the news story you usually scrolled past. Each time, the weight in your chest grew lighter. By 11 p.m., you thought you were empty. Then you saw your wife sitting on the couch, staring at an old photo of her late mother.

Her shoulders shook. Normally, you’d have hovered in the doorway, unsure, hoarding a big fuck about being a good partner. This time you sat down beside her, reached into your chest, and found one last, tiny, flickering fuck.

“I give this one to you,” you whispered.

It floated out of your mouth and settled over her like a blanket. She turned, eyes wet, and hugged you so tight you felt something in your ribs crack. The clock struck midnight.

You blinked. You were back at the pearly gates. The warehouse was empty. Dust motes swirled in golden light.

The angel looked up from his clipboard and smiled. “Well. That’s more like it.”

“Did I make it?” you asked.

“You gave all the fucks you had,” he said. “Come on in.” He swung the gates open. Inside, you could see a thousand other fucks floating around, bright and warm, dancing between the residents of heaven.

“What are those?” you asked.

“Those are the fucks everyone else gave away. That’s the whole point, friend. A fuck given is a fuck received. It never really leaves you. It just finds a new home.”

You stepped inside. And for the first time in your life, you didn’t have a single fuck left. It felt exactly like heaven.
samples.Muse-Spark-1.2-Contributor_story:
You didn't think you'd die because of a pigeon.

You were carrying two bags of groceries up the three flights to your apartment, the Tuesday rain hammering the fire escape, when a pigeon spooked off the railing right into your face. You flinched, your foot slipped on the wet concrete step, and the back of your head found the corner of the metal railing with a dull, stupid thud. That was it. No lightning strike, no heroic sacrifice. Just wet socks, a dropped carton of eggs, and then nothing.

Then there is light, and it is not nothing.

You are standing barefoot on what feels like warm marble, even though you are still wearing your wet socks. In front of you are gates so tall they disappear into cloud, pearly white and faintly humming. A man in a loose linen suit that looks like it was made for someone else sits at a folding table in front of them. He has a clipboard, tired eyes, and a name tag that says ST. PETER.

"Hey," he says, not unkindly. "Tough break with the pigeon."

You try to say something, but your voice doesn't work right. You look down at yourself and you are exactly as you were, grocery bags gone, head no longer bleeding.

He flips a page on his clipboard. "So, we usually do the whole life-review thing. Deeds, sins, that balance sheet. But we've changed the system. More efficient."

He gestures to the side of the table and you see it.

It is a mountain. A literal, sagging mountain of small, glowing glass jars, each one stoppered with cork and filled with a faint, amber light. There are thousands of them. Tens of thousands. They are stacked in crates, in laundry baskets, spilling out of cardboard boxes marked FRAGILE. Each jar is labeled in your handwriting.

*Fuck I didn't give when Maya said she was tired.*
*Fuck I didn't give when Mom called on Thursday.*
*Fuck I saved for later when my boss took credit for your presentation.*

"You hoarded them," St. Peter says.

"What?"

"Most people come here empty. They spent them all. Anger, love, worry, pity, obsession — they gave a fuck all over the place until they had nothing left. You," he taps his pen against the mountain, and a few jars clink, "you conserved. You walked around for thirty-four years acting like you had an unlimited supply by never spending any. That's why you're a hoarder."

You stare at the jars. You recognize every single one. The fuck you didn't give when your downstairs neighbor knocked because your music was too loud. The fuck you didn't give when your best friend texted you that his dad was in the hospital and you replied 'damn that sucks' and went back to scrolling. The fuck you didn't give when you told yourself you'd start caring tomorrow.

"So I don't get in?" you ask.

"Not like that. You can't bring them with you. Heaven has no storage." He slides a dented duffel bag across the table. It unzips itself, hungry. "Here's the deal. We send you back. You get to relive your last twenty-four hours. Same pigeon, same rain, same ending. But you take these with you. Every single one. You don't get through the gates until the bag is empty. You have to actually give a fuck."

Before you can ask what that even means, the marble tilts.

You wake up to your alarm at 6:47 AM on Tuesday. The rain is already hitting the window. Your phone says you have three missed calls from Mom from last night that you meant to return. Maya is asleep next to you with her back turned, the way she has been for two weeks since the fight you never really apologized for. On the floor next to your bed is the duffel bag, zipped shut but vibrating faintly, light leaking from the seams.

You understand immediately. You have twenty-four hours to spend a lifetime of not caring.

You start small. You get up and you don't hit snooze. You make coffee the way Maya likes it, not the way you like it, and you bring it to her while she's still half-asleep. You look at her properly. You say, "Hey, I was an asshole last week. I wasn't listening. Tell me again, for real this time." She blinks, surprised, and then she does. You listen until your chest hurts. When you reach down, you feel the bag get lighter. One jar, gone. The amber light just dissipates into the air between you.

At work, you don't swallow it when your boss, Daniel, presents your mockups as his. You stand up in the meeting. Your voice shakes. You say, "Actually, I worked on those all weekend, and I'd like to walk everyone through my thinking." The room goes quiet. Daniel turns red. You feel another dozen jars evaporate all at once, not because you were brave, but because you finally gave a fuck about your own work.

On your lunch break you call your mom back. You don't text. You call. You ask about her doctor's appointment that you pretended to forget. You ask about Dad. You stay on the phone for twenty-two minutes even though you have emails piling up. Two more jars gone.

You apologize to Mrs. Chen downstairs in person for the bass. You help her carry her trash to the chute. You text your friend back, "I'm so sorry about your dad. Can I come over? Do you need anything?" You mean it.

By 6 PM you are exhausted. Giving a fuck is so much heavier than hoarding it, you realize. Hoarding was easy. It was just not doing anything.

The bag is almost empty. One jar left, glowing brighter than the rest. It says: *Fuck I didn't give about myself.*

The rain is still falling. You are walking home with the groceries. You see the pigeon on the railing. You remember the slip. You could step differently, avoid it. But you understand now that this isn't about cheating death.

You stop on the wet step. You look at the rain, at your shitty apartment building, at the cracked plastic bags cutting into your fingers, and you finally, truly, give a fuck that you are alive, that you were alive, that you wasted so much of it trying not to care so you wouldn't get hurt.

You shift your weight. The pigeon startles.

You slip.

Your head finds the railing.

You are back on the warm marble. The duffel bag is empty and gone. St. Peter is standing now, and the gates are open behind him, light spilling out that doesn't hurt your eyes at all.

"About time you spent them," he says, and smiles for real this time.

You walk through.

You didn't expect to die on a Tuesday, let alone via a runaway parade float shaped like a giant ear of corn. But there you stood before the Pearly Gates, brushing fiberglass kernels off your jacket.

Saint Peter didn't have a golden ledger. Instead, he stood beside an industrial-sized granary siloing millions of glowing, amber spheres.

"Arthur," Peter sighed, pinching the bridge of his nose. "We have a problem. You’re a hoarder."

"A hoarder?" you gasped. "I lived in a sixty-square-meter apartment with two chairs and a single plate!"

"Not physical items," Peter snapped, tapping the clear wall of the silo. The amber spheres clinked softly. "Fucks. You hoarded your fucks. Look at this! 'Not my circus, not my monkeys.' 'It is what it is.' 'Whatever.' Forty-two years of emotional constipation. You died with a full tank of empathy, passion, and outrage, and you didn't give a single one to a soul who needed it."

He slammed a large red button on his podium. "We don't allow emotional miserliness in Paradise. I'm sending you back twenty-four hours. You have until the corn float strikes again to give every last one of these fucks away. Empty the silo, or spend eternity in the cosmic lost-and-found."

*Gasp.* You bolted upright in bed, your alarm blaring 7:00 AM—yesterday morning.

You didn't waste a second. In your chest, you could feel the heavy, thrumming weight of forty-two years of withheld caring. It was time to clear out inventory.

You burst out of your apartment building. Your landlord, Mr. Henderson, was in the lobby grumbling about a leaky pipe. Usually, you’d nod, mutter "bummer," and scurry past. Not today.

"Mr. Henderson!" You grabbed his shoulders. "Your dedication to this building’s plumbing is heroic, but you look exhausted! Have you taken a vacation since 2012? I genuinely care about your mental health!"

The old man blinked, stunned into silence. You felt a subtle *pop* in your chest. One down.

At the local cafe, you didn't just take your black drip. You stared deeply into the eyes of the sleepy barista. "Chloe. The foam on this latte is an artistic miracle. You are capable of great things. Don't let the corporate grind dull your shine!" You tipped her fifty dollars and gave her a tearful hug. *Pop. Pop. Pop.*

At work, you didn't stay quiet when your boss, Greg, tried to steal credit for Sarah’s marketing strategy.

"Actually, Greg," you slammed your hands on the conference table, your voice booming, "that was all Sarah! She spent three weekends on this, and she deserves a raise! Furthermore, your micromanagement is stifling the creative soul of this department, and I give a massive, overwhelming fuck about the workplace culture here!"

The room went dead silent. Sarah teared up. Greg looked terrified. Inside you, a whole avalanche of amber spheres dissolved.

By afternoon, you were a force of nature. You stopped to pet every dog and told their owners exactly why their retrievers were good boys. You called your estranged sister, cried into the phone for forty minutes, and promised to be a real brother. You helped an elderly woman cross the street, then spent an hour listening to her tell stories about her late husband's button collection, hanging on every single word.

As 6:59 PM approached, you stood on the corner of 5th and Main. Your chest felt impossibly light, like a balloon ready to lift off. You were exhausted, raw, and completely open to the world.

Around the corner, you heard the faint, terrifying music of the Harvest Festival parade. The giant corn float was careening down the hill again, its brakes screaming.

A teenager stood in the crosswalk, mesmerized by their phone, oblivious to the runaway cob of doom.

You didn't hesitate. You sprinted, shoved the kid safely onto the sidewalk, and turned to face the oncoming yellow tide. As the giant fiberglass kernel made impact, you screamed at the top of your lungs, "I CARE ABOUT ALL OF YOU!"

You blinked. The Pearly Gates materialized around you once more.

Saint Peter stood by the silo. It was completely clear, sparkling clean. He looked up from his clipboard, a faint smile breaking through his stern demeanor.

"Well played, Arthur," Peter said, gesturing to the open gates. "Turns out, you had plenty to give."

You stepped through, lighter than air.

The vending machine falls on you on a Tuesday, which is fitting, because you didn't even want the chips. You were just killing time. You were always killing time.

The gates are real—pearlescent, flaking a little—but behind them stretches a warehouse that goes on forever. A man with a name tag that says PETE walks you down the aisle. The shelves rise into darkness, and every shelf is stacked with small glowing coins, warm as embers that never cool.

"Fucks," Pete says. "Yours."

You laugh. He doesn't.

"Seventy-three thousand, four hundred and twelve, issued at birth. Number given: zero." He consults his clipboard. "Forgotten birthdays. Calls you let ring out. A funeral you skipped because of traffic. Your mother's voice asking 'you still there?' while you watched a video of a man making pancakes shaped like celebrities." He sighs. "You're a hoarder, kid. And we don't have room."

You ask what you're supposed to do.

"Relive your last twenty-four hours. Spend every last one. Come back empty, you're in."

You wake up in yesterday. Your pockets sag with coins. When you pull one out, two more take its place.

You try cheating first. At the coffee shop you announce, loudly, that the barista's tattoo is awesome. Nothing happens. The coin sits in your palm like an accusation. *They know when you don't mean it,* Pete had said, in the way of people who have said it ten thousand times.

So you actually look. It's a heron, mid-flight, along her wrist. You ask about it. She tells you about her grandmother's lake house, about being nine and fearless, and somewhere in the middle of the story the coin warms and is gone.

One down.

You carry Mrs. Abernathy's groceries up four flights—the same Mrs. Abernathy you've lived beside for six years without learning her name. It's Ruth. Her husband built that bookshelf. He died in March. You sit in her hallway and let her tell you, and coins spill out of you like a busted slot machine.

You answer when your sister calls. The first time through this day you let it ring. Now you listen for an hour while she cries about the divorce. You don't fix anything. You just stay on the line.

You call your mother. "You still there?" she asks, braced for no. "I'm here," you say. "Tell me about the garden." The coins come off in handfuls.

You stop for the violinist on the subway stairs and give him your actual attention, which costs more than money. You pet the dog tied outside the pharmacy, and he leans his whole warm weight against your shin, and you give a fuck about that too. You watch the sunset from the roof instead of scrolling through pictures of other people's.

By nine o'clock your pockets are almost light. Almost. One coin remains—the oldest one, heavy as a manhole cover—and it will not move.

Then you're passing the corner store and you see it through the glass: the vending machine, *that* machine, rocking on its bolts—and a kid beneath it, reaching for a bag of chips stuck on the coil.

You don't decide. Deciding is for people with time. You just move, get your shoulder into the kid, and send him sprawling clear, and the last coin finally leaves you—the oldest, heaviest fuck you own, the one that says somebody else's life matters more than your own—right before the world comes down.

The warehouse is dark now. Every shelf, bare. Pete checks his clipboard, and for the first time in recorded eternity, he smiles.

"Zero," he says. "Clean."

The gates swing open and you walk through lighter than you have ever been, because that's the trick of it, the thing nobody tells you while you're alive: the weight was never other people.

It was all the fucks you carried, and never gave.

You die on a Tuesday.

Not gracefully, either.

One second you're standing in a supermarket parking lot, arguing with a parking meter that has eaten your last two coins. The next, a delivery van loses a tire, the tire hits a lamppost, the lamppost falls onto a decorative sign, and the sign comes down directly on your head.

You approach.

He looks at you.

You look at him.

"Name?"

You tell him.

"Occupation?"

You answer.

"Cause of death?"

He almost smiles.

You relax.

**I give a fuck about winning.**

**I give a fuck about being right.**

**I give a fuck about that asshole from accounting.**

Thousands upon thousands of them.

"What are these?"

"Every fuck you've ever given."

You stare.

He gestures toward the mountain.

"You've accumulated quite a collection."

You pick up a slip.

**I give a fuck whether the neighbors think my lawn looks terrible.**

"I don't remember this."

"You gave a fuck about it for three weeks in 2019."

Another slip.

**I give a fuck about proving Dad wrong.**

That one hurts.

Another.

**I give a fuck about being remembered.**

You sit down.

"So what's the problem?"

"The problem is that you gave too many fucks about things that didn't deserve them."

He points toward the gates.

"Heaven has limited storage."

"You're joking."

"I'm an angel."

"Right."

"You have one chance. Relive the last twenty-four hours of your life. Give every fuck you have to something that truly deserves it. If you can do that before your death, the gates open."

"And if I can't?"

He shrugs.

"You become a cloud."

You look at the mountain of paper.

"Can I at least keep some?"

"No."

---

You wake up in your bed.

Tuesday morning.

Alive.

For a few seconds, you just lie there, breathing.

Then you notice the box sitting beside your bed.

Your box.

Every fuck.

You start with the obvious ones.

Your phone buzzes.

A message from your boss: *Need that report by noon.*

Normally, you'd panic.

Today, you pick up one of the slips.

**I give a fuck about looking competent.**

You tear it in half.

The anxiety disappears.

At work, your boss criticizes the report.

You don't defend yourself.

You fix the mistake.

When your coworker takes credit, you don't spend twenty minutes imagining his funeral.

You give that fuck away, too.

By lunchtime, you're strangely light.

You call your mother.

She answers on the fourth ring.

"What's wrong?"

"Nothing."

"You never call during work."

"I just wanted to hear your voice."

There's silence.

Then she says, "Are you sick?"

You laugh.

"Apparently not."

You talk for forty minutes.

You realize you haven't asked her about her garden in months.

So you ask.

She tells you everything.

You listen.

And when the box whispers that you should hurry because you're wasting time, you ignore it.

Some things deserve a fuck.

At six, you visit your father.

He's been gone for three years.

You stand outside his old house, now occupied by strangers, and finally understand that you don't need to prove anything to a dead man.

You tear up the slip.

**I give a fuck about winning an argument Dad isn't here to hear.**

Then you cry.

Not because you're sad.

Because you're finished carrying it.

At 10:47 p.m., you remember the parking meter.

The delivery van.

The tire.

The sign.

Your death is coming.

You could avoid it.

You could stay home.

But then you look at the last remaining slips.

There is only one.

**I give a fuck about living.**

You hold it tightly.

At 11:12, your phone rings.

It's your mother.

You answer.

She tells you she forgot to mention something.

The garden has finally bloomed.

You smile.

"Tell me about it."

She does.

You listen until midnight.

And at 12:03, you walk outside.

The accident happens exactly as you remember.

But this time, you aren't angry.

You aren't thinking about money or reputation or tomorrow's meeting.

You're thinking about your mother's garden.

You're thinking about your father's laugh.

You're thinking about how ridiculous parking meters are.

You're thinking that, somehow, despite everything, life was worth giving a fuck about.

Then the world goes white.

---

You open your eyes.

The pearly gates stand before you.

The angel is waiting.

He checks his book.

Then he looks at the empty box in your hands.

"Well?"

You shrug.

"I gave them all away."

He smiles.

"Good."

The gates begin to open.

You step forward.

Then you stop.

"One question."

"Yes?"

"Can I have one back?"

The angel raises an eyebrow.

You point behind you, toward the life you just left.

"I think I'd like to give a fuck about that."

The angel laughs.

"That's not how it works."

You grin.

"Shame."

And you walk through the gates anyway.
samples.Claude-Sonnet-5-High_story:
# The Ledger of Fucks Given

The truck came out of nowhere. One second I was crossing Fifth and Main, thinking about whether I'd left the stove on, and the next I was standing before gates so white they hurt to look at.

"Name?" A figure in robes consulted a tablet that looked suspiciously like an iPad.

"Margaret Chen. Am I—is this—"

"Dead? Yes. Well, mostly administrative purgatory right now." The figure swiped. "Oh dear."

"What?"

He turned the tablet toward me. Instead of a list of good deeds or sins, I saw a massive, sprawling inventory titled: **FUCKS GIVEN: A COMPREHENSIVE HOARD**

"You've been sitting on these," the angel said, not unkindly, but with the weary tone of someone who'd seen this before. "Seventy-three years of fucks, barely given away. You're what we call a Fuck Hoarder, Margaret."

"I don't understand."

"You worried about everything. Your neighbor's opinion of your lawn. Whether you said the wrong thing at your cousin's wedding in 1987. Traffic. The weather. Strangers' judgments. Meanwhile"—he scrolled—"the fucks that actually mattered? Barely touched. Your daughter called you crying last Tuesday and you gave her four minutes before mentioning you needed to let the dog out."

I felt something cold settle in my chest. "So what happens now?"

"Normally, nothing good. Hoarding fucks means you never really lived—you spent them on kindling instead of fire. But." He tapped the screen. "You get a rare opportunity. Twenty-four hours, relived, one more chance to spend your fucks where they belong. Succeed, and you're through the gates. Fail, and, well." He gestured vaguely at a door marked ADMINISTRATIVE PURGATORY, ONGOING.

---

I woke up in my bed, sunlight exactly as it had been, phone buzzing with the same morning news alert. My last day, again.

The stove *was* on. I turned it off without the usual spiral of self-recrimination—no fuck given, filed away for later use.

Sarah called at 9 AM, same as before. Last time, I'd been distracted, folding laundry, saying "mm-hmm" while she talked about her divorce. This time, I sat down. I put the laundry away in my mind and gave her the whole fuck—all of it, undiluted. I asked questions. I cried when she cried. When she said, "Mom, thank you for actually listening," I felt something in my chest unclench that had been tight for decades.

I gave a fuck to the barista who looked exhausted, asked her name, learned her mother was sick. I gave a fuck to my ex-husband when he called about something trivial, and instead of my usual clipped politeness, I told him I was sorry for how things ended, that I'd carried resentment like a stone in my pocket for twenty years and I was finally setting it down.

I skipped worrying about my lawn. I skipped the elaborate justification I'd prepared for a friend about why I couldn't make her dinner party. I just told her the truth: I was tired, and I loved her, and could we do coffee instead.

By evening, I felt lighter than I had in decades—like I'd been carrying invisible luggage my whole life and had finally set it down at the right doors.

At 6:47 PM, I saw the truck. Fifth and Main. I stepped off the curb.

This time, I gave a fuck about the moment itself—really *saw* the sky, orange and torn with clouds, felt the ordinary miracle of my own heartbeat, gave it to my life, fully, right up until the end.

---

The gates again. Same robed figure, same tablet.

"Well," he said, scrolling through a much shorter, much different list. "Look at that. All spent. Every last one."

"Did I make it?"

He smiled, and swiped the gates open. "Turns out, Margaret, you had exactly enough. You just needed to stop saving them for a rainy day."

I walked through, empty-handed, and it was the fullest I had ever felt.
samples.MiniMax-M3_story:
The last thing I remember being alive was a rogue Amazon drone, its propellers whirring like angry hornets. My last thought — whether my life insurance covered "drone strike" — turned out to be irrelevant. I was dead.

I expected darkness. What I got was a small bureaucratic office with a fluorescent light that buzzed like an irritated wasp, and a man with a long beard and a nameplate that simply read: PETER.

"Sit down," he said. I sat.

Peter did not open a book. He reached into his desk drawer and pulled out a glass jar the size of a small child. Inside, something glowed like a thousand crushed glow sticks. It pulsed. It hummed. It felt, somehow, like the inside of my chest on a particularly anxious Tuesday.

"What," I said, "is that?"

"Your fucks," Peter said. "Every one you've ever given."

I stared at the jar. The things inside looked like tiny origami cranes, perhaps shrunken teabags, luminous lint. They were innumerable. They were a hoard.

"You're a hoarder," Peter read from a form, sighing like a man who'd been filing these since the invention of guilt. "Specifically, of fucks. You gave so many about so many things — taxes, haircuts, strangers on the internet — that upstairs is full. The angelic downspouts are clogged. There's a waiting list at the wing we set aside for these."

"I—" I began.

"You worried about a barista judging your order. About a crooked tie on a Zoom call. You hoarded cares, plural." He gestured upward. "It's a fire hazard. It's gauche."

"So what do I do?"

Peter slid another form across. "We're sending you back. Twenty-four hours. Your last day, but lived knowing what you now know. The deal: you have to give all the fucks you have."

I must have looked confused, because he added: "Not zero — that's the monk queue. You have to actually give them. Fully. Without packing them in plastic and storing them in the attic of your soul." He waved a hand. "Go."

I woke up twenty-four hours before the drone.

I won't catalogue the small hours, the long, embarrassing inventory of things I'd spent my life pretending not to care about while caring intensely, alone, in the dark, with the lights off and the door locked. I'll tell you only this:

I called my mother. She asked, as she always did, why I never called. I didn't have a joke. I said: "Because I love you, and I'm sorry I made it weird." She said, "Well, finally." Then: "Wait, are you dying?" "Mom," I said, "I love you." We stayed on the phone for an hour. I gave a fuck so big it could've powered a small city.

I told my best friend I was proud of him. Not in the safe, jokey way — in the way where my voice cracked and I had to clear my throat. He said, "Are you okay?" I said, "I'm giving a fuck. Watch." He laughed. I laughed. I cried a little. The fuck went out of me like a held breath.

I told my sister I forgave her. I didn't want to. I wanted to keep that fuck forever, polish it, store it in a velvet-lined box. But I gave it anyway, in one sentence, on a Tuesday afternoon, in a coffee shop. The world did not end. It felt, for the first time in years, like it might actually be holding together.

And here is the strange thing: I did not run out of fucks.

I thought I would — by sunset hollow as a bone, the drone taking me empty-handed, Peter shrugging, stamping me through anyway. But every fuck I truly gave made room for another. The jar emptied, and emptied, and somewhere around dusk, sitting on my back step watching the light die over the neighbor's fence, I felt the last one go — a small warm coal of concern for the world itself, which I'd been hoarding in case I needed it later. I gave it to the world. The world said: thanks, that's enough.

The drone hit me at 8:47 a.m. the next day. I didn't see it. I was already gone.

Peter was waiting at the gates. He held up the jar. It was empty, except a faint warmth, like a teacup someone had just set down.

"Welcome," he said, stamping something in a book I didn't get to see. "Try not to start collecting again on the way in. We've just unclogged the spouts."

I walked in. The light was very warm. Behind me, faintly, I could hear a thousand tiny origami cranes folding themselves into birds.

samples.MiMo-V2.5-Pro_story:
The air in the Grand Concourse of the Galactic Alliance tasted of ozone and something like cinnamon. I stood there, a lone human in a sea of beings that defied every biology textbook I’d ever skimmed. Ambassador Vex, a being of shimmering, shifting light, had just finished the formal introduction. Humanity, it seemed, had been granted provisional membership. We were the new kids on a cosmic block so vast it made our entire history feel like a single footnote.

The first few cycles were a blur of diplomatic functions. I met the Crystalline Hegemony of Xylos, whose members communicated through intricate, slow-motion light patterns and considered any form of spontaneous speech a sign of profound mental instability. I dined with the Groln, massive, slug-like beings who found our concept of "appetite" barbaric; they absorbed nutrients through osmosis and viewed the act of chewing as a grotesque, violent ritual. Every species had its own rigid, often baffling, code of conduct. What was polite to one was a declaration of war to another.

The real education began in the Archives. As a junior cultural liaison, my job was to study. And what I found wasn't just a catalog of alien customs; it was a compendium of galactic-grade neuroses.

The Vrell, a hive-mind insectoid species, had achieved perfect social harmony. Their solution to any internal conflict? The dissenting consciousness was simply… pruned. Not killed, but edited. They lived in a state of perpetual, lobotomized consensus. To them, our human debates, our passionate arguments, our very capacity for dissent, were symptoms of a species-wide psychotic break.

Then there were the Ethereals of Nebula-7. They existed partially in a higher dimension and perceived time non-linearly. A single Ethereal could be simultaneously experiencing its birth, its death, and a thousand points in between. This led to a civilization paralyzed by existential dread. They couldn't act, because every action was already a memory and a future echo. They saw our linear, forward-marching perception of time as a form of blissful, almost tragic, ignorance. We were, to them, children playing in a sandbox, unaware of the ocean just over the dunes.

The most unsettling were the K’tharr. They were biologically incapable of deceit. Their society was built on absolute, brutal honesty. There was no diplomacy, no white lies, no social cushioning. A K’tharr would tell you your symphony sounded like a dying star, and that your face was aesthetically displeasing, with the same calm it would use to state the chemical composition of water. They viewed our social niceties, our polite fictions, as a form of collective madness, a deliberate poisoning of the informational well.

I sat in my sterile quarters, the data-slate glowing with case studies. The Xylosians, frozen in their crystalline perfection. The Groln, repulsed by their own biology. The Vrell, who had sacrificed individuality for peace. The Ethereals, trapped in a prison of omniscience. The K’tharr, who had traded kindness for clarity.

A slow, dawning horror mixed with a strange, defiant pride settled over me. We weren't the barbarians. We weren't the chaotic, emotional children of the galaxy.

We were the only ones who had figured out how to *function*.

Our emotions weren't a bug; they were a feature. Our capacity for irrational love, for creative madness, for hope in the face of certain oblivion, for lying to spare a friend's feelings, for arguing passionately and then sharing a meal—these weren't signs of insanity. They were the very tools that allowed us to build complex, resilient societies without lobotomizing ourselves or being paralyzed by cosmic truth.

We were messy. We were contradictory. We were gloriously, beautifully flawed. And in a galaxy of extremes—of perfect order, of absolute honesty, of temporal paralysis—that messy, human middle ground was the sanest place to be.

The next morning, I walked into the Concourse with a straighter back. When Ambassador Vex pulsed a greeting, I didn't just bow in the Xylosian style. I smiled—a wide, human, slightly irrational smile. The Ambassador’s light flickered in what I now recognized as confusion. Let them be confused. Humanity had finally found its place in the galaxy. Not as the most advanced, or the most peaceful, but as the most balanced. We were the galaxy's therapists, and we hadn't even known we were applying for the job.
samples.DeepSeek-V4-Flash_story:
We thought we were the least civilised species in the room. Our ambassador had spent six months learning which tentacle to extend, which eye to avoid, which chime to answer. The Galactic Alliance chamber smelled of ozone and wet rot and something like burnt coral. We had rehearsed humility. We had prepared for our insignificance.

Then the Hssith delegate offered us a cup of water. We drank. It was a gift. Under Hssith law, a gift creates a debt equal to the giver’s emotional value. We asked what it was worth. The Hssith shivered all four nostrils and said, "It is worth the memory of my mother’s final breath, which is worth 4,000 years of servitude." The chamber went quiet. Our treaty was in danger because we had accepted water.

That was when we first suspected something odd about the galaxy.

The Vrul ambassador laughed for no reason. "Do not worry," she said, "in my dream, I am the one who broke your ship. In the waking world, I am merely a projection. All is permitted." She began to eat her own chair. The Skaldir delegate began a ritual screaming at the Hssith, because the Hssith had not screamed back at him yesterday, and silence between species is a declaration of war unless accompanied by a handwritten apology in the direction of the Skaldir’s home sun. The Hssith responded by calculating the emotional cost of the scream, and the Vrul tried to trade a dream-self for a real cup of water, and the Skaldir accused everyone of existing.

We sat frozen. Then our diplomat, a woman named Osei, did something terrible. She said, "This is a misunderstanding. Let us all take a deep breath and state what we actually need."

The chamber stopped.

The Alliance Coordinator, a gelatinous creature called the Amenable, rippled in alarm. "You are not playing a role," it said. "You see a fact, then you name it, then you expect the fact to remain. That is… sane."

Osei blinked. "Thank you?"

"No! Do not thank! That is not how the universe works!" The Amenable quivered. "Every species in this Alliance is held together by a shared sacred madness. The Hssith know that gift is love and love is arithmetic. The Vrul know that reality is a dream and dreams are true. The Skaldir know that only through unspoken grievance can one be free. These are not beliefs. They are survival mechanisms. They are the walls we built against chaos."

Osei said, "And what do humans have?"

The Amenable turned its one huge eye toward the ceiling. "We thought you had a wall. But you do not. We ran every test, every deep survey, every interpretive datastream. Humanity sees what is there. You call a rock a rock. You disagree without declaring a blood feud. You apologize and mean it. You are capable of changing your minds when evidence appears."

A Hssith delegate made a sound like a collapsing bridge. "It is an abomination."

"Is it?" said Osei. We waited. The creature’s eye pulsed.

"To us," the Amenable said, "sanity is a perverse truth. It means you can see the universe without blinking. It means you cannot be comforted by a beautiful lie. It means you can stand in the middle of a room and say, 'We are all afraid, and that is all right.' We have been hiding from that for a billion years."

The Skaldir stopped screaming. The Vrul stopped eating her chair. The Hssith stopped counting. They all looked at us with something like pity.

Osei looked at us. We looked back. We realized then that being sane was not strength. It was a kind of nakedness. We walked around without armor, without a divine madness to make the dark bearable. And the Alliance knew it.

But then Osei smiled. "Maybe," she said, "that is why you need us. Not because we are strong. Because we are willing to sit with you in the dark and keep our eyes open."

The Amenable was silent for a long time. Then it extended a pseudopod to our ambassador.

"Welcome," it said, "to the Galactic Alliance. Please do not take this personally, but your sanity terrifies us."

Osei bowed. We bowed. And when we left, we heard them arguing behind us—about debts, dreams, grievances—but this time, they were arguing in front of us, and for the first time, they seemed almost sane.

We have not yet decided if that is a good thing.
samples.Muse-Spark-1.2-Contributor_story:
We had rehearsed for this moment for a century.

We sent the golden discs and the mathematical primes and the careful warnings about our wars, expecting judgment. When the Galactic Alliance finally answered, with a ship that folded space like paper and voices that sang in our minds without sound, we assumed we were the children being called to the table of adults.

We were wrong.

The Alliance envoy met us on Luna, because Earth was deemed "too noisy with unshielded thought." There were three of them. The Aurelian, a lattice of crystal and trapped light that rearranged itself every time we looked away. The Choir, a colony of fungal threads sharing one slow consciousness spread across six bodies that breathed in unison. And the Maw-kin, who introduced itself by vomiting up its own stomach to show us it meant no harm. We smiled politely through our translators and tried not to flinch.

At first, they seemed impossibly wise. The Aurelian spoke in proofs. The Choir sang in harmonies that made our mathematicians weep. The Maw-kin offered us energy, medicine, a place in the Alliance. We, humanity, offered in return what we thought was appropriate humility. We gave them our history unedited — the genocides, the famines, the world wars, the way we had nearly boiled our own planet because we couldn't agree to stop.

We expected horror. Pity, maybe.

The Aurelian shimmered and said, "How restrained."

We thought there was a translation error.

In the middle days of the summit, we began to understand. We were given access to the Alliance cultural archive, a courtesy to new members. We watched their histories because we wanted to learn.

The Aurelians, who live for ten thousand years, spend the first two thousand in a ritual called the Shattering, where they deliberately fracture their own mind-lattice to see what patterns grow back. Most never fully recover. They consider those who do "dull."

The Choir once went to war with itself because one hemisphere of its planet thought the color of a particular star was disrespectful. The war lasted eight thousand years. It ended only when both sides forgot what they were fighting about but continued out of politeness.

The Maw-kin — we learned that their reproduction requires one partner to willingly be consumed alive by the other, and they have entire philosophical schools debating whether being eaten without proper enthusiasm is murder or bad manners. Their ambassadors are chosen from those who beg not to be chosen, because desire disqualifies you.

And they are not the outliers. The soft, gas-bag Drifters navigate by intentionally inducing hallucinations and then believing them. The Architects of Glass build magnificent cities, then abandon them the moment they are finished because completion is considered obscene.

Every species we met was brilliant, ancient, capable of wonders we could barely comprehend — and utterly, cosmically mad. Not cruel. Not evil. Just mad in the way a mind breaks when it has looked at infinity for too long without blinking.

We held a private meeting on the third night. Us. Just humans, in a cramped conference room on Luna, with bad coffee and recycled air. No translators. No crystal lattices.

"Are we... okay?" someone asked.

We laughed, which was a hysterical sound, because we finally understood the perverse truth that had been eluding us since we first looked up at the stars and felt small.

We are the sane ones.

We, who still fight over borders and bury our dead and weep at funerals and write laws to protect the weak. We, who think eating your spouse is a tragedy, not a tradition. We, who consider hearing voices a symptom, not a navigation system. We, who flinch when someone suggests fracturing their own mind for art.

We had spent centuries assuming the galaxy would judge us and find us wanting — too violent, too petty, too broken. And the galaxy looked at us and saw a species that could actually agree on what reality was, most of the time, and could course-correct when it was wrong. To them, that was a superpower.

On the last day, the Aurelian asked us if humanity would serve as mediators for a border dispute that had lasted twelve millennia. "You are still linear," it said, with something like reverence. "You can still remember what a beginning and an end are."

We said yes. What else could we say?

We left Luna with an embassy, a trade route, and a terrible, quiet responsibility we had never wanted. We are not the wisest. We are not the strongest. But in a galaxy of dreaming gods and beautiful lunatics, we are the only ones still awake.

We are going to have to be the adults.
samples.Gemini-3.6-Flash_story:
We expected demigods. For centuries, humanity’s philosophers had predicted that any civilization capable of mastering faster-than-light travel would have long surpassed the messy, emotional baggage of primitive life. We prepared our diplomatic corps with profound humility, ready to sit at the feet of the cosmic masters of logic, peace, and enlightenment.

Instead, I found myself standing in the Grand Rotunda of the Galactic Alliance, watching the High Prime of the Vultharians aggressively sob into a potted fern because the room’s ambient lighting was set to a prime number of lumens.

"It's seventeen hundred!" High Prime K'thrak wailed, his six ocular stalks twitching in manic rhythm as he clutched his ornate silk robes. "The universe is built on symmetry, but seventeen hundred leads to seventeen! It bodes ruin! Absolute, cosmic ruin!"

"Could we... just turn off one light?" I offered gently, smoothing the front of my tailored suit.

"And make it sixteen hundred and ninety-nine?!" a nearby delegate shrieked. This was Grand Marshal Vex of the Zorrillians, a terrifying apex predator whose bio-armored species had conquered three star systems. Vex was currently hyperventilating into a metallic bag. "Sixteen ninety-nine is a prime too, you idiot! We're trapped! The numbers are hunting us!"

My diplomatic team exchanged bewildered, terrified glances. Dr. Aris, our lead xenopsychologist, leaned over to whisper, "Ambassador... I don't think this is a diplomatic test. I think they are genuinely losing their minds."

"They aren't losing them," I whispered back, watching a giant insectoid delegate attempt to hide beneath a coffee table. "They never had them."

Over the next two hours, the grand assembly of thirty-two star-faring species descended into absolute, unbridled paranoia. It didn't take long for the perverse truth to dawn on us: humanity wasn't the unevolved brute at the cosmic table. We were, by an impossible fluke of biology, the only species in the known galaxy that possessed basic cognitive sanity.

As Dr. Aris frantically explained over our secure comms, the math was absurdly simple. The neurological mutations required to comprehend high-dimensional slipspace mechanics were so complex that they obliterated every species' baseline mental stability. To build a hyperdrive, an alien mind had to operate on a plane of terrifying hyper-awareness. The tradeoff? Massive, species-wide psychiatric disorders.

The Koraxian Hive-Mind was an ultra-intelligent collective of ninety billion nodes currently paralyzed by severe obsessive-compulsive disorder, unable to launch their fleet because they couldn't agree on which warship to clean first. The hyper-advanced Aethelgardians, beings of pure plasma, were so profoundly paranoid that they refused to step out of their ships without four layers of lead foil to stop "the invisible moon-demons from eating their thoughts."

And then there was the Supreme Chancellor of the Alliance—a gelatinous, floating leviathan named Oorun.

"Ambassador Miller," Oorun bubbled, floating toward me on a flickering repulsor-throne. His voice resonated telepathically, thick with existential dread. "The floor tiles. Do you see the pattern? It repeats every four meters. It is a sign that time has folded upon itself! We are trapped in a temporal loop!"

"It’s just a mass-produced linoleum tile, Chancellor," I said slowly, adopting the calm, measured tone one might use with a panicked toddler. "It doesn't mean time is looping. It just means the contractor took a shortcut."

Oorun gasped, his gelatinous form quivering. The entire rotunda fell deathly silent. Dozens of terrifying, god-like alien entities stared at me in stunned, reverent awe.

"He... he defied the tile prophecy," a Koraxian drone whispered. "He spoke to the floor without screaming!"

Chancellor Oorun lowered his throne, tears of profound relief leaking from his central sensory mass. "Human... your mind is like iron. Unshakeable. Rational. How do you endure the crushing, nonsensical horror of existence without clawing your own eyes out?"

"We take deep breaths," I said, improvising wildly. "We take naps. And sometimes, we drink tea."

A collective murmur of holy wonder swept through the rotunda. 

We had come to the Galactic Alliance seeking cosmic enlightenment and advanced technology. Instead, we realized our true place in the stars. The galaxy didn't need our weapons, our science, or our trade. 

They needed a quiet room, a box of tissues, and someone to listen.

I took a deep breath, pulled a notepad from my jacket, and set down my chair. "Alright, everyone. Let me get my pen. Who wants to go first?"

# The Sanity Clause

The day the Galactic Alliance made contact, I was eating a gas station burrito in the parking lot of the United Nations. I mention this because Ambassador Vex'thar later told me it was the most reassuring thing any human did that entire week.

"You were *eating*," she said, her translator rendering the word with something like awe. "While awaiting the most significant moment in your species' history. You simply... ate."

I didn't understand what she meant until the orientation briefing.

There were forty-seven species in the Alliance, and over the following months, I met them all. The Krell, a warrior race of terrifying reputation, turned out to be pathologically incapable of leaving a room without checking the door lock exactly nine times. Entire Krell wars had been fought because one general's lock-checking ritual was interrupted by another general's lock-checking ritual, and honor demanded bloodshed.

The Melodians communicated exclusively in opera. Not metaphorically. Every trade negotiation, every treaty, every casual request to pass the salt was a forty-minute aria. Their diplomats considered our spoken language "disturbingly abrupt," like we were constantly hanging up on each other.

The Sss'peth had achieved faster-than-light travel but refused to use odd-numbered star systems. Their trade routes looked like a drunk spider's web. When I asked why, their ambassador went pale (a remarkable feat for a silicon-based lifeform) and whispered, "You *use* the odd systems? All of them? Even... *thirteen*?"

And the Vorath — oh, the Vorath. Brilliant engineers. They'd built the Alliance's entire communications network. They also held weekly funerals for their houseplants, whether the plants had died or not. "Pre-grieving," they called it. "It saves time later."

I sat through six months of this before I finally cornered Vex'thar in the observation deck of the orbital station.

"Level with me," I said. "Why did you really contact us? Every species here is—" I searched for a diplomatic word and failed. "—*a lot*."

Vex'thar's frills rippled in what I'd learned was deep embarrassment. "The Alliance has a classification system for member species," she said. "Based on psychological stability. Species are ranked from Category One — dangerously unstable — to Category Ten."

"And humanity?"

"Category Ten has been empty for eleven thousand years," she said quietly. "We began to believe it was theoretical. A mathematical ideal. Then our probes reached Earth."

I laughed. She didn't.

"Ambassador, your species *watches* horror films. Voluntarily. For *fun*. You consume poison — alcohol, caffeine, capsaicin — recreationally. You keep predators in your homes as companions." Her voice dropped. "And when your planet faces catastrophe, you do not fragment into ritual civil war. You... organize. You form committees. You hold *fundraisers*."

"That's just—" I stopped. "That's just normal."

"Yes," Vex'thar said. "That is precisely the problem. For you, it is normal. For the rest of the galaxy, it is a superpower."

She explained the rest. The Alliance wasn't contacting us to welcome us. They were contacting us because they were desperate. The Krell and the Sss'peth were on the brink of a war over whether the peace treaty should be signed in an even- or odd-numbered system. The Melodians had been singing their grievances for three years without resolution. The Vorath had pre-grieved so hard about the coming war that they'd already built the memorial.

They needed a mediator. A species that could look at an interstellar crisis and say, with complete sincerity, *okay, let's just talk this out like reasonable people.*

"You want humanity to be the galaxy's therapist," I said.

"We want humanity to be the galaxy's *adult*," Vex'thar corrected.

I thought about it. I thought about my species — our wars, our cruelties, our reality television. By our own standards, we were a mess. But standing there, watching a Krell warship do its ninth ceremonial flyby of the airlock before docking, I understood. We were a mess the way a family is a mess. Loud, flawed, occasionally on fire — but fundamentally able to sit down at the same table.

"One condition," I said.

"Name it."

"The Krell check the airlock *eight* times. We're negotiating them down gradually. Baby steps."

Vex'thar stared at me for a long moment. Then her frills lifted in the gesture her people reserved for profound hope.

"Category Ten," she murmured. "Confirmed."

I went back to my quarters and ate a burrito. Some burdens are easier to carry on a full stomach.

# The Sane Ones

The first thing the Galactic Alliance did after welcoming humanity was apologize.

Not formally, of course. Formally, the representatives of forty-three civilizations applauded, flashed bioluminescent patterns, emitted ceremonial spores, or performed whatever passed for clapping among species without hands.

But when the doors closed and the humans were alone with Ambassador Qel, he lowered all four of his eyelids and whispered, “We are terribly sorry.”

Captain Mara Vance stared at him.

“For what?”

“For everything.”

That was how humanity discovered the truth.

The Galactic Alliance was not a collection of advanced, peaceful civilizations. It was a collection of catastrophically unstable civilizations that had somehow survived long enough to invent faster-than-light travel.

The discovery began with the diplomatic tour.

The insectoid Kharuun considered eating one's enemies a sacred form of conflict resolution. The crystalline Velori routinely erased their own memories during arguments because remembering an insult was considered “emotionally aggressive.” The amphibious Nemm insisted that every government decision be made by singing, which explained why their parliament had spent eleven years deciding whether to repair a bridge.

Then there were the Jax.

The Jax had six arms, two brains, and an instinctive distrust of straight lines.

“They believe geometry is authoritarian,” Qel explained.

Mara watched a Jax engineer attempt to repair a circular airlock by making it triangular.

“Why?”

“He says the circle knows what it did.”

Mara slowly turned toward Qel.

“Are all of you like this?”

Qel's antennae drooped.

“Worse.”

The Alliance had spent centuries trying to understand humanity.

Humans were aggressive, emotional, territorial, competitive, and apparently obsessed with inventing new ways to kill one another. Their history was, by Alliance standards, horrifying.

And yet humans possessed one deeply unusual characteristic.

They could recognize when they were being idiots.

The revelation came during humanity's first session of the Galactic Council.

A delegate from the Vey Collective accused humanity of cultural irrationality.

“You have nations,” she said. “Why?”

“Historical reasons,” Mara replied.

“You fought wars over borders.”

“Yes.”

“You still have borders.”

“Yes.”

“You permit individuals to disagree with their governments.”

“Usually.”

“You possess thousands of religions.”

“Yes.”

The Vey delegate shuddered. “And you consider yourselves sane?”

Mara shrugged. “Not particularly.”

Silence filled the chamber.

Qel leaned toward her.

“That's the answer.”

“What is?”

“You don't consider yourselves sane.”

The Alliance representatives exchanged nervous glances.

Qel explained that every other major species believed its own behavior was perfectly reasonable. Their customs were sacred. Their instincts were correct. Their politics were inevitable.

Humans alone had developed an elaborate cultural tradition of looking at themselves and saying, *What the hell are we doing?*

Humans called this self-awareness.

The Alliance called it miraculous.

The situation became clearer when the council was attacked.

An extremist Kharuun faction detonated a device beneath the station. Emergency alarms screamed. Gravity failed. Delegates panicked.

The Velori erased their memories.

The Jax began dismantling the escape pods because they suspected the pods were conspiring.

The Nemm started singing.

Mara grabbed the nearest emergency console.

“Evacuate everyone!”

A dozen delegates stared at her.

“How do you know that is correct?” asked the Vey.

“I don't!”

That shocked them into silence.

Mara continued.

“We're going to make mistakes. So we'll make the best ones we can, check each other, and fix whatever goes wrong.”

Humans moved.

They carried injured aliens. They stabilized the station. They opened escape routes. They argued constantly while doing it.

At one point, Mara screamed at her chief engineer.

“You idiot! That was the wrong valve!”

“I KNOW!”

“Then why did you turn it?”

“BECAUSE YOU TOLD ME TO!”

“Fair enough!”

They fixed it anyway.

Three hours later, the station was secure.

The council gathered in the damaged chamber.

Qel approached Mara.

“You saved everyone.”

“So did hundreds of people.”

“You admitted you might be wrong.”

“Of course.”

“Even while giving orders.”

“That doesn't make me right.”

Qel was silent for a long moment.

Then he laughed.

It was an odd sound, like glass marbles rolling down metal stairs.

“What?” Mara asked.

“The Alliance has searched the galaxy for a perfect species.”

“And?”

“We found one that knows it isn't perfect.”

The Galactic Alliance formally admitted humanity the following week.

The treaty included only one unusual clause:

**In matters of psychological stability, the humans are to be consulted.**

Humanity accepted.

There was, however, one final complication.

At the first interstellar summit, the Kharuun asked humanity for advice on avoiding war.

The Velori requested counseling.

The Jax wanted help understanding geometry.

And the Nemm asked humanity to settle a bridge dispute.

Mara looked at the enormous crowd of aliens waiting for guidance.

She sighed.

“Fine,” she said. “But we're going to need a committee.”

Every alien in the room gasped.

“A committee?”

“Yes.”

“That sounds terrifying.”

Mara smiled.

“Now you're learning.”

# First Contact Protocol

Ambassador Reyes told us not to stare when the Vel'tharic delegation floated in. Three meters tall, translucent, humming a chord that made my molars ache. I stared anyway. Everyone did.

"They communicate in prime numbers during greetings," our liaison whispered. "It's considered a show of respect. Try to hum back."

I did not hum back. Neither did anyone else on our seventeen-person delegation, and somehow that was fine, because the Vel'tharic ambassador simply drifted past us to argue with a floating cube about whether the number seven was "morally compromised."

That was our first hour inside the Chorus Spire, seat of the Galactic Alliance. It did not get less strange.

By the third day, I had watched the Krissenor delegation set fire to their own credentials as a gesture of "sincere vulnerability," listened to the Ophidi Concordance explain that their entire legal system was based on the outcomes of a board game none of them remembered the rules to, and sat through six hours of the Ith'kolo Matriarchy debating whether time moved backward on Tuesdays, a debate they insisted was not metaphorical.

"They're joking," I kept telling myself. "This is a stress test. They're seeing how we react."

They were not joking.

The turning point came during the Trade Subcommittee meeting, when a representative of the Glassmind Assembly proposed that all interstellar contracts be signed in a font that "screamed slightly" when read aloud, for security purposes. The Vel'tharic ambassador supported this. The Ophidi delegate abstained, citing the board game. The Krissenor representative had, by this point, set fire to something again.

Ambassador Reyes, who had spent thirty years in Beijing, Geneva, and low-orbit trade negotiations, and had therefore seen a great deal of human nonsense, put her head in her hands.

"Does anyone," she said slowly, "want to propose we simply write the contract in a font that people can read?"

Silence. Then the Glassmind representative made a sound like a dial-up modem, which we later learned was applause.

That night, over recycled protein that tasted faintly of cardboard and ambition, our science attaché, Priya, said what none of us had wanted to say out loud.

"I think we might be the normal ones."

We laughed. Then we stopped laughing, because we ran the numbers. Of the forty-one species in the Alliance, thirty-eight had governmental systems built on some combination of superstition, sensory hallucination, or ritual self-harm. Two more ran their economies on debts owed to ancestors who were, by their own admission, imaginary. One species had abolished the concept of "no" and was, as a direct result, currently at war with itself over a misunderstanding about breakfast.

Humanity, by comparison, had shown up with a written agenda, name tags, and a translator app. We were, it turned out, boringly, gloriously reasonable.

It should have felt like a victory. Instead it felt like standing in a room full of people convinced the floor was lava, holding a folding chair, and realizing you're the only one who brought a chair because you're the only one who remembered chairs exist.

At the closing ceremony, the Alliance Speaker — a being who communicated via smell and had spent the summit smelling faintly of cinnamon and regret — addressed us directly for the first time.

"Humanity," it said, translated through six layers of software, "you are strange to us. You do not believe the walls are listening. You do not fear the color your leaders wear. This unsettles many delegates."

Reyes, diplomatic to the last, simply nodded. "We'll try to be less alarming."

"Please do not," the Speaker said. "We have decided. Sanity is now a resource. You will be consulted."

We flew home with a treaty, a trade agreement, and the unshakable knowledge that somewhere out there, forty other species were still arguing about whether Tuesdays counted. Reyes filed her report under a single line: *Recommend humanity export nothing but common sense. Market is virtually untapped.*
samples.MiniMax-M3_story:
Ambassador Mara Chen had prepared for the worst. She had memorized seventeen alien dialects, rehearsed forty-two cultural taboos, and spent a year in psychological conditioning to remain calm when faced with the unknown.

Nothing could have prepared her for the Freln.

She stood on the polished obsidian platform of the Galactic Assembly, her delegation of six humans arranged in their crisp charcoal uniforms, and watched as the Freln representative introduced itself. The creature resembled a translucent jellyfish the size of a horse, with seven trembling eye-stalks and a brain visible through its crown.

"GREETINGS, YOUNG SPECIES," it said through its translator. "WE WELCOME YOUR ENQUIRING MINDS TO OUR COMMUNION. PLEASE CONFIRM THAT YOU INTEND NO PSYCHIC AGGRESSION TOWARD ANY MEMBER TODAY."

Mara nodded carefully. "We confirm."

By the end of the first hour, Mara had learned:

The Freln communicate exclusively through what humans would call screaming. Their normal conversation is a 110-decibel howl that they find soothing. They consider whispering obscene.

The Skaaden believe all conflict in the universe stems from debts owed across reincarnations. Half of their diplomacy is genealogical accounting.

The Vellimor are incapable of lying but are also incapable of tolerating disagreement. They must flee any room where conflict might arise, and their civilization is therefore mostly empty.

The Hroth are compulsively honest and compulsively violent. They have solved this by being very honest about their violence, which they consider a noble tradition called "the Clarity."

The Zelantti cannot perceive any being they love clearly; everyone they cherish becomes a vague glowing blur. This has made their entire culture extremely lonely.

Mara sat in her quarters that night, staring at her reflection in the viewport as the strange suns of the Alliance capital set in five colors at once.

"Dr. Tanaka," she said quietly. "I need you to tell me I'm not losing my mind."

Tanaka sat beside her. "You're not."

"They're all insane."

"Yes."

"We declared war on ourselves for sixty years and called it various things. We had an era where we thought leeches cured depression. We elected a reality television host to lead a nuclear arsenal."

"And yet," Tanaka said, "we also have therapy. We have apologies. We have art that tries to understand people who are different from us. We have the concept of 'I was wrong.' Most of these species have never once, in their entire histories, admitted a mistake, because their cultures cannot even frame the concept."

Mara considered this.

The next morning, she stood before the Grand Assembly of two hundred and twelve species, all of whom had been staring at the humans with the polite condescension reserved for particularly confused children.

"You have asked us," she said, "to demonstrate our fitness for membership. I am told several of you have concerns about our 'instability.'"

Murmurs rippled through the chamber, translated into a symphony of clicks, hums, and one agonized screech.

"So I would like to propose a test. I would like each of your representatives to tell this assembly one thing you have changed your mind about in the last decade. One belief you once held that you no longer hold. One thing you were wrong about."

The silence that followed was louder than the Freln's hospitality.

The Vellimor ambassador turned, with visible effort, to the Skaaden delegate, and said, "I have always believed the Skaaden debt-records were superstitious nonsense."

It was the first time in three thousand years a Vellimor had voluntarily stayed in a room with a contradicting voice.

Klik-7 tilted its head. "I confess I had privately believed the Vellimor were cowards for leaving rooms. I no longer believe this. I believe they were brave enough to admit they could not tolerate us, which is more honest than pretending."

The Hroth envoy stood. "I admit I once thought humans were savage because they hid their violence behind euphemism. I see now that you do this because you wish to be better than your impulses. That is not weakness. It is the only kind of strength that lasts."

Mara looked out at two hundred and twelve species, each of them, for perhaps the first time in their long and varied histories, saying the four hardest words any sentient being can say.

*We are not the sanest*, she thought, *because we have no madness. We are the sanest because we can name ours, and try, and fail, and try again.*

"Welcome," she said softly, "to the Alliance."

And the Galactic Alliance, after some considerable debate, welcomed them back.

The cold seeped through my jacket, a familiar companion on these long nights at the observatory. The dome hummed softly above me, a mechanical lullaby. My eye was pressed to the eyepiece of the old 12-inch refractor, a telescope my grandfather had installed. I was tracking the Pleiades, that delicate cluster of blue jewels, when it happened.

One of the sisters, Merope, simply vanished. Not a cloud, not a flicker. One moment it was a crisp point of light, the next, a void. I blinked, assuming fatigue. I checked the coordinates, recalibrated the finder scope. Nothing. I pulled back and looked up at the naked sky. There, in the cluster, was a gap, a missing tooth in a celestial smile.

A cold dread, entirely separate from the night air, trickled down my spine. I swung the telescope to Orion. Betelgeuse, the ruddy shoulder, was there. I moved to Rigel, the brilliant foot. It was there. Then, as I watched, Rigel’s light contracted into a pinprick and extinguished. It was as if a giant, unseen hand was pinching out the stars one by one.

I scrambled out of the dome, my boots crunching on frost. The sky was a tapestry being unraveled. Vega, the summer star, winked out. Deneb followed. The Summer Triangle became a Summer Line, then nothing. I watched, paralyzed, as the Milky Way, that soft, glowing river of light, began to fade from its edges inward, like a photograph left in the sun. Constellations lost their meaning. The Big Dipper became a broken scoop. Cassiopeia’s ‘W’ dissolved into a ‘V’, then a single, lonely point before it, too, was gone.

My scientific mind raced through explanations. A global atmospheric event? Impossible. A simultaneous supernova dimming? Nonsensical. This was systematic, deliberate. It was a countdown.

The last visible stars were the brightest, the stubborn anchors of the sky. Sirius, the Dog Star, blazed defiantly. I held my breath, my hands clenched. For a long moment, it held. Then, it began to pulse, a frantic, desperate rhythm. Once. Twice. On the third pulse, it collapsed into darkness.

The sky was now utterly, profoundly black. Not the black of a cloudy night, which has texture and depth. This was an absolute, featureless void. It felt solid, heavy, pressing down. The silence was no longer peaceful; it was a vacuum. The hum of the dome behind me seemed obscene, a noise from a world that no longer existed.

I stood there for what felt like hours, a speck on a rock, staring into an abyss that had swallowed eternity. The universe had gone blind. Then, in that perfect, terrifying darkness, a new light appeared.

It wasn’t a star. It was a point of light that grew, not with a fiery tail, but with a soft, expanding luminescence, like a drop of ink in water. It hung directly overhead, silent and serene. It didn’t twinkle. It simply *was*. As I watched, mesmerized, a pattern emerged within its glow. It wasn’t random. It was a complex, shifting lattice of light, a language written in photons.

My communicator, forgotten on the console, crackled to life. A voice, calm and genderless, spoke in every language at once, yet I understood it perfectly in my own tongue. It wasn't coming from the device; it was resonating in my bones.

*“Observer of the Third Planet. Your night sky was a broadcast. A beautiful, chaotic, random broadcast. We have been listening. Now, we wish to speak.”*

The lattice of light above pulsed, and in its structure, I saw not just patterns, but equations, star charts of places I’d never dreamed of, the blueprints of nebulae, the life cycles of suns. It was a library, a greeting, a revelation.

The stars hadn’t been extinguished. They had been *replaced*. The old, distant, silent lights had been switched off, and in their place, a single, direct, and overwhelming signal had been turned on. The universe hadn’t ended. It had just introduced itself.

I lowered my head from the empty sky, my eyes adjusting to the faint glow of the observatory lights. The fear was gone, replaced by a awe so profound it was painful. I picked up my logbook, my hand shaking not with terror, but with the weight of what I now knew. The first entry would be simple. The last entry of the old world.

*“The stars are gone. We are no longer alone. And they are talking.”*
