It started as a small irritation, the kind you feel when a bug crosses your laptop screen during a long night of data. I was at the observatory, as I had been for every clear night that month, tracking a variable star in Cygnus. The coffee had gone cold. My logbook was open. And then, without warning, the star I was watching simply wasn’t there.

Not dimmed. Not flickering. Gone.

I blinked, rubbed my eyes, and frowned at the spectrograph. Equipment malfunction, I decided. The software must have slipped a decimal, or a fleck of dust had drifted across the sensor. But when I leaned away from the eyepiece and looked up at the sky with my own eyes, the northeast quadrant of Cygnus was darker than it should have been. A hole in the pattern. A missing stitch.

Then another star vanished two degrees to the west.

I stood up so fast my chair rolled across the concrete and hit the wall. My heart was doing something strange, a mixture of wonder and cold dread. This was not a satellite. Not a cloud. Not a power flicker. I stepped outside, into the dome’s shadow, and stared at the naked sky.

A third star went out. Then a fourth.

It was like watching someone erase a chalkboard from left to right, one dot of white at a time. The constellations I had known since childhood—my first star maps, my first telescope, my first lies to my parents about staying up late—were being unmade. Orion’s shoulder vanished. Then his belt. Then the bright pinprick of Rigel at his foot. Each extinction was absolute and silent. There was no flash, no residual glow, no burst of radiation in any wavelength I knew. The stars were just... switched off.

I found myself whispering a prayer, which was odd because I had never been religious. Then I ran back inside and checked the all-sky camera. It confirmed what my eyes were telling me. Dark patches were spreading like ink in water across the entire celestial sphere. Not clouds. Not shadows. *Absence*.

I tried the other observatories. No signal. I tried the internet. It went down. The backup phone line was dead, too. The silence was the worst part. A universe that had always chattered in radio hiss and cosmic microwave hum had gone mute.

I stumbled back outside. By then, perhaps half the stars were gone. The Milky Way, that great river of light that had flowed across the sky since before humans were human, had thinned to a trickle, then to a pale ghost, and then to nothing. The stars were dying in order of brightness, I realized. The faint ones went first, then the brighter ones, as if something was sweeping from the edge of the galaxy inward. A great hand, or a great wall, was eating the light.

One by one, the last few brilliant points of light held on. Sirius. Canopus. Arcturus. The ones I had always used to calibrate the telescope, to navigate the sky, to feel small in the best possible way. They stood alone for a long, terrible minute. Then Arcturus flickered twice, like a candle in a draft, and went out.

I was weeping by then. I don’t remember deciding to cry. The tears were simply there, cold on my cheeks in the mountain air. I thought of all the generations before me who had looked up and seen a living sky—and the generations after me who would look up and see only a black ceiling. I thought of the light that had travelled for millennia, only to arrive in the last instant before some cosmic shutter closed.

Finally, there was one star left. I didn’t know its name. It was faint, near the southern horizon, maybe a red dwarf a thousand light-years away. It pulsed, small and lonely. I thought, *maybe they missed one*. I thought, *maybe this is a gift*. And then it, too, blinked out.

The sky was pure black. Not the cheerful black of a new-moon night, full of hidden treasures and faint nebulae. This was a flat, velvet, absolute black. A lid had been put on the universe.

I stood in the dark for a long time, listening to the wind and the rattle of dry grass. Then I went back inside, sat down at my desk, and wrote this entry in my log. I don’t expect anyone to read it. But if they do, I want them to know: the stars did not die. They were taken. And somewhere, beyond the black, something is looking back at us—and it is not kind.
samples.Muse-Spark-1.2-Contributor_story:
You've been cold for so long you've stopped feeling it. That's how you know you've been at the eyepiece too long. It's 2:17 a.m. on a Tuesday in late October, and you are alone in the dome on Mount Locke. The 107-inch mirror below you breathes with its low coolant hum, and your thermos sits empty at your feet. You are tracking Barnard's Loop in Orion, logging the same patch of sky you've logged for four years for a survey no one but your advisor and two reviewers will ever read. You love it anyway. You love the quiet that is not quite silence, the way the dome smells like old oil and ozone, the way the sky feels endless and indifferent. 

You blink, and Rigel is gone. 

You frown. You tap the focus. You assume you've blinked at the wrong second, or a cloud has slipped in from the west where the weather report said no clouds would be. You lean in again. Rigel should be there, blue-white and arrogant at the foot of Orion. There is only black where it was, a perfect, star-shaped hole punched out of the dark. You check the CCD readout. The pixel where Rigel burned is now reading background noise. You swing the scope a few arcminutes to Betelgeuse. It is still there, red and swollen. You exhale, tell yourself it is a transient detector error, a cosmic ray, a glitch in the readout. 

Then Betelgeuse goes out. 

It doesn't fade. It doesn't flicker. It simply ceases, as if someone flipped a switch. One frame it is there, the next it is not. Your hand jerks back from the controls. On the monitor, the familiar shape of Orion is now missing its two brightest points, like eyes gouged out. You stand up so fast your chair squeaks. You switch to wide-field, your heart hammering so loud you can hear it over the coolant fans. 

Bellatrix goes. Then Saiph. Then the three stars of the belt go one after another, Alnitak, Alnilam, Mintaka, each vanishing in the same clean, instantaneous way. You are no longer logging. You are just watching, your mouth open, your breath fogging the cold air. You try to tell yourself this is an instrument failure, a cascading short, but you know what instrument failure looks like. It tears, it streaks, it leaves artifacts. This leaves nothing. Perfect black. 

You throw open the dome slit and stumble out onto the catwalk without your coat. The wind hits you, sharp with pine and dust. You tilt your head back and look up with your own eyes, unaided, desperate to prove the telescope is lying. 

It isn't. 

Above you, the Milky Way is unzipping itself. You watch the Pleiades wink out like someone blowing out candles. You watch Polaris, which has not moved in your entire lifetime, simply not be there anymore. Sagittarius goes dark. Cassiopeia, which you learned to find when you were nine in your backyard with a plastic telescope, loses a star, then another, then is gone. There is no sound, no flash, no explanation. Just absence spreading. You want to call someone, but you know that by the time anyone picks up the phone, there will be nothing to see. 

You sink to your knees on the metal grating. The wind rattles the dome behind you. The sky is now almost entirely black, a black you have never seen before, because even the darkest night you have ever known was full of light. This is a different kind of dark, a true dark, heavy and complete. Only a few stubborn stars remain low on the eastern horizon, and as you watch, they too go out, one, one, one, until there is nothing left. 

You stare into it. For a long, terrible minute you are the only person on Earth who has ever seen a sky with no stars, and you understand with a sudden, vertiginous clarity why ancient people feared the dark. It is not empty. It is waiting. 

Then, in the absolute black above you, a single new point of light kindles. Faint at first, then brighter. Then another, and another. You don't recognize the pattern. They are not your stars. They are something else, something on the other side, and as they bloom, you realize the darkness was not an ending at all, but something vast and silent moving between you and the light.
samples.Gemini-3.6-Flash_story:
The hum of the observatory’s cooling systems was the only sound breaking the mountain silence. At three thousand meters above sea level, the air was crisp, thin, and impossibly clear. For twenty-two years, I had spent my nights inside this dome, tracking the slow, predictable dance of the cosmos. I knew the night sky better than I knew the streets of my own hometown. To me, the universe was an elegant clock of incandescent light—precise, mathematical, and reassuring.

Until 2:14 AM.

I was recalibrating the optical sensors on the main telescope, focused on the northern cross of the Cygnus constellation. I leaned over the secondary monitor, taking a slow sip of lukewarm coffee. That was when Deneb vanished.

It didn’t flicker. It didn’t dim behind a patch of high-altitude cirrus. Humidity readouts were at a bone-dry one percent, and the atmospheric telemetry showed absolute clarity. Deneb simply ceased to exist. One frame of the high-resolution capture showed the bright supergiant blazing brilliantly; the next frame, captured three seconds later, showed only dead, empty grid space.

"Sensor glitch," I muttered to myself, tapping the glass of the monitor. "Thermal bleed."

I swung the guide scope manually to double-check through the optical eyepiece. When I looked up through the open slit of the dome, my breath caught.

Deneb was gone. Where a magnitude 1.25 anchor of the Summer Triangle should have been glowing, there was only blackness.

Before my mind could process the impossibility of a star four hundred light-years away instantly vanishing, the next one went out. Gamma Cygni blinked into nonexistence. Then Delta. Then Albireo. The constellation of the Swan wasn't just losing its light; it was being systematically erased.

A cold knot tightened in my chest. Light takes time to travel across the cosmos. For a star to go dark from Earth's perspective, the physical event had to happen centuries ago. But stars light-years apart were winking out seconds after one another. Whatever was happening was ignoring the speed of light entirely—or it was happening right on our galactic doorstep.

"Think," I whispered into the silent room, my hands trembling over the control console. "Think."

I zoomed out the wide-field camera array. The darkness was spreading outward in a perfect, expanding ring of absolute void. Lyra went next. Vega—a sapphire beacon that had guided human sky-watchers for millennia—simply snuffed out. Then Altair. The entire Summer Triangle was swallowed.

I scrambled to the shortwave radio comms, slamming the switch to connect to the neighboring array fifty miles south.

"La Silla, this is Mount Solitude, do you read me? Are you seeing the northern sector?"

Static crackled violently through the speaker. Then, a voice sharp with sheer panic replied: "They’re gone! David, it’s not atmospheric! We’re losing Ursa Major! Polaris is gone—god, Polaris just went out!"

I dropped the headset and bolted out the side hatch onto the observatory’s catwalk.

The freezing wind bit at my face, but I barely felt it. I stared up at a sky I no longer recognized. The void was accelerating. The great, shimmering band of the Milky Way was being devoured from the inside out, like ink spreading across a silk sheet, consuming billions of distant suns in a silent, terrifying sweep.

Pegasus vanished. Cassiopeia fell. Boötes was consumed.

It wasn't that the stars were dying. Something was closing. It was as if an incomprehensible, cosmic curtain was being drawn across the universe, isolating our solar system in a shrinking pocket of reality.

Within two minutes, only our closest neighbors remained. Alpha Centauri winked out. Sirius flared briefly before plunging into the abyss.

Then, Betelgeuse.

And then, total, absolute night.

I stood high above the desert, wrapped in a darkness so absolute it felt physical, pressing against my eyes and weightless in my lungs. There were no stars. No distant galaxies. No cosmic dust. The sky above was an empty, dead vault.

I looked down at the valley floor, where the faint, fragile lights of human cities still flickered, blissfully unaware that the rest of the universe had just vanished. I turned my eyes back to the empty sky, waiting for the moon, waiting for the sun, terrified of what would happen when it was time for the morning light to return.
samples.Kimi-K3_story:
# The Last Light

I've spent thirty years looking up. My colleagues joke that I know the night sky better than my own backyard, and they're right. I could find Polaris blindfolded. I could tell you the magnitude of Betelgeuse without checking a chart. The stars were my oldest friends—constant, reliable, always exactly where they should be.

Until the night they weren't.

It started at 2:14 AM on a Tuesday in October. I was at the observatory in the mountains, alone, running routine spectrographic analysis on a cluster in Cygnus. I glanced up through the dome's open slit to stretch my neck, the way I always did, and something felt wrong. It took me a moment to place it.

Deneb was gone.

I laughed at first. A cloud, obviously. Some wisp of atmosphere I hadn't noticed. But the rest of Cygnus shone clear and sharp, and when I checked the satellite feed, the sky was pristine. Not a cloud for two hundred miles.

I was still staring when Albireo blinked out. Not faded—*blinked*. Like an eye closing. Like a switch being flipped.

My hands were shaking as I pulled up the telescope feeds. I told myself it was equipment failure, atmospheric distortion, anything rational. But the instruments confirmed what my eyes already knew. Two stars, gone. Not exploded. Not collapsed. Just... absent. No radiation burst, no gravitational signature, nothing. As if they had never existed at all.

Then Vega went. Then Altair. Then Arcturus, one of the brightest lights in our sky, there one moment and swallowed by nothing the next.

I called everyone. Chen at Mauna Kea answered on the second ring—she was already watching. "You see it too," she said. It wasn't a question. Within the hour, every observatory on the planet was awake. The pattern became clear quickly, and it was worse than random. The stars were going out in order of distance. The nearest ones first.

Whatever was happening, it was coming toward us.

I did the math three times because I didn't want to believe it. The phenomenon was moving faster than light, which should have been impossible, which meant we weren't seeing it happen in real time—we were seeing the *absence* arrive. Something had already consumed everything between here and there, and the darkness was just the news catching up.

By dawn, half the sky was empty.

The world reacted the way the world does. Panic in some cities, prayer in others. Markets collapsed, then stopped mattering. People gathered in fields and on rooftops, watching the sky erase itself. I stayed at the observatory. Someone had to record it. Someone had to bear witness, even if there would be no one left to read the record.

On the second night, only a handful of stars remained. Sirius. Alpha Centauri. Our closest neighbors, our oldest companions. I watched them through the eyepiece one by one, whispering their names like a prayer I'd forgotten I knew.

Sirius went at 11:48 PM.

Alpha Centauri at 3:02 AM.

And then there was nothing. The sky was a sheet of black velvet with nothing behind it. No stars. No galaxies. The moon still hung there, pale and confused, reflecting sunlight that suddenly felt borrowed. I stood under that empty sky and felt smaller than I had ever felt in my life—and I had spent my career studying just how small we are.

But here's the thing I keep coming back to, the thing I write down now in case it matters: the sun rose that morning. It rose the next day too, and the day after that. Whatever took the stars passed us by, or spared us, or never noticed us at all. A single pale dot around an ordinary star, too small to be worth swallowing.

It's been a year now. The night sky is still empty, and children are growing up who will never see a star. They ask me what it was like, and I tell them the truth: it was like living inside a jewel box, and we never knew it until the lid closed.

I still go to the observatory. I still look up. Some nights I think I see something—a flicker, a ghost of light at the edge of perception. Probably imagination. Probably hope dressed up as data.

But I keep watching. That's what astronomers do. We look into the dark and wait for light.

And if even one star comes back, I'll be the first to see it.
samples.GPT-5.6-Luna_story:
The observatory was quiet enough to hear the clock ticking.

I had always loved that sound. Out beneath the dome, with the telescope turning slowly toward the heavens, the world seemed reduced to simple things: the steady machinery, the cold metal beneath my hands, and the ancient light of stars arriving from distances I could barely comprehend.

That night, I was alone.

It was nearly two in the morning when I leaned away from the telescope and looked directly through the open slit in the dome. The sky above me was brilliant. Thousands of stars scattered across the darkness, sharp and white against the Milky Way. I smiled.

Then one disappeared.

At first, I thought I had imagined it.

A small star near the eastern horizon vanished without a flicker. One moment it was there; the next, there was only empty blackness.

I checked the telescope.

The star was gone from the monitor too.

I adjusted the focus, checked the tracking system, and pulled up the observatory's catalog. The coordinates showed nothing unusual. No cloud covered that section of the sky. No satellite passed in front of it.

I stared upward.

Another star vanished.

This one was brighter.

My smile disappeared.

"Impossible," I whispered.

Then a third went out.

I hurried to the computer and opened the observatory's network. If this was happening to me, perhaps the other astronomers would see it too.

I sent a message to the research station two hundred kilometers away.

**Are you seeing anything unusual in the sky?**

The reply came almost immediately.

**Yes. Stars are disappearing.**

Before I could answer, another message appeared.

**What is happening?**

I had no explanation.

The stars continued to vanish.

One after another, they blinked out. Some disappeared every few seconds; others remained for nearly a minute before suddenly going dark. Bright stars, dim stars, familiar constellations—all of them were being erased.

I watched Orion lose its shoulder, then its belt. The Big Dipper became a broken pattern of darkness. The Milky Way thinned until only scattered points remained.

I stopped taking notes.

There was nothing scientific about what I was feeling anymore.

I was afraid.

I called the observatory director, but he didn't answer. I tried the emergency line. Static. I contacted the other stations. Some responded with frantic voices. Others were already silent.

Then the power flickered.

The telescope stopped turning.

The computers went black.

For several seconds, the only light came from the stars above.

Then another one disappeared.

And another.

I stepped outside.

The air was perfectly still.

I looked up as the remaining stars vanished across the sky. There was no pattern I could see, no direction from which the darkness advanced. It was as if an invisible hand were sweeping across the universe, extinguishing every light it touched.

Ten stars remained.

Nine.

Eight.

I began counting.

Seven.

Six.

Five.

My hands were trembling.

Four.

Three.

Two.

One.

The final star was directly overhead.

It was the brightest object I had ever seen.

I stared at it, holding my breath.

Then it disappeared.

The sky was completely black.

Not dark.

Black.

There was a difference.

For the first time in my life, I understood what the night would look like if there were no stars at all. There was no depth to it. No distant glow. No sense of space. Just an enormous, empty darkness pressing down from above.

I stood there for what felt like hours.

Then something happened.

A point of light appeared.

Not where a star had been.

Closer.

Much closer.

It grew slowly until it became a pale blue circle hanging above the horizon.

I realized I was looking at Earth.

But that was impossible.

I could see continents.

Oceans.

Clouds.

And thousands of tiny lights scattered across the surface.

Cities.

Our planet had become the only light left in the universe.

I heard a voice behind me.

"You see it too?"

I turned.

The observatory director stood in the doorway, pale and breathless.

I looked back at the blue world in the sky.

"Maybe," I said, "we were never looking at the stars."

He frowned.

"What do you mean?"

I pointed upward.

"Maybe they were looking at us."

For several seconds, neither of us spoke.

Then, far beyond Earth, something moved in the darkness.

It was too large to be a star.

Too bright to be a planet.

And slowly, one enormous eye opened.
samples.Claude-Sonnet-5-High_story:
The observatory dome hummed its familiar hum, the one I'd fallen asleep to more nights than I could count. I had the telescope trained on the Perseus cluster, nothing urgent, just routine cataloguing for a paper nobody would read until the next funding cycle. I sipped cold coffee and watched the eyepiece the way other people watch television.

Betelgeuse went first.

I almost didn't notice. I was looking slightly to the left of it, jotting coordinates, and when I glanced back the familiar red smear was simply gone. I blinked, rubbed my eyes, checked the focus. Instruments fail. Eyes fail more often. But when I looked through the wide-field finder, Rigel had gone dark too, and Bellatrix, and the whole shape of Orion was collapsing into itself like a drawing being erased one line at a time.

I ran outside without my jacket. The night was warm for October, unnaturally warm, and the sky above the ridge was doing something skies are not supposed to do. Stars were winking out in slow procession, not all at once, but in a wave, as though someone were walking across the ceiling of the world switching off lights they no longer needed.

I called the university. Nobody answered on the first three tries. On the fourth, a graduate student named Priya picked up, her voice thin and fast. "You're seeing it too," she said, not a question.

"How far has it spread?"

"Everything past the moon. The moon's still there. For now."

I looked up. She was right. The moon hung fat and yellow, indifferent, while behind it the sky had gone the black of a closed eye. Not the black of empty space, which is never truly empty, always flecked and glittering even in bad seeing conditions. This was different. This was a black that had weight to it, that pressed downward like a lid.

"What's the last thing you saw disappear?" I asked her, because I didn't know what else to ask.

"Polaris," she said. "The North Star. Went out like someone snuffed a candle."

We stayed on the phone for an hour, the two of us narrating a funeral to each other. Vega. Deneb. Altair. The summer triangle collapsing into itself. Cassiopeia's crooked W folding shut. I kept the phone against my ear with my shoulder and kept looking, unable to stop, the way you can't stop watching a car go off a bridge even though you know how it ends.

Somewhere around three in the morning the moon went.

After that there was only the black, and under it, the ordinary world continuing as if nothing had happened. Crickets still sang. A dog barked twice somewhere down the valley and quieted. The observatory dome still smelled like machine oil and dust. I realized I could hear my own heartbeat because there was nothing else left large enough to compete with it.

Priya's voice had gone quiet on the line. "Do you think anyone's coming to explain this?" she asked.

I didn't answer right away. I was thinking about all the light I had spent my life chasing, light that had traveled centuries and millennia to end its journey in my eye, in this small dome, on this small hill. I was thinking that maybe the extinguishing wasn't sudden at all. Maybe I was only now, tonight, finally watching the true and patient dark arrive, the one that had always been coming, ancient and unhurried, closing every door behind it as it came.

"No," I said. "I don't think anyone's coming."

We stayed on the phone anyway, two small voices, keeping each other company under a sky that had forgotten how to shine, waiting to see what the dark intended to do with us now that it finally had the whole house to itself.
samples.MiniMax-M3_story:
You adjust the eyepiece for the third time, certain something is wrong with your eyes. A faint ache has settled behind your left temple from staring too long, and you've been hunched over this scope for three hours. Vega should not be doing what you just thought you saw Vega do.

You pull back from the eyepiece and look up with your naked eye. The summer triangle is high and bright, Vega burning blue-white at its apex. You mark its position against the faint outline of your observatory roof, then lean back in.

Vega is gone.

You jerk back, then forward, then back again. Your heart is doing something embarrassing. You check the finder scope—empty. You swing the main scope ten degrees east and back. Vega is not there. Vega, fifth-brightest star in the sky, is not there.

You tell yourself there must be a power issue. Some glitch with the tracking motor, maybe a loose cable. You check the controls, the cables, the mount. Everything is fine. You check the weather data on your tablet. Clear skies, low humidity, no anomalies. You check the satellite tracker to make sure nothing is passing in front of your view. The path is clear.

You look up again.

Altair is out.

You stand up so fast your chair rolls backward and slams into the desk behind you. You walk out onto the observing platform and look straight up. The Milky Way is still smeared across the sky, a pale river of ten billion stars. So many stars. Too many to count. And yet, on the eastern edge of the triangle, Altair is just… not.

You wait. You count your breaths. One. Two. Three.

Deneb flickers. Holds. Fades. Is gone.

You take out your phone with hands that do not feel like your hands. You open the astronomy forum you frequent—the one with fifteen thousand members, mostly amateurs, mostly awake at this hour because the sky is good. You start typing: *Has anyone else noticed—* You delete it. Too crazy. You type instead: *Vega and Altair missing?* You stare at the message for a long time, then hit send.

A reply comes in eleven seconds. From someone in Belgium. *Yeah. And Deneb. I'm losing it.*

Another, from Australia: *I've got six friends on a video call right now. We can see it happening. It's moving west to east. Wait. Capella just went.*

You look west. Capella is there. You look east. Capella is there. You look again. Capella is there. You blink. Capella is not there.

The sky is going out.

You watch as if your watching could stop it. You watch as stars you've known since childhood wink into nothing—Rigel, then Aldebaran, then Pollux, then Castor. The constellations unravel like loose thread. Orion loses his shoulder, then his foot, then his belt. The Big Dipper's handle dissolves star by star, the bowl last.

You think of Carl Sagan. Billions and billions. You think of how small you are, how small Earth is, how small your whole solar system is against the backdrop you are now watching die. You think of your mother, who told you when you were nine that the stars were the lights of heaven, and that every person who had ever lived had one. You had looked up that night and tried to find hers. You had never been able to pick which one.

The Milky Way is the last thing. It thins, like fog burning off, and for a moment the sky is the deepest gray you have ever seen—a gray that has weight, that has texture. Then it goes black. True black. Not the black of a moonless night with distant suns, but the black of nothing, of no light anywhere, of an eye that has never seen.

Your phone buzzes. A message from the forum. It is from someone you don't know, somewhere in the southern hemisphere. The message is only three words:

*It's getting closer.*

You look up. There is nothing to see. You lower your phone. The screen's blue glow is the only light in the world. Somewhere, miles away or inches away—you cannot tell—something breathes.

You turn off your phone.
